short_description: Cerebral perfusion analysis using computed tomography with contrast administration, including post-processing of parametric maps with determination of cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and mean transit time Notes: (For carbon monoxide, expired gas analysis [eg, ETCOc/hemolysis breath test], use 84999) (For mammary duct[s] catheter lavage, use 19499)
lay_term: The provider obtains a measurement of regional cerebral blood flow through analysis of computed tomography (CT) scans by taking sequential images of sections of the brain while administering intravenous contrast. This procedure is done to evaluate patients suspected of having a stroke. Explanation In this procedure, the provider administers contrast, typically an iodine tracer through an IV, which travels to the brain in the blood and perfuses, or spreads through, the brain tissue. The provider then measures the level of absorption of the tracer in the brain, which is seen as brighter tissue on CT images. He does this by taking sequential images of a section of the brain and mapping changes to the density of the contrast in the tissue over time. Using computer software, he then calculates the resulting measurement of brain tissue blood perfusion, or the amount of blood taken up by the brain cells. The program also determines the amount of blood in the brain, or the cerebral blood volume, and the time it takes the blood to pass through the cerebral capillaries, referred to as the mean transit time. Terminology Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Contrast: A chemical, such as barium or iodine, or a radioactive substance used in radiologic imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral, intravenously, and as an enema; also known as contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, contrast dye, or tracer. Parametric mapping: Statistical technique to examine difference in brain activity through the analysis of brain imaging data sequences. short_description: Focused ultrasound ablation of uterine leiomyomata, including MR guidance; total leiomyomata volume greater or equal to 200 cc of tissue Notes: (Do not report 0071T, 0072T in conjunction with 51702 or 77022)
lay_term: The provider uses magnetic resonance imaging guided focused ultrasound, or MRgFUS, to heat and destroy a noncancerous growth of the uterus, called a leiomyomata, whose total volume is 200 cc of tissue or greater. The procedure is done with a patient inside a magnetic resonance imaging scanner, which monitors temperature and guides the provider to the precise location of the leiomyomata, or uterine fibroids. Explanation In this noninvasive procedure, the provider preps and places the patient in an MRI scanner that has a high energy ultrasound transducer, or focused ultrasound energy probe. The provider then focuses the ultrasound beam on the target, which penetrates the soft tissues and heats parts of a uterine fibroid while avoiding nearby structures, such as the bowel and bladder. She uses the MRI to guide each sonication, or ultrasound energy application, and to monitor the tissue temperature to ensure she completely ablates, or destroys, the fibroid tissue but does not damage the surrounding tissue. She repeats the thermal ablation until she destroys most of the fibroid. Each sonication lasts approximately 20 to 25 seconds. The provider typically applies multiple sonications during a treatment session to destroy a fibroid for a total leiomyomata volume greater than or equal to 200 cc of tissue, but depending on the size and number of fibroids, more sonications or a second treatment may be necessary. Terminology Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): Radiographic imaging using magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Transducer: A device that converts one form of energy to another; an ultrasound transducer produces sound waves, captures the echoes created when those waves bounce off body structures, and transfers that data to a computer to create the ultrasound image. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Uterine fibroid: A benign tumor made up of muscular and fibrous tissues, typically found in the wall of the uterus; also known as a leiomyomata. Thermal ablation: The application of high localized temperatures to destroy tissue. Tips Report this code only once for leiomyomata with a total volume greater than or equal to 200 cc of tissue. For uterine leiomyomata less than 200 cc in volume, see 0071T. short_description: Transcatheter placement of extracranial vertebral artery stent(s), including radiologic supervision and interpretation, open or percutaneous; initial vessel
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a stent through an incision in the skin into a vessel of the extracranial vertebral artery, to treat a stenosis or blockage. This code includes imaging for determination of the need for stenting along with radiological supervision and interpretation of same. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the leg to gain access to the constricted artery and inserts a guide wire through the incision. He then advances a catheter over the guide wire and performs angiographic imaging. He begins by using a catheter to place an emboli protection device beyond the site of stenosis to ensure that the device captures any clot that may detach. Next, again using the catheter, the provider places a stent across the site of stenosis in the extracranial vertebral vessel through an open procedure directly into the artery or percutaneously, through the skin and confirms its position using angiography. The provider finally removes all the equipment, achieves hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, and closes the wound in layers. The provider may employ imaging to determine the need for stent placement; if he does, do not report radiological supervision and interpretation separately. Terminology Angiography:Imaging of internal organs including blood vessels, arteries, veins, and heart chambers. Artery: A blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the body tissues. Carotid artery: Two large main arteries in the neck, passageway carrying blood from the heart to other parts of the body, which supply blood to the brain. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Embolic protection device: A medical device that a provider uses to capture an embolus, a detached blood clot, during surgical intervention on the carotid artery. Extracranial: Situated outside the skull. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and stent. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Stent:A thin expandable tube placed through a narrowed area of a tubular structure, such as the esophagus, small intestine, or a vessel, to prevent obstruction and provide support after dilation. Transcatheter: Through the catheter. Tips For additional stent placement on the same side, report +0076T in addition to 0075T for stent placement in the initial vessel. If the provider does not place a stent, report codes for selective catheter placement, including imaging, instead. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provides the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. short_description: Placement of a subconjunctival retinal prosthesis receiver and pulse generator, and implantation of intraocular retinal electrode array, with vitrectomy Notes: (For initial programming of implantable intraocular retinal electrode array device, use 0472T)
lay_term: The provider attaches a retinal prosthesis (artificial retina) to the patient’s retina to induce some visual perception by restoring the distinction between the presence and absence of light. The prosthetic, made of silicone and platinum, replaces lost light sensitivity of the retina by transmitting external images to an array of electrodes the provider also places in the epiretinal space. This procedure is done for retinal diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa, hereditary retinal disorders, and some forms of age–related macular degeneration. Explanation An artificial retina involves a tiny video camera on the frame of a pair of eye glasses. The camera captures images of the surrounding area and sends the image to a video microprocessing unit with battery pack that the patient wears or carries. The processing unit takes these electronic images, converts the images to an electronic signal, and wirelessly sends them to the retinal prosthesis receiver. The receiver sends the signal to an array of electrodes on the surface of the retina that the provider implants and secures to the retina. The implanted receiver takes the data and stimulates the electrodes, which the retina responds to by sending the pulses to the optic nerve of the brain. The brain then perceives the pulses as a pattern of light and dark spots, allowing a patient to distinguish images and movement. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider dilates the patient’s eye and performs a 360–degree incision in the conjunctiva to expose the rectus muscles. He isolates each of the rectus muscles and using forceps, grabs the implant, rinses it with sterile saline, and places it under the muscles, securing the implant receiver in place with a suture. Next, he removes any epiretinal membrane from the location where he will place the electrode array in a procedure called a vitrectomy. Then he releases the array in the vitreous cavity, positions it, and secures the retinal electrode array in place with micro retinal tacks. He sutures over the extraocular portion of the cable to secure it to the sclera, and he sutures closed all remaining wounds using grafts as necessary. He tests the unit and then places a patch and shield over the eye. Terminology Conjunctiva: Lining that covers the inside of the eyelids and the eyeball. Electrode array: Device that contains multiple electrodes. Epiretinal space: Inner retinal layer partially covering the surface of the retina. Extraocular: Outside the eye. Macular degeneration: Slowly progressive eye disease that causes deterioration of the photoreceptor cells, or the cells for detecting light and enabling site. Microretinal tacks: Small barbed, tapered tip fastener to fix prosthetic devices to the retina. Rectus muscles: The eye muscles that control the rotation of the eye. Retina: Light sensitive layers of tissue present at the back of the inner eye. Retinitis pigmentosa: A group of inherited, degenerative eye diseases where the light sensitive retina of the eye slowly and progressively degenerates. Sclera: White of the eye. Subconjunctival: Underneath the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane that covers the eyeball and the under surface of the eyelid. Vitrectomy: Surgical removal of some or all of the eye’s vitreous humor, the clear gel like tissue that fills the eyeball behind the lens. Read Less

short_description: Extracorporeal shock wave performed by a physician, requiring anesthesia other than local, and involving the lateral humeral epicondyle
lay_term: The physician applies a shock wave treatment to the lateral humeral epicondyle of an anesthetized patient. This procedure requires anesthesia other than a local anesthetic. This service typically is done to treat epicondylitis, or tennis elbow, a repetitive or overuse injury of the elbow. Explanation In extracorporeal shock wave treatment, the provider delivers high pressure sound waves to the affected body area. A physician identifies and marks the affected area of the elbow, specifically, the lateral humeral epicondyle, that is the most sensitive. This procedure requires the patient to have anesthesia other than local anesthesia. The physician applies a water–based conductive coupling gel to conduct the shock waves. They then place the shock head of the therapy unit over the area of tenderness on the elbow and bring the elbow into the shock wave path. The physician verifies the shock head’s positioning and contact to ensure the shock head remains in the treatment area during the entire procedure. The physician sets the power setting and generates the power pulses at the target. They increase the power incrementally, keeping the head of the therapy unit constantly coupled to the elbow. The physician treats the entire area, moving the patient’s arm as necessary until the maximum power level and number of shocks for the treatment protocol is reached. This service typically is done to treat epicondylitis, or tennis elbow, a repetitive or overuse injury of the elbow. Terminology Epicondylitis: Inflammation of the epicondyle, the bony projection on the outside and inside at the end of a long bone where muscles attach to the bone. Extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT): Administration of powerful sound waves to promote healing of tissues, such as in plantar fasciitis, a condition in which the connective tissue supporting the arch of the foot becomes inflamed and painful, and lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), in which the tendons of the elbow become inflamed and painful from repetitive use; extracorporeal means outside the body. Lateral humeral epicondyle: The bony projections on the outside and inside of the elbow where muscles of the forearm attach to the bone of the upper arm. short_description: Removal of total disc arthroplasty, (artificial disc), anterior approach, each additional interspace, lumbar (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0164T in conjunction with 22865)
lay_term: In this add on procedure, the provider removes another artificial disc in another lumbar interspace at the same operative session as an initial disc placement. Total disc arthroplasty describes the use of an artificial disc to replace a disc of the lumbar spine to treat conditions such as degenerative disc disease or damage due to trauma. Explanation To access the site for the initial disc removal, the provider uses an anterior approach and incises the abdomen at the site of the original incision, then dissects down through the scar tissue to expose the rectus muscle, which he identifies within the rectus sheath and mobilizes. He carefully removes adhesions from the previous surgical exposure, taking care not to harm the peritoneum. He places retractors to hold back the tissues. He identifies, protects, and mobilizes structures as needed to obtain the necessary exposure. He identifies the first target segment, separates the bone surfaces, then loosens the arthroplasty device from any adhesions, and removes the artificial device. In this procedure, after the provider performs the initial artificial disc removal described above, he removes another artificial disc from another lumbar interspace. He identifies the subsequent target segment and removes the device. He achieves hemostasis, closes the posterior rectus sheath, releases all retractors from surrounding muscles and reapproximates all tissue and muscle. He may place drains, closes the incision in layers and applies sterile dressing. Terminology Anterior: Situated in front. Arthroplasty device: Device used to replace or reconstruct a joint. Degenerative disc disease: Age related changes in the spine causing spinal deterioration. Disc or Intervertebral disc: This is a round, flat fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae that consists of a hard outer layer called annulus fibrosis and a gel like central part called nucleus pulposus; The intervertebral disc acts as a flexible cushion between the two vertebrae that helps in load bearing and shock absorption . Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also called the intervertebral space. Lumbar vertebrae: Five vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest level vertebrae, and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Posterior rectus sheath: The portion of the sheath of the rectus abdominis muscle, the two parallel vertically aligned muscles on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen that lies behind the muscle and covers only its upper two thirds. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Rectus muscle, rectus abdominis muscle: the two parallel vertically aligned muscles on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen Rectus sheath: Sleeve of fibrous connective tissue that surrounds the rectus abdominis muscle. Retractors: Surgical instrument used to separate the edges of a surgical incision or wound, or to hold back tissue or organs. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine; there are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 4 coccygeal. Tips Because this is an add–on code, it must be reported in conjunction with a code for the initial disc removal, 22865. Assign code 0164T once for removal of each additional lumbar artificial disc. lay_term: In this add on procedure, the provider revises and replaces another artificial disc in another lumbar interspace at the same operative session as an initial lumbar artificial disc repair. The provider performs this procedure for movement or damage of an arthroplasty device. Total disc arthroplasty describes the use of an artificial disc to replace a disc of the lumbar spine to treat conditions such as degenerative disc disease , or damage due to trauma. Explanation To access the site for the initial artificial disc revision and replacement, the provider uses an anterior approach and incises the abdomen at the site of the original incision, then dissects down through the scar tissue to expose the rectus muscle, which he identifies within the rectus sheath and mobilizes. He careful removes adhesions from the previous surgical exposure, taking care not to harm the peritoneum. He places retractors to hold back the tissues. He identifies, protects and mobilizes structures as needed to obtain the necessary exposure. He identifies the first target segment, removes the artificial device, repairs and replaces it. In this procedure, after the provider performs the initial artificial lumbar disc revision described above, the provider identifies the next implant level for repair, then accesses and loosens the device from the vertebral segments. He removes the device and uses retractors to keep the disc space open. He may take new measurements to verify the appropriateness of the disc prosthesis. He may also adjust and reshape the space as necessary to contain the implant perfectly. Finally, he reshapes and preps the prosthesis for reinsertion and the implant is guided into the lumbar space using fluoroscopy. He secures the device in place. He achieves hemostasis, closes the posterior rectus sheath, releases all retractors from surrounding muscles and reapproximates all tissue and muscle. He may place drains, closes the incision in layers and applies sterile dressing. Terminology Anterior: Situated in front. Arthroplasty device: Device used to replace or reconstruct a joint. Degenerative disc disease: Age related changes in the spine causing spinal deterioration. Disc or Intervertebral disc: This is a round, flat fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae that consists of a hard outer layer called annulus fibrosis and a gel like central part called nucleus pulposus; The intervertebral disc acts as a flexible cushion between the two vertebrae that helps in load bearing and shock absorption. Hemostasis: The stoppage of blood flow. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also called the intervertebral space. Lumbar vertebrae: Five vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest level vertebrae, and the sacral, or bottom vertebrae, in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Posterior rectus sheath: The portion of the sheath of the rectus abdominis muscle, the two parallel vertically aligned muscles on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen, that lies behind the muscle and covers only its upper two thirds. Reapproximates: To align or rejoin tissue. Rectus sheath: Sleeve of fibrous connective tissue that surrounds the rectus abdominis muscle. Retractors: Surgical instrument used to separate the edges of a surgical incision or wound, or to hold back tissue or organs. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine; there are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 4 coccygeal. Tips Because this is an add–on code, it must be reported in conjunction with a code for the initial disc revision, 22862. Assign code 0165T once for revision and replacement of each additional lumbar artificial disc. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider identifies and removes a rectal tumor using a proctoscope with the goal of leaving the anus unharmed. He does this using the transanal endoscopic microsurgical approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses the transanal endoscopic microsurgical approach for identification and removal of a rectal tumor. In this approach, he inserts the proctoscope to identify the tumor. He then insufflates the lumen of the rectum with high flow carbon dioxide. The provider dissects the tumor from its lower edge by keeping a macroscopic margin of 5 mm from the tumor. He continues full–thickness resection circumferentially and safeguards the normal surrounding mucosa. The provider then irrigates the rectum with antimicrobial agents like iodopovidone solution and sutures the rectal wall. Finally, he examines the rectum through the proctoscope for appropriate closure. Terminology Anus: Lower opening of the digestive tract through which fecal matter is excreted. Lumen: Space inside any hollow, tube–like structure in the body. Mucosa: Lining in the internal, tube–like organs of the body. Proctoscope: Instrument used to visualize and examine the rectum and anus. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that comes to an end at the anus. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inserts one or more drainage devices into tissue in the anterior segment (front–most region) of the eye.?The device helps drain fluid from the eye, which may help reduce pressure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision or inserts the needle of a delivery device through the cornea (the clear covering in the front of the eye) into the anterior segment (the front–most region of the eye). The provider inserts the small drainage device into the trabecular meshwork, which is tissue that drains most of the thick watery substance called aqueous fluid from the eye. The fluid goes into a circular drainage canal in the eye called Schlemm’s canal. The provider may place one or more drainage devices during the session. The provider removes the instruments and completes the procedure. Providers may insert the drainage devices to help reduce pressure in the eye, such as in patients with glaucoma. short_description: Percutaneous sacral augmentation (sacroplasty), unilateral injection(s), including the use of a balloon or mechanical device, when used, 1 or more needles, includes imaging guidance and bone biopsy, when performed
lay_term: The provider injects cement material through a needle to one side of a fractured sacrum. The provider may perform this augmentation by creating a cavity in the vertebral body using a balloon or mechanical device. The provider may use imaging guidance and bone biopsy in this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, usually by local anesthesia, the provider may create a cavity in the sacral region of the vertebra using a balloon or a mechanical device. The provider performs the technique with the inflatable balloon with the help of a specialized bone tamp that expands the collapsed vertebra for injection of cement. He then uses a needle to inject polymethylmethacrylate or other bone cement into the cavity of the fractured zone of the sacrum. The provider may or may not employ computed tomography or fluoroscopic guidance to inspect the application of the injection. This technique alleviates pain and provides mechanical support to patients with a compression fracture or metastatic malignancy of the spine. Although the code does not essentially require the provider to perform imaging guidance and bone biopsy, but the code does include these services when the provider performs them. Terminology Augmentation: Adding to, such as by placing a graft. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Bone tamp: A straight cylindrical surgical tool a provider uses to channel and create a cavity in the bone and to pack artificial bone into place. Compression fracture: Collapse of vertebra due to its weakening; mostly due to osteoporosis. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Metastatic malignancy: The spread of a tumor or cancerous tissue to another part of the body. Sacroplasty: Procedure to stabilize a compression fracture of the sacral region. Sacrum: Large, triangular bone at the end of vertebral column. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Vertebral body: Main or largest part of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips For bilateral augmentation of the sacrum, use 0201T, Percutaneous sacral augmentation, sacroplasty, bilateral injections, including the use of a balloon or mechanical device, when used, 2 or more needles, includes imaging guidance and bone biopsy, when performed. lay_term: The provider replaces one or more joints, at a single lumbar vertebral level, with a prosthetic device under fluoroscopic guidance. The procedure stabilizes the spine and retains the normal motion of the vertebrae. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the affected lumbar vertebrae to the level of the fascia. He then retracts the paravertebral muscles to gain access to the lumbar vertebrae. The provider further uses partial resection to remove the posterior lumbar component and insert the facet prosthesis. He may perform facetectomy, laminectomy, foraminotomy, and inject cement material in the vertebra to fix the prosthetic device. He performs the procedure under fluoroscopic guidance. Finally he ensures hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, and closes the excised area in layers. Terminology Arthroplasty: Surgical procedure to replace and reconstruct a joint. Facet joints: Joints connecting one vertebra to another. Facetectomy: Excision of the facet joints of vertebrae. Fascia: Fibrous connective tissue that encloses and binds organs, muscles, blood vessels, and nerves together. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Foraminotomy: Surgical procedure to enlarge the intervertebral foramen, the passages through which nerve bundles pass to the body via the spinal cord. Laminectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the posterior portion of the vertebra known as the lamina. Lumbar vertebrae: Five vertebrae situated between the thoracic, or chest level vertebrae, and the sacral, or bottom, vertebrae in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols L1 through L5. Posterior: The back surface of the body. Read Less

short_description: Speech audiometry threshold, automated; with speech recognition
lay_term: The provider presents the patient with series of words at varying volumes and measures the patient’s ability to recognize familiar words and repeat them. This test measures the patient’s ability to understand speech and helps determine whether the patient could benefit from a hearing aid. Explanation The provider places headphones or earphones over the patient’s ears and asks him to repeat the words he hears. The words begin at a lower volume so that the provider may determine the speech reception threshold which is the lowest level of sound that the patient easily understands and repeats the words. Further, the provider presents the patient with some words that we use in ordinary conversation at a louder level than the speech recognition threshold and asks him to repeat the words. This helps the provider determine if the patient could benefit from a hearing aid. Terminology Audiometry: Testing of a person's hearing sensitivity to hear various sound frequencies. Hearing threshold: Minimum sound frequency that a person can hear. Tips Code 0211T represents the technical component of the service only, so you should not append modifier 26 or TC. Read Less

short_description: Placement of a posterior intrafacet implant(s), unilateral or bilateral, including imaging and placement of bone graft(s) or synthetic device(s), single level; cervical
lay_term: The provider implants an allograft or a synthetic spacer into the facet joint of the cervical vertebrae under image guidance. This procedure expands and stabilizes the facet joint space and lessens pain due to degenerative changes or trauma in the cervical vertebrae region. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the cervical region of the vertebral column, extends the incision down to the fascia and muscle, and then exposes the bone. He places a synthetic spacer or an allograft, typically made from the bone of the femur or tibia, into the facet joint at a single level of the cervical vertebra. He performs the procedure under fluoroscopic guidance or other imaging technique. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called an allogeneic graft or homograft. Cervical vertebrae: Seven vertebrae situated within the neck, between the head and thoracic vertebrae in the spinal column, designated by the symbols C1 through C7. Degenerative: Progressive decline or loss of function in the body or tissues that cause the body or part of the body to become weaker. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Femur: Thigh bone. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structures with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, or joining, of two structures. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Intrafacet: Within a facet joint, a joint connecting one vertebra to another. Paravertebral facet, or zygapophyseal, or Z joint: A synovial joint containing synovial fluid and connecting two spinal vertebrae. Tibia: Shin bone. Tips For placement of an intrafacet implant at each additional vertebral segment, use code +0222T, Placement of a posterior intrafacet implants, unilateral or bilateral, including imaging and placement of bone grafts or synthetic devices, single level; each additional vertebral segment. short_description: Placement of bone marrow sampling port, including imaging guidance when performed Notes: (Do not report 0901T in conjunction with 77002, 77012)
lay_term: The provider places a bone marrow sampling port, which allows for repeated bone marrow sampling without multiple needle insertions. The provider may use imaging guidance, such as ultrasound or X–ray, to ensure correct placement of the port. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a bone marrow sampling port, a small device implanted under the skin, typically near the hip bone, to facilitate easy access to bone marrow. Bone marrow is the soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are produced. The port allows for repeated sampling without the need for multiple needle sticks. In a typical procedure, the provider makes a small incision and creates a small pocket under the skin to house the port. The provider inserts the port and tunnels a catheter, a thin, flexible tube attached to the port, under the skin and into the bone marrow cavity. The provider may use imaging guidance, such as ultrasound or X–ray, to help position the port accurately. The imaging guidance helps the provider visualize the internal structures to ensure the port is correctly placed in the bone marrow cavity. Once the port is placed, the provider verifies its position and secures it in place. short_description: Transluminal peripheral atherectomy, open or percutaneous, including radiological supervision and interpretation; renal artery
lay_term: The provider restores the blood supply in a narrowed or blocked renal artery. He removes the deposited plaque through an open or percutaneous approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the femoral artery and inserts a guide wire over which he inserts a catheter to the area of stenosis in the renal artery. Alternatively, he punctures the skin directly over the suspected area of stenosis in the renal artery. He then inserts a catheter with a shaving device, e.g., a burr or blade, at its tip. He guides the catheter over the guide wire under image guidance, usually fluoroscopy, into the area of stenosis in the renal artery. He dissects or shaves off the arterial plaque from the vessel walls with the blade or burr at the end of the catheter. The provider then aspirates out the excised plaque from the artery. The provider finally removes all the instruments, controls any bleeding, and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Abdominal aorta: Largest artery in the abdominal cavity supplying oxygenated blood to the abdomen. Aspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach. Atherectomy: Removal of plaque from the lining, or intima, of an artery; also called endarterectomy. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Femoral artery: Large artery in the thigh that supplies oxygen rich blood to the legs. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and stent. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Plaque: Yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material, that is, fat, in the lining, or intima, of the arteries. Renal artery: Large blood vessels branching off from abdominal aorta and supplying blood to the kidneys. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Transluminal:Along or across the interior of a tubular structure, such as a blood vessel or the intestines. The provider reporting the catheterization of renal artery should report 36251 through 36254 to demonstrate the catheterization of renal artery to investigate any blockage, narrowing, or clots in the renal blood vessels. short_description: Intramuscular autologous bone marrow cell therapy, with preparation of harvested cells, multiple injections, one leg, including ultrasound guidance, if performed; complete procedure including unilateral or bilateral bone marrow harvest Notes: (Do not report 0263T in conjunction with 38204-38242, 76942, 93925, 93926)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider extracts bone marrow from the patient, prepares it, and injects it into the muscles of the patient to treat diseases like end stage peripheral artery disease. Explanation The provider inserts a large bore needle into the bone marrow cavity of bones, such as the sternum, iliac crest, or ribs, and extracts bone marrow from the area. He collects the bone marrow in a container and centrifuges it at high speed to prepare cells for injection. This centrifugation causes the bone marrow to separate into individual components. The provider collects the desired part of the bone marrow. Using ultrasound guidance, he administers the bone marrow either intra arterially or through multiple injections into the muscle usually the gastrocnemius muscle. This bone marrow injection enhances the repair process and increases the diameter of existing arterial vessels. Terminology Arterial vessels: Vessels that carry oxygen rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. Bone marrow: Substance within the internal cavity of a bone; a source of stem cells, which ultimately develop into red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Centrifugation: Process that rotates a mixture around a fixed axis at a high speed to separate it into its constituents. Gastrocnemius: Large muscle located on the back of lower leg, originating at the back of thighbone and knee, and joined to the muscle of the heel; also called as leg triceps. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Iliac crest: Upper edge of the ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone; also called the crest of the ilium. Intra arterial: Within the artery. Peripheral artery disease: Circulatory problem characterized by narrowing of arteries of limbs, thereby resulting in decrease in blood flow; abbreviated as PAD. Sternum: Breastbone, at the front of the rib cage. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips If the provider just prepares the cells and transplants them to the patient, use code 0264T, Intramuscular autologous bone marrow cell therapy, with preparation of harvested cells, multiple injections, one leg, including ultrasound guidance, if performed; complete procedure excluding bone marrow harvest. If the provider only harvests the bone marrow and preserves it for future use, use code 0265T, Intramuscular autologous bone marrow cell therapy, with preparation of harvested cells, multiple injections, one leg, including ultrasound guidance, if performed; unilateral or bilateral bone marrow harvest only for intramuscular autologous bone marrow cell therapy. short_description: Implantation or replacement of carotid sinus baroreflex activation device; total system (includes generator placement, unilateral or bilateral lead placement, intra-operative interrogation, programming, and repositioning, when performed)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider implants or replaces a device consisting of leads and a pulse generator, into the carotid sinus to lower the heart rate and blood pressure of the patient. This occurs due to stimulation of baroreceptors in the carotid arteries that helps to treat resistant hypertension. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision near the clavicle on each side of the neck to reach the carotid sinus. He then places electrodes in the carotid sinus and attaches wires to them. He connects these wires to the generator placed subcutaneously beneath the skin. He then tests the system for accuracy. On initiation, the generator stimulates the electrodes to activate the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, which results in dilation of the vessels leading to reduction in heart rate and blood pressure. Finally, the provider achieves hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Baroreceptors: Pressure receptors located in the carotid sinus that reduces blood pressure upon activation. Baroreflex: Spontaneous reaction through which the baroreceptors maintain the blood pressure. Bilateral: On two sides; opposite of unilateral. Blood pressure: Force of blood against the wall of the blood vessels. Carotid artery: Two large main arteries in the neck, passageway carrying blood from the heart to other parts of the body, which supply blood to the brain. Carotid sinus: Area in the neck marked by the divergence of coronary arteries contains baroreceptors. Clavicle: Collar bone. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Intraoperative interrogation: Cross examination during the procedure. Pulse generator: A programmable device that emits electrical pulses. Resistant hypertension: Increase in blood pressure despite the treatment with at least three antihypertensive drugs. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. Tips If the provider implants or replaces only unilateral leads of baroreflex activation device, use code 0267T, Implantation or replacement of carotid sinus baroreflex activation device; lead only, unilateral. If the provider implants or replaces only pulse generator of baroreflex activation device, use code 0268T, Implantation or replacement of carotid sinus baroreflex activation device; pulse generator only. short_description: Percutaneous laminotomy/laminectomy (interlaminar approach) for decompression of neural elements, (with or without ligamentous resection, discectomy, facetectomy and/or foraminotomy), any method, under indirect image guidance (eg, fluoroscopic, CT), single or multiple levels, unilateral or bilateral; cervical or thoracic
lay_term: The provider alleviates painful pressure on the nerve by increasing the amount of space available for the nerve root to exit the spinal canal. He may use different percutaneous techniques under indirect imaging guidance to treat a herniated or bulging disc at a single or multiple levels of the cervical or thoracic region. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin of the affected cervical or thoracic spinous process and inserts a specially designed endoscope and obturator sheath. Using imaging guidance, he advances an obturator through the sheath along the base of the spinous process above the lamina below and to the interlaminar space or until the obsturator and sheath reach the bony surface, depending on the patient's anatomy. After dividing tissue and fat as necessary and after confirming the epidural space, he drills the center of the superior edge of the lamina under the lesion as far as the attachment of the ligamentum flavum and dissects the ligament. He also drills the superior facet process. If the ligamentum flavum cannot be detached, he may perform a laminotomy as far as its attachment and debulk the ligamentum flavum using a punch.. If the approach is difficult, the provider may use a 30–degree beveled or duck–billed sheath. In similar fashion, the provider may perform a ligamentous resection, discectomy, facetectomy, or foraminotomy at the same level through the endoscope and obturator sheath to decompress the herniated disc(s) at one or multiple levels. For bilateral procedures, the provider repeats the service on the opposite side of the vertebra. Finally, he removes all the equipment, controls any bleeding, and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Cervical vertebra: Seven vertebrae situated within the neck, between the head and thoracic vertebrae in the spinal column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Decompression: Reduction in the pressure.Discectomy: Surgical procedure to remove herniated disc material that presses on a nerve root or the spinal cord. Disc herniation: Medical condition in which the vertebral disc degenerates and tears down leading to leakage of inner core through the outer portion of the disc. Endoscope: A stiff (rigid) or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, stomach, or eye; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Epidural space: Area between the wall of the vertebra and the outer most membrane of the spinal cord i.e., the dura mater. Facetectomy: Invasive surgical procedure performed to relieve pressure on the spinal nerves by excision of a facet. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Foraminotomy: A type of back surgery used to widen the size of the neuroforaminal spaces and treat pinched nerves in the neck and lower back to relieve pressure on nerves. Herniated disc: Degeneration or tearing down of fibrous cartilaginous disc between the vertebrae.Interlaminar: Between the lamina. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Laminectomy: Surgical excision of the lamina, one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Laminotomy: Surgical removal of part of a lamina to relieve pain and pressure on the spinal cord. Ligamentum flavum: Yellow elastic tissue that connects the bones of the adjacent vertebrae. Ligamentous resection: Surgical removal of part of ligament which is the fibrous band connecting bones and joints. Lumbar spine: The lower back region containing vertebrae L1 through L5. Obturator: A surgical device placed through a sheath or cannula during insertion to prevent blockage of the sheath by tissue. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Thoracic vertebra: 12 vertebrae situated between the cervical, or neck level vertebrae, and the lumbar vertebrae in the spinal column, indicated by T1 through T12. Trocar: A hollow pointed puncturing device, typically part of a cannula and trocar combination. Tips For the same procedure ont he lumbar spine, see 0275T. short_description: Visual evoked potential, screening of visual acuity, automated, with report Notes: (For visual evoked potential testing for glaucoma, use 0464T)
lay_term: This is an automated test that records the response from visual stimuli in the form of electrical signals produced by the brain's occipital region. The responses are recorded through electrodes placed on the patient's scalp and interpreted through an output of EEG study, and the provider prepares a report. Explanation The provider places electrodes at appropriate locations on the patient's scalp, mainly over the occipital area, the brain's vision center. The patient is positioned in front of a computer screen where his vision is exposed to brief visual stimuli, such as an alternating checkerboard pattern. The electrodes record the electrical potential responses to the visual stimuli on the screen and display the result as an electroencephalogram (EEG) study. The data from the EEG result is interpreted to determine the visual evoked potential (VEP) result of the test, which shows the response time to visual stimuli. VEPs are used to evaluate nerve dysfunction from the retina to the visual cortex and to evaluate the integrity of visual pathways. The visual acuity of the patient is then determined by the provider with the help of the test results. This process of testing is done one eye at a time. The electrodes are removed at the end of the process. Finally, the provider prepares a report. Terminology Visual evoked potential (VEP): Electrical signals produced or evoked mainly in the brain's occipital region in response to visual stimuli, such as an alternating checkerboard pattern on a computer screen. short_description: Visual evoked potential, testing for glaucoma, with interpretation and report Notes: (For visual evoked potential screening of visual acuity, use 0333T) (To report percutaneous/minimally invasive [indirect visualization] arthrodesis of the sacroiliac joint with image guidance, use 27279)
lay_term: Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing measures the electrical activity of the brain in response to a visual stimulus such as an alternating checkerboard board pattern on a computer screen. The provider performs this test when the patient is experiencing changes in vision that can be due to problems along the pathways of certain nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider places electrodes on the occipital area, the back of patient’s head. This area of the brain receives and interprets visual signals. Visual evoked potential measures the time taken by a visual stimulus to travel from the eye to the occipital cortex. The provider compares the amplitude (the intensity of response) and the latency (the length of time it takes to respond) to established normal values. Patients with early glaucoma have problems with low contrast images and their processing of these images may be slow. A provider uses this information to ensure that optic nerve pathways are working normally. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of sinus tarsi implant Notes: (Do not report 0335T in conjunction with 28585, 28725, 29907)
lay_term: The provider attaches a synthetic implant on the soft tissues between the ankle and heel bones to treat hyperpronation of the foot. Explanation With the patient in the supine position, appropriately prepped, and using local anesthesia, the provider makes a small, usually less than one inch, incision on the lateral side (outside) of the ankle/heel region over the sinus tarsi. If posterior tibial tendon (PTT) lengthening is needed, he may make a small percutaneous medial incision and release the PTT. He debrides the sinus tarsi, removing fatty contents and nerve endings, taking care not to injure the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament. He introduces a blunt lever through the sinus tarsi and underneath the neck of the talus. He pushes the lever distally to supinate the foot while an assistant pronates the forefoot to move the head of the talus upward, outward, and backward and reposition it so that pronation is corrected. He inserts trial prostheses of increasing size until the correct size is determined, choosing the smallest implant that corrects the deformity and holds the sinus tarsi stable. At this point, if he has released the PTT, he reattaches it to achieve optimum tension. After this, he inserts the actual implant the same size as the trial implant and closes the incision in routine fashion. He may apply a compression cast. A sinus tarsi implant, also referred to as subtalar arthroereisis, treats hyperpronation (flexible flatfoot deformity); it may also be used to treat dysfunction of the posterior tibial tendon, tarsal coalition (an abnormal connection between the tarsal bones on the back of the foot), and accessory navicular syndrome (an extra navicular bone near or attached to the posterior tibial tendon). Terminology Arthroereisis: A surgical procedure using a bone graft or implant to re–establish a medial foot arch and limit movement of the subtalar joint without blocking it; the procedure treats flat foot and other conditions involving the arch and ankle bones; the word is derived from arthro– meaning joint and –ereisis meaning to sustain, support, or push against (something). Calcaneus: Heel bone, located at the back of the tarsus (ankle) bone. Cuneiform bones: Three small wedge–shaped bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral) in the foot just before the first, second, and third metatarsals. Navicular bone: A boat–shaped bone between the talus and the cuneiform bones in the ankle; former name of the scaphoid bone in the wrist. Posterior tibial tendon: FIbrous tissue that attaches the calf muscle to the bones on the inside of the foot; it holds up the arch of the foot and supports the foot when walking. Pronation: Rotation of the hands and forearms so that the palms face downward or rotation of the foot so that the plantar surface (underside) of the foot rolls outward. Subtalar joint: A joint between the talus (ankle bone) and calcaneus (heel). Supination: Rotation of the hands and forearms so that the palms face upward or rotation of the foot so that the plantar surface (underside) rolls inward. Talus: A small bone that sits between the calcaneus (heel bone) and the two long bones of the lower leg. Read Less

short_description: Removal and reinsertion of sinus tarsi implant Notes: (For unilateral or bilateral endothelial function assessments, using peripheral vascular response to reactive hyperemia, noninvasive [eg, brachial artery ultrasound, peripheral artery tonometry], use 93998)
lay_term: The physician removes an implant previously attached to soft tissues between the ankle and heel bones to treat hyperpronation of the foot and then places a new implant in the same region. Explanation With the patient in the supine position, appropriately prepped, and using local anesthesia, the provider makes a small on the lateral side (outside) of the ankle/heel region over the sinus tarsi. He removes the initial implant. He debrides the sinus tarsi, if necessary, taking care not to injure the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament. He introduces a blunt lever through the sinus tarsi and underneath the neck of the talus. He pushes the lever distally to supinate the foot while an assistant pronates the forefoot to move the head of the talus upward, outward, and backward and reposition it so that pronation is corrected. He inserts trial prostheses of increasing size until the correct size is determined, choosing the smallest implant that corrects the deformity and holds the sinus tarsi stable. At this point, if he has released the PTT, he reattaches it to achieve optimum tension. After this, he inserts the actual implant the same size as the trial implant and closes the incision in routine fashion. He may apply a compression cast. A sinus tarsi implant, also referred to as subtalar arthroereisis, treats hyperpronation (flexible flatfoot deformity); it may also be used to treat dysfunction of the posterior tibial tendon, tarsal coalition (an abnormal connection between the tarsal bones on the back of the foot), and accessory navicular syndrome (an extranavicular bone near or attached to the posterior tibial tendon). Terminology Arthroereisis: A surgical procedure using a bone graft or implant to re–establish a medial foot arch and limit movement of the subtalar joint without blocking it; the procedure treats flat foot and other conditions involving the arch and ankle bones; the word is derived from arthro– meaning joint and –ereisis meaning to sustain, support, or push against (something). Calcaneus: Heel bone, located at the back of the tarsus (ankle) bone. Cuneiform bones: Three small wedge–shaped bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral) in the foot just before the first, second, and third metatarsals. Navicular bone: A boat–shaped bone between the talus and the cuneiform bones in the ankle; former name of the scaphoid bone in the wrist. Posterior tibial tendon: Fibrous tissue that attaches the calf muscle to the bones on the inside of the foot; it holds up the arch of the foot and supports the foot when walking. Pronation: Rotation of the hands and forearms so that the palms face downward or rotation of the foot so that the plantar surface (underside) of the foot rolls outward. Subtalar joint: A joint between the talus (ankle bone) and calcaneus (heel). Supination: Rotation of the hands and forearms so that the palms face upward or rotation of the foot so that the plantar surface (underside) rolls inward. Talus: A small bone that sits between the calcaneus (heel bone) and the two long bones of the lower leg. Read Less

short_description: Therapeutic apheresis with selective HDL delipidation and plasma reinfusion
lay_term: The provider draws blood from the patient and removes the low density lipoprotein, or LDL, the so called bad cholesterol, from the plasma. He infuses the red blood cells and the remaining filtered plasma back into the patient. The provider performs this procedure to treat hypercholesterolemia. Explanation The provider inserts a sterile needle into the arm in the region of the elbow and withdraws venous blood. He collects the blood in a container layered with an anticoagulant and centrifuges it at high speed, which causes the blood constituents to separate. The provider separates the plasma and administers the red blood cells back into the blood stream. He then treats the plasma with different chemicals and centrifuges, which splits the cholesterol into different components, such as high density lipoprotein, low density lipoprotein, triglycerides, and very low density lipoprotein. Finally, the provider infuses delipidated plasma, i.e., the plasma with the lipids removed, along with the high density lipoprotein, the so called good cholesterol, into the bloodstream once a week for seven weeks continuously. Terminology Anticoagulant: Substance that prevents blood clotting; an anticoagulant deficiency that can lead to thrombosis in veins or arteries. Apheresis: Technique to collect blood from the patient and separate it into individual components and reinfuse some of the blood, plasma, or components into the patient; also called pheresis or therapeutic pheresis. Cholesterol: An important fatlike substance found in most tissues; an important component in certain processes but excessive accumulation can cause atherosclerosis and circulation problems. Delipidation: Removal of lipids from plasma using chemicals. High density lipoprotein, or HDL: A constituent or fraction of total cholesterol that transfers cholesterol from body tissues to the liver, essential and good for the body. Hypercholesterolemia: Excessive cholesterol in the body. Low density lipoprotein, or LDL: A constituent or fraction of total cholesterol that transports cholesterol into body tissues, considered bad for the body. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Red blood cells, or RBCs or erythrocytes: One of three primary cell types in blood that primarily carries oxygen through the body on the hemoglobin molecule; RBCs have surface antigens to which people can form antibodies, typically through exposure via pregnancy or blood transfusion; at a future time, these antibodies can cause hemolytic anemia, killing fetal RBCs during pregnancy, or transfused RBCs during a blood transfusion, or possibly the patient’s own RBCs due to an autoimmune response. Triglyceride: A major lipid, or fat, formed from cholesterol and stored in fat cells; considered neither good nor bad in terms of its effect on the body, but elevated triglyceride typically indicates a high fat and or a high sugar diet. Very low density lipoprotein, or VLDL: Combination of very high proportion of lipids with less of proteins that carry cholesterol from the liver to the tissues. Read Less

short_description: Placement of interstitial device(s) in bone for radiostereometric analysis (RSA)
lay_term: The provider places multiple tantalum beads in the interstitial spaces of the bones and obtains a two dimensional image to measure the motion, quality, and wear of an implant or prosthesis. Explanation The provider performs this procedure during surgery to place an implant or prosthesis in the spine, upper extremities, or lower extremities. The provider inserts multiple tiny tantalum beads about the size of sesame seeds as markers into the interstitial tissues of bone around the implant or prosthesis. The beads become imbedded in the bone over time. The provider then exposes the site of the implant to a pair of X–rays in order to capture simultaneous images from two different directions. A special device frames the area and ensures that future images will be taken from the exact same projection. Images taken periodically following the surgery identify alterations in the position or condition of the implant or prosthesis. Terminology Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Interstitial: Situated in the small gaps or spaces between tissues. Prosthesis: An artificial or man made replacement for a body part. Radiostereometric analysis, or RSA: An imaging procedure that uses two dimensional images to locate the position of an object and to detect changes in the position over time. Tantalum: An element with a high anatomic number easily identifiable on radiographic images. X–rays, or radiographs: The use of radiation to image and examine specific body structures in order to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tips Code 0347T is for the placement of the interstitial tantalum beads. For Radiologic examination, radiostereometric analysis (RSA) of the spine, upper extremities, and lower extremities, use codes 0348T, 0349T, and 0350T respectively. Read Less

lay_term: The provider uses optical coherence tomography imaging to detect the cancer cells in the surgical cavity left after breast excision. The procedure gives the provider immediate feedback on whether the surgical margins are clear of cancer cells or if he needs to excise more tissue. After the surgery, he or a radiologist interprets the data and reports the findings. Explanation In the operating room, the provider applies a probe to the surgical cavity left after the breast excision. The probe is connected to a computer which displays the microscopic images of the tissue. The provider uses the probe to expose the tissue to light waves and measures the reflection of light from the tissues. The computer displays the images and shows the provider in real time during the surgical procedure whether the margins reveal the presence or absence of malignant cells. After the procedure, the provider or a radiologist interprets the images and reports the findings. Terminology Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Mammography: An X–ray of the breast, which providers use to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases, including cancer. Optical coherence tomography: Noninvasive imaging that uses light waves to process and provide three dimensional images of tissue. Probe: An instrument placed to explore in a wound or the inside of a vessel, organ, or the body; to explore a wound or the inside of a vessel, organ, or the body with such an instrument. X–ray, or radiographs: A procedure that involves the use of radiation to image specific body structures in order to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Tips If the provider performs optical coherence tomography without interpretation and report, use code 0353T, Optical coherence tomography of breast, surgical cavity; real time intraoperative. If the provider performs optical coherence tomography of the excised tissue of the breast, with interpretation and report, use code 0352T, Optical coherence tomography of breast or axillary lymph node, excised tissue, each specimen; interpretation and report, real time or referred. short_description: Bioelectrical impedance analysis whole body composition assessment, with interpretation and report Notes: (For bioimpedance-derived physiological cardiovascular analysis, use 93701) (For bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS), use 93702)
lay_term: The provider uses the resistance of water, fat, and tissues to electrical conductivity to estimate body composition. He calculates body composition using the difference between body weight and total water in the body. He prepares a report of the findings. Explanation The provider places electrodes on various parts of the body. He then passes mild electric current through the electrodes. The provider measures the resistance shown by the different tissues of the body. The current passes easily through water and tissues like muscle with higher water content, but the tissues with high fat content slow down the signals. The provider uses the resistance to the flow of current to estimate the amount of water and fat in the body and uses the difference in body weight and total water in the body to calculate body composition. He prepares a report of the findings. Terminology Bioelectrical impedance analysis: Technique to estimate the body composition by passing mild electric current through the body. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses. Explanation Adaptive behavior treatment addresses one or more specific severe destructive behaviors, such as, self–injurious behavior, aggression, or property destruction. short_description: Visual field assessment, with concurrent real time data analysis and accessible data storage with patient initiated data transmitted to a remote surveillance center for up to 30 days; review and interpretation with report by a physician or other qualified health care professional
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an examination of the visual field of each eye of a patient. Report this code if there is concurrent real time data analysis and accessible data storage with patient initiated data transmission to a remote surveillance center for up to 30 days and there is interpretation with report by the provider. Explanation Visual field testing, also known as perimetry, is the measure of the area in which an individual can see objects in side vision while his eyes focus on a central point. In a common form of this examination, the patient focuses on the center of an instrument called a perimeter, a concave, or bowl type device and presses a button each time he sees a flash of light, which occur all around the device. A computer records the location of the flash and if the patient presses the button and then identifies areas of vision loss where the patient did not see the flashes. The provider then reviews and interprets the data. The provider performs the patient visual examinations at a preset time over a period of 30 days and testing includes concurrent real time data analysis and accessible data storage, along with the provider review, and interpretation of the examination recordings. The provider performs a visual field assessment test to detect the central and peripheral vision problems caused by stroke, glaucoma, and other eye or brain problems. This code represents the professional components of this service. Terminology Central vision: Describes the person’s vision when he sees straight ahead for example when one drives or read. Glaucoma: A condition that damages the eye’s optic nerve causing vision loss. Peripheral vision: Describes the person’s vision outside the direct line of vision. Stroke: A condition in which the blood supply to the brain interrupts causing the brain damage. Read Less

He uses a catheter inserted through the scope deliver a retrograde (backward) injection of dye or contrast material into the pancreatic and biliary ducts to obtain X–ray images. short_description: Collagen cross-linking of cornea, including removal of the corneal epithelium, when performed, and intraoperative pachymetry, when performed Notes: (Report medication separately) (Do not report 0402T in conjunction with 65435, 69990, 76514)
lay_term: The provider uses vitamin B2 eyedrops activated by ultraviolet light to strengthen crosslinking of corneal fibers, leading to a stiffer stronger cornea (clear covering of the eye). The provider also may remove the thin layer (epithelium) over the cornea and use pachymetry to determine the cornea’s thickness. Explanation The provider may mildly sedate the patient and apply numbing anesthetic drops to the patient’s eyes. The provider then applies riboflavin (vitamin B2) drops into the eyes. These drops saturate the cornea, the clear transparent covering in front of the eye. The provider then exposes the eye to ultraviolet rays to activate the riboflavin, strengthening natural attachments between corneal structures. This helps retain the normal shape and strength of the cornea and enhances its thickness. The provider also may remove the corneal epithelium, the thin layer over the eye’s surface, to improve absorption of the riboflavin. The provider also may use a device to measure the corneal thickness (pachymetry). Terminology Cornea: The clear transparent outer layer in the front of the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber that refracts light entering the eye and provides almost two–thirds to three–quarters of the focusing power. Epithelium: The tightly packed outer layer of cells that covers all the free surfaces of the body, including the skin, lining of tubular structures and cavities of organs, and mucous membranes that communicate with the outside of the body. Keratoconus: A degenerative eye disease, which causes a change in the normal gradual curve of the cornea to a more conical shape and results in the distortion of vision and multiple images. Pachymetry: A noninvasive ultrasound exam for measuring corneal thickness. Riboflavin: A vitamin essential for normal growth, red cell production, carbohydrate metabolism, and for the glutathione reductase enzyme to function; also known as vitamin B2. Ultraviolet light: A part of the light spectrum not visible that is able to break some chemical bonds. Tips Providers may perform this procedure for patients with keratoconus, in which the cornea doesn’t have enough collagen fiber crosslinks for structural support. lay_term: The provider educates a group of patients using an intensive standard curriculum of behavior modification and lifestyle changes for preventing diabetes for an hour or more on a single day. Unlike pacemakers, these systems stimulate for specific time intervals in order to improve myocardial function. lay_term: The provider implants a cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) system, or removes and replaces a previously implanted system, in a pocket created in the right upper chest and attaches electrodes at the end of wire leads that transmit electrical impulses to the right ventricular septum and the atrium to increase the strength of the heart's contractions and treat moderate–to–severe congestive heart failure in a patient not controlled by optimal medical therapy. This code covers the entire procedure including evaluating contractility if performed, programming, and the generator and electrodes. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the right upper chest region and creates a "pocket" for a cardiac contractility modulation device, which is similar to a pacemaker. Alternatively, he may make the incision over a previously placed device and remove the device. He places the device into the pocket. He attaches three leads (wires that transmit electrical impulses) to the device. He threads two of the leads through a vein to the right ventricle and attaches them at least 2 cm apart to the septum, or wall, between the right and left ventricles, the pumping chambers of the heart. He threads the third lead to the atrium, the upper chamber of the heart, to sense atrial activity. The two leads on the right ventricular septum emit electrical impulses to the ventricular during the absolute refractory period, just after the excitation impulse that stimulates the ventricle to contract. The provider evaluates the contractility of the heart and determines the optimum position of the leads and the heart's response to the impulses. The impulses, unlike a pacemaker or defibrillator which controls the heart rhythm, increase the strength of the contraction itself. Once the provider determines the optimum settings for the device, he checks for bleeding and closes the incision(s). If replacing a system, the provider will have removed prior components and disconnected the leads prior to the insertions described above. short_description: Removal of permanent cardiac contractility modulation system; pulse generator only
lay_term: The provider removes a cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) pulse generator from a pocket previously created in the right upper chest. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the pulse generator previously placed in a "pocket" in the right upper chest region. Report this code only for the removal of the pulse generator. short_description: Relocation of skin pocket for implanted cardiac contractility modulation pulse generator

guidelines: Cat III Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 0408T-0418T describe procedures related to cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) systems. These systems consist of a pulse generator, ventricular pacemaker electrodes (leads), and one atrial pacemaker electrode (lead), when performed. In contrast to a pacemaker or a defibrillator, which modulate the heart’s rhythm, the CCM system's impulses are designed to modulate the strength of contraction of the heart muscle. Unlike pacemakers, these systems stimulate for specific time intervals in order to improve myocardial function. Each CCM procedure code includes all imaging guidance in addition to placement of right ventricular leads and, when performed, placement of the atrial pacemaker lead. short_description: Destruction of neurofibroma, extensive (cutaneous, dermal extending into subcutaneous); face, head and neck, greater than 50 neurofibromas Notes: (For excision of neurofibroma, use 64792) (Report 0419T once per session regardless of the number of lesions treated)

short_description: Transperineal laser ablation of benign prostatic hyperplasia, including imaging guidance; prostate volume less than 50 mL
lay_term: The provider uses laser to ablate (destroy) benign tissue of an enlarged prostate. The approach is transperineal, going through the area between the scrotum and anus. This code includes imaging guidance and applies when the prostate volume is less than 50 mL. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may use an imaging probe, such as an ultrasound probe inserted into the rectum, or other imaging guidance to view the prostate on a screen during the procedure. The prostate is a small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder. For transperineal laser ablation (TPLA) of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), the provider inserts the laser device through the perineum (the area between the anus and scrotum) and into the prostate. This approach may involve placing multiple needles as introducers and then inserting fibers that connect to a laser machine. The provider applies power, and the laser light turns into heat energy to ablate (destroy) the targeted prostate tissue. The provider then removes the fibers and needles to complete the procedure. This code applies when the prostate volume is less than 50 mL. Terminology Ablation: Destruction of abnormal tissue by various methods including but not limited to application electrical energy, laser heat, intense cold, or chemicals. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, typically in older males; may compress the flow of urine. Perineum: The surface area between the scrotum and anus in men, bounded by the thighs, and the external genitalia and skin between the genitalia and anus in women. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen.
