lay_term: The provider uses ultrasound guidance and a robotic guidance system to deliver saline at high velocity through a catheter inserted into the urethra to destroy (ablate) the prostate to treat benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH), an enlargement of the prostate, which commonly occurs in older men and results in urinary urgency, frequency, straining, weak flow, and incomplete bladder emptying. This code includes other procedures on the urethra and seminal vesicles when performed. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized and using real–time ultrasound guidance, the provider performs prostate ablation using preprogrammed robotically guided high–velocity jet of saline delivered through a cystoscope placed through the urethra to destroy the prostate. The prostatic tissue is collected for analysis. If necessary, bleeding is controlled using a low–pressure water stream encompassing a low–power laser beam. The provider removes the cystoscope, a tubular lighted instrument to examine the interior of the urinary bladder and ureter through which other instruments may be passed. Other procedures may be performed to carry out the ablation. These include vasectomy, resection of the tube that carries sperm; meatotomy, incision to enlarge the meatus, the opening of the urethra; cystourethroscopy, examination of the bladder and urethra using a specially designed lighted tubular instrument; urethral calibration (measurement of dimensions) or dilation (widening, typically by expanding a balloon on the tip of a catheter); and internal urethrotomy, incision to extend the opening of the bladder end of the urethra. When performed, these procedures are included and should not be reported separately. Tips For other resection/ablation procedures on the prostate, see 52601–52649, 53850–53852, and 55873. Read Less

short_description: Ablation of benign prostate tissue, transrectal, with high intensity-focused ultrasound (HIFU), including ultrasound guidance Notes: (For ablation of malignant prostate tissue, transrectal, with high intensity–focused ultrasound [HIFU], including ultrasound guidance, use 55880)

The transducer focuses sound waves to generate heat at a lesion site to destroy the targeted tissue. This process is repeated as many times as is necessary until all the targeted prostate tissue is destroyed. When enough of the prostatic tissue has been destroyed, the provider withdraws the instrument. short_description: Cardiac acoustic waveform recording with automated analysis and generation of coronary artery disease risk score
lay_term: The provider uses a device that records heart sounds, analyzes them, and generates a coronary artery disease risk score. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider performs cardiac acoustic waveform (heart sound) recording. The service includes automated analysis and creation of a coronary artery disease (CAD) risk score. In a typical encounter, the provider has the patient relax and lie down prior to the test. Then the provider prepares the device, such as by entering patient demographic and health information, and attaching a component that allows the device to be placed comfortably on the patient. Then the provider marks and preps the target site on the patient’s chest. The provider places the device on the patient’s chest with a sensor on the marked target site. When the device is in place, the provider starts recording the heart sounds. The provider may instruct the patient to hold their breath at specific intervals. After recording, the device analyzes the data using CAD–score specific algorithms to identify abnormal sounds. The device performs calculations based on this analysis and the patient’s demographic and health information to generate the patient’s CAD risk score. The provider removes the device from the patient’s chest. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Coronary artery disease (CAD): A condition in which the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle become stenosed (narrowed) due to the deposit of plaques (fatty substances) on the inner walls of the blood vessels, resulting in decreased blood flow and ultimately heart failure, if not treated; also known as coronary heart disease or atherosclerotic heart disease. lay_term: The provider glides a hand–held tactile sensing device over the surface of the breast and under the arms, which transmits data to a computer that converts the data into two– and three–dimensional images and displays a surface map of the breast and any lesions in real time on a monitor that can be viewed by both the provider and the patient. short_description: Myocardial contrast perfusion echocardiography, at rest or with stress, for assessment of myocardial ischemia or viability (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0439T in conjunction with 93306, 93307, 93308, 93350, 93351)
lay_term: The provider performs myocardial contrast perfusion echocardiography, a technique that uses tiny gas–filled bubbles (microbubbles) to enhance visualization of capillaries in tissues; he performs the procedure when the patient is at rest or during stress to assess the heart for ischemia, reduced blood supply, or whether the heart muscle is healthy (viable). Explanation While performing echocardiography on a patient, the provider decides to incorporate myocardial contrast perfusion technique to assess circulation in the capillaries, the smallest blood vessels. Blood flow in these capillaries is important to maintain the viability of the heart muscle. He infuses gas–filled microbubbles intravenously into the blood stream. High–energy ultrasound destroys the microbubbles. The provider can tell by the rate of microbubble replenishment whether the resting flow is normal or reduced. Calculations carried out give the provider the blood volume fraction and flow velocity values. The provider may repeat the procedure with the patient at rest and with the patient under stress. short_description: Ablation, percutaneous, cryoablation, includes imaging guidance; nerve plexus or other truncal nerve (eg, brachial plexus, pudendal nerve)
lay_term: The provider uses cryoablation, the application of freezing temperature, to destroy a nerve plexus (a weblike collection of nerves) in the trunk of the body or genital area (pudendum) to treat complex regional pain syndrome or other neuropathy. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically with moderate sedation, and after localizing the area to be treated, the provider injects lidocaine to provide local anesthesia. He makes a small skin incision over the area to be treated and, using imaging guidance, inserts a special cryoablation needle down to the nerve. Through the needle he delivers an "ice ball" to destroy (ablate) the nerve. He may or may not follow a freeze–thaw, freeze–thaw protocol. When he is satisfied that the nerve has been destroyed, he removes the needle and closes the small incision. Terminology Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high–frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Neuropathy: Nerve damage resulting in symptoms such as numbness, pain, or weakness. Percutaneous: Through the skin. Plexus: A weblike collection of lymphatic vessels, nerves, or veins. Truncal: Pertaining to the torso, which includes the chest and abdomen. Tips This procedure includes imaging guidance, so do not report that service separately. Read Less

short_description: Real-time spectral analysis of prostate tissue by fluorescence spectroscopy, including imaging guidance (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0443T in conjunction with 55700) (Report 0443T only once per session)
lay_term: While performing a prostate biopsy and under imaging guidance, the provider uses fluorescence spectroscopy, an imaging technology that employs various wavelengths of light, to provide real–time spectral analysis of the prostate to identify potentially cancerous tissue. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized for a needle or punch biopsy of the prostate, the provider uses a special biopsy needle with an integrated optical sensor to expose the prostate tissue to certain wavelengths of light. Substances, such as collagen, in the prostate tissue naturally fluoresce (emit light) as well. Sensors in the biopsy needle detect the absorption and emission of light by the tissue and transmit it to the imaging system, which interprets the results as benign or cancerous tissue. This enables the provider to biopsy the tissue most likely to be cancerous. Tips This is an add–on code and must be reported with a primary procedure. This code can be reported only once per procedure session. Imaging guidance is included in this procedure, so do not report it separately. Read Less

short_description: Initial placement of a drug-eluting ocular insert under one or more eyelids, including fitting, training, and insertion, unilateral or bilateral
lay_term: The provider places a clear, flexible device, somewhat like a contact lens, that contains a drug, such as timolol to treat glaucoma, under one or more eyelids of one or both eyes; the procedure includes fitting, training the patient, and initial insertion. Glaucoma is an eye disorder characterized by increased intraocular pressure, the pressure caused by the fluid inside the eye, the aqueous humor, that helps maintain the shape of the eye. Explanation A drug–eluting ocular insert is a clear, flexible device made of a polymer or plastic material designed to slowly release a drug in measured increments. Although somewhat like a contact lens, the insert is placed under the eyelid on the sclera, not over the cornea. The provider measures the shape and curvature of the patient's eye to fit the insert. He shows the patient how to insert the device and performs the initial insertion. Tips This code is for the initial fitting, training, and insertion of the insert. For a subsequent placement, report 0445T. Read Less

short_description: Creation of subcutaneous pocket with insertion of implantable interstitial glucose sensor, including system activation and patient training Notes: (Do not report 0446T in conjunction with 95251, 0447T, 0448T)
lay_term: The provider creates a pocket beneath the skin, typically in the upper arm of the patient, and places an interstitial glucose sensor in the pocket; he activates the system and trains the patient on its use. Explanation This procedure can usually be performed in the provider's office. The patient may or may not be sedated, i.e., under the influence of a drug that reduces anxiety or apprehension; the level of sedation determines whether the patient is awake and aware or asleep. With the patient appropriately prepped and using local anesthesia, the provider makes an incision in the skin, generally in the patient’s upper arm. He creates a small pocket into which he places the sensor of an interstitial continuous glucose monitoring system and closes the incision. The sensing device uses fluorescence (light–emitting) technology to measure the glucose in interstitial fluid (fluid that surrounds cells in the body). He places a rechargeable device directly over the area. This device powers the implant. The implant wirelessly transmits the glucose levels to the transmitter on top of the skin, and it calculates glucose values other data, which it sends to a smart phone. The transmitter can be taken off and put back on, but it must be in place to get glucose values. Before releasing the patient, the provider trains the patient on how to use the device. The device helps providers and patients predict hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia (high and low glucose levels) continuously throughout the day, thus helping maintain better control of diabetes, a disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs. Terminology Glucose: The main type of sugar in the blood; the major source of energy for the body's cells. Tips To report the removal of the device, use 0447T. For replacement of the entire system, report 0448T. To report placement of a similar system without an implantable sensor that is for temporary use, report 95250. Read Less

short_description: Removal of implantable interstitial glucose sensor with creation of subcutaneous pocket at different anatomic site and insertion of new implantable sensor, including system activation Notes: (Do not report 0448T in conjunction with 0446T, 0447T) (For placement of non-implantable interstitial glucose sensor without pocket, use 95250)
lay_term: The provider removes a previously implanted sensory, and creates a new pocket beneath the skin, perhaps in the opposite upper arm of the patient, and places an interstitial glucose sensor in the pocket; he activates the system and trains the patient on its use. Explanation This procedure can usually be performed in the provider's office. The patient may or may not be sedated, i.e., under the influence of a drug that reduces anxiety or apprehension; the level of sedation determines whether the patient is awake and aware or asleep. With the patient appropriately prepped and using local anesthesia, the provider opens the incision over the previously implanted sensor, removes the sensor and closes the incision. Next, the provider makes an incision in the skin in a new location, possibly on the patient's other arm. He creates a small pocket into which he places the sensor of an interstitial continuous glucose monitoring system and closes the incision. The sensing device uses fluorescence (light–emitting) technology to measure the glucose in interstitial fluid (fluid that surrounds cells in the body). He places a rechargeable device directly over the area. This device powers the implant. The implant wirelessly transmits the glucose levels to the transmitter on top of the skin, and it calculates glucose values other data, which it sends to a smart phone. The transmitter can be taken off and put back on, but it must be in place to get glucose values. Before releasing the patient, the provider trains the patient on how to use the device. The device helps providers and patients predict hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia (high and low glucose levels) continuously throughout the day, thus helping maintain better control of diabetes, a disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs. Terminology Glucose: The main type of sugar in the blood; the major source of energy for the body's cells. Tips To report initial placement of the sensor, activation of the device, and patient training, use 0446T. To report only the removal of the device, use 0447T. To report placement of a similar system without an implantable sensor that is for temporary use, report 95250. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of aqueous drainage device, without extraocular reservoir, internal approach, into the subconjunctival space; initial device
lay_term: The provider inserts the first aqueous drainage device into the interior of the eye with its end in the subconjunctival space; the device does not include a reservoir to hold the fluid. The device drains aqueous fluid from the eye and lowers intraocular pressure in a patient with glaucoma, i.e., increased pressure within the eye from buildup of fluid. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically by topical anesthesia, the provider makes a small fornix–based corneal incision (under the eyelid on the cornea, the clear transparent covering of the front of the eye) or a limbus–based corneal incision (on the cornea near its junction with the sclera, the white of the eye). He places the aqueous drainage device, e.g., a Baerveldt® glaucoma implant or an Ahmed® glaucoma valve, into the interior of the eye so that it drains into the space under the conjunctiva, i.e., the interior lining of the eyelids and external lining of the eyeball. No reservoir is implanted. The provider controls any bleeding and closes the incision in the cornea. Terminology Aqueous humor: Transparent fluid between the cornea and anterior chamber of the eye. Tips Use modifiers LT and RT for left and right eye respectively. For the insertion of each additional device, report 0450T. Read Less

short_description: Retinal polarization scan, ocular screening with on-site automated results, bilateral Notes: (Do not report 0469T in conjunction with 92002, 92004, 92012, 92014) (For optical coherence tomography [OCT] for microstructural and morphological imaging of skin, use 96999) (For ocular photoscreening, see 99174, 99177)
lay_term: Retinal polarization scanning is a type of visual screening test to detect retinal fixation; it is particularly useful for diagnosing strabismus and amblyopia (lazy eye) in patients whose eyes are not suitable for standard fixation testing and in uncooperative patients, such as infants and children. This code includes ocular screening of both eyes and on–site automated results. Explanation Retinal fixation refers to pinpointing the area of most acute vision, which is generally in the fovea centralis, a pit in the center of the retina. Standard testing for retinal fixation is referred to as birefringence, which involves directing polarized light into the eye to the retina and analyzing the reflection. Retinal polarization scanning improves on this technique by directing modulated polarized light through a specific pattern of nerve fibers to identify and define the region on the retina where fixation occurs. This technique avoids interference from corneal birefringence. This code represents scanning of both eyes and incorporates on–site automated (computer–generated) results. Terminology Amblyopia: Decreased vision due to a disconnect between the eye and the brain. Strabismus: A condition in which the eyes are misaligned and point in different directions; one eye may look straight ahead, while the other eye turns inward, outward, upward, or downward. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of anterior segment aqueous drainage device, with creation of intraocular reservoir, internal approach, into the supraciliary space Notes: (For recording of fetal magnetic cardiac signal, data scanning, transfer data, signal extraction, review, and interpretation and report, use 93799)
lay_term: The provider uses an internal approach to place an aqueous drainage device in the anterior segment (between the cornea and the lens) of the eyeball and creates a reservoir in the area of the eye just below the eyebrow (supraciliary space) to drain aqueous fluid from the eye and to lower intraocular pressure in a patient with glaucoma. The provider ensures hemostasis (stoppage of bleeding) during the procedure and places a temporary patch over the eye. Terminology Aqueous humor: Transparent fluid between the cornea and anterior chamber of the eye. Choroid: Vascular connective tissue of the eye between the retina and white portion of the eye. Gonioscopy: Painless examination of the eye to scan between the cornea and iris, which is the colored part of the eye. Intraocular pressure: Pressure of fluid inside the eye. Reservoir: A created space for storage; it may be a replacement for an anatomical cavity like the stomach or an artificial container for storage of medicine or other fluid. Sclera: Outer white layer of the eyeball. Suprachoroidal space: Space between sclera, white portion of the eye, and choroid of the eye. Read Less

short_description: Fractional ablative laser fenestration of burn and traumatic scars for functional improvement; first 100 cm2 or part thereof, or 1% of body surface area of infants and children
lay_term: The provider creates openings or windows (fenestrations) in burns and traumatic scars using a fractional ablative laser technique. Report this code for the first 100 cm2 in adults or 1 percent of body surface area (BSA) in infants and children. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider creates an opening or fenestration in the burn or traumatic scar wound using a fractional ablative laser technique. A fractional ablative laser focuses the light in such a way that it targets a small portion (fraction) of the scar at a time. It is less destructive than standard laser ablation techniques. Once the scar tissue is destroyed, an opening is created to surgically drain off any fluid below the scar or created during the fractional ablation. The provider may submit the specimen to a laboratory for analysis. He checks for bleeding and then closes the wound in a single layer. Use this code to report the first 100 cm2 in adults or 1 percent of body surface area treated in infants and children. Terminology cm2: Abbreviation for square centimeter, a metric unit of measure of area; the 2 is usually superscripted; 1 cm equals approximately 0.39 inches, or just over a third of an inch, so a square centimeter would be 1 cm x 1 cm; alternative sq cm. Tips For each additional 100 cm or 1 percent of BSA, report +0480T in addition to 0479T for the primary procedure. Read Less

lay_term: The provider implants a prosthetic mitral valve, or replaces one, through a catheter that he inserts through a small incision in the skin and which he threads through a vessel to the heart; he may or may not puncture the wall between the ventricle and atrium in order to place the valve. The procedure is performed to treat mitral valve prolapse or malfunction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision through the skin and dissects down to the vessel, such as the femoral artery, selected for access. He inserts a catheter with the prosthetic valve compressed within its lumen and threads the catheter through the vessel to the left ventricle of the heart. If necessary, he punctures the septum (wall) between the two chambers to place the prosthetic valve. He may have to modify (enlarge or make smaller) the existing valve opening to place the implant. He implants the artificial valve between the left ventricle and atrium. The provider then ensures a return to normal heart function in the patient. He withdraws the catheter and applies pressure over the artery to control any bleeding and closes the small incision. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Mitral valve: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, name because its two cusps look like a bishop's hat or a mitered joint in carpentry. Percutaneous: Minimally invasive approach through the skin. Transcatheter: Performed through the interior channel, or lumen, of a catheter. Read Less

short_description: Transcatheter mitral valve implantation/replacement (TMVI) with prosthetic valve; transthoracic exposure (eg, thoracotomy, transapical)
lay_term: Through a transthoracic exposure, the provider inserts a catheter through which he implants, or replaces, a prosthetic mitral valve to treat mitral valve prolapse or malfunction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the chest and exposes an artery, such as the brachial, selected for delivery of the catheter. He then inserts a catheter, and approaches the valve through the apex (top) of the ventricle (transapical approach). He may need to revise the valve opening to make it larger or smaller. He implants an artificial valve between the left ventricle and atrium. The provider ensures a return to normal heart function in the patient, checks for bleeding, and closes the wound after withdrawing the catheter. short_description: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of middle ear, with interpretation and report; unilateral
lay_term: The provider uses optical coherence tomography (OCT) to examine the middle ear. This code is specific to one side, right or left. OCT is a noninvasive imaging technique that uses light waves to process and provide three–dimensional images of tissue. The code includes interpretation and report, so do not report those services separately. Explanation The provider positions the patient on the chair and places the OCT machine at the ear. The patient remains still while the provider uses the scanner to take images of the target anatomy of the middle ear. From these scans, a computer creates images called slices. The images help the provider identify tumors and other anatomic abnormalities as well as foreign bodies. After completing the procedure, he interprets the images and prepares a report. Terminology Auditory ossicles: The three small bones (malleus, incus, and stapes) of the middle ear, which transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window. Middle ear: The space behind the tympanic membrane in the temporal bone that contains the tympanic cavity, auditory ossicles, and auditory tube. Tips For OCT of both middle ears, report 0486T. short_description: Noncontact near-infrared spectroscopy (eg, for measurement of deoxyhemoglobin, oxyhemoglobin, and ratio of tissue oxygenation), other than for screening for peripheral arterial disease, image acquisition, interpretation, and report; first anatomic site Notes: (Do not report 0640T in conjunction with 0860T) Noncontact near-infrared spectroscopy is used to measure cutaneous vascular perfusion. Codes 0640T, 0859T describe noncontact near-infrared spectroscopy for measurement of cutaneous vascular perfusion (other than for screening for peripheral arterial disease) that does not require direct contact of the spectrometer sensors with the patient's skin. Codes 0640T, 0859T may only be reported once, when performing noncontact near-infrared spectroscopy of multiple wounds in one anatomic site (eg, multiple diabetic ulcers involving the plantar surface of the foot). For noncontact near-infrared spectroscopy studies for screening for peripheral arterial disease, use 0860T.
lay_term: The provider examines the target tissue by exposing it to near–infrared light and analyzing the tissue’s absorption and emission of light. The provider acquires images, interprets the results, and completes a report. This code is specific to noncontact studies, meaning the device’s spectrometer sensors do not have direct contact with the skin. Use this code for the first or only anatomic site studied for a reason other than peripheral arterial disease screening. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider uses a device that uses near–infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) to complete a study. The instrument does not require direct contact of sensors with the patient’s skin. NIRS measures cutaneous vascular perfusion, checking blood flow to the skin area tested. The technology uses reflected light to assess perfusion based on color changes. For instance, small color changes occur when hemoglobin is oxygenated (oxyhemoglobin). By comparing the amount of oxygenated to deoxygenated hemoglobin, the provider can assess the percent of oxygenated blood reaching the skin. The level of oxyhemoglobin is indicative of the condition of the tissue. The provider interprets the images and completes a report. This code is specific to the first or only anatomic site studied for a reason other than peripheral arterial disease screening. Terminology Infrared light: An invisible form of light with a wavelength beyond the visible range; light waves invisible to the human eye; also referred to as infrared waves. Spectroscopy: Study of absorption and emission of radiation or light from an object usually reflected by the object. Tips See +0859T for each additional site. For peripheral arterial disease screening, see 0860T. short_description: Surgical preparation and cannulation of marginal (extended) cadaver donor lung(s) to ex vivo organ perfusion system, including decannulation, separation from the perfusion system, and cold preservation of the allograft prior to implantation, when performed
lay_term: This code represents the surgical preparation and preservation of cadaver donor lung(s) including attaching the lung to an organ perfusion system and its removal from the system for implantation. Explanation Marginal organs are organs once considered unsuitable for transplantation due to the length of time the organ was without blood and oxygen circulation. An ex vivo organ perfusion system is a small cardiopulmonary bypass machine that maintains temperature and oxygenation and can supply nutrients and medication to keep marginal donor organs viable while in transit. Report this code when a provider makes the necessary surgical modifications to a cadaver donor lung, including cannulating (inserting a thin tube) to vessels to attach the lung to an organ perfusion system as well as removing the tubes (decannulation) and detaching the lung from the perfusion system. short_description: Endovenous femoral-popliteal arterial revascularization, with transcatheter placement of intravascular stent graft(s) and closure by any method, including percutaneous or open vascular access, ultrasound guidance for vascular access when performed, all catheterization(s) and intraprocedural roadmapping and imaging guidance necessary to complete the intervention, all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, when performed, with crossing of the occlusive lesion in an extraluminal fashion Notes: (0505T includes all ipsilateral selective arterial and venous catheterization, all diagnostic imaging for ipsilateral, lower extremity arteriography, and all related radiological supervision and interpretation) (Do not report 0505T in conjunction with 37224, 37225, 37226, 37227, 37238, 37239, 37248, 37249, within the femoral-popliteal segment) (Do not report 0505T in conjunction with 76937, for ultrasound guidance for vascular access)
lay_term: The provider restores blood flow to the femoral–popliteal arteries by inserting a stent within the femoral–popliteal arterial system via a catheter inserted through a vein, typically via a small puncture over a vein in the groin or open vascular access on the opposite (ipsilateral) side; the procedure includes closure by any method, all imaging including ultrasound guidance and mapping using arteriography during the procedure, and radiological supervision and interpetation (RS&I). This procedure is performed to treat peripheral arterial disease or severe ischemia or claudication in the lower extremities. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under regional or general anesthesia, the provider makes a small incision through the skin or an open incision over a vein in the groin, usually on the opposite side from the occlusion. Using ultrasound guidance, he inserts a guidewire and advances it to and into the femoral–popliteal arteries. He then advances a catheter over the guidewire. He may inject a contrast material to visualize the arteries and map the blood circulation to outline the occlusion. If the obstruction is long or difficult to cross, the provider intentionally creates a subintimal channel in the vessel wall to bypass the occlusion using a specially designed catheter or guidewire. Once he has crossed the occlusion, he inserts a stent graft through the catheter or over the guidewire across the occlusion. He opens and expands the stent to keep the vessel open and maintain blood flow. Finally, he repairs all incisions, checks for bleeding, and concludes the procedure. All imaging guidance, angiography, and associated RS&I, when performed, are included in this procedure. Terminology Arteriography: The provider injects a radiopaque dye into an artery, thereby making the vessel visible under X–ray; he can then diagnose any blockage, obstruction, or pathology within the artery being examined; also known as angiography. Catheterization: Placement of a long, thin, flexible tube (catheter) into a blood vessel, heart, or any other tubular structure in the body. Claudication: Difficulty walking; leg pain, or cramping that occurs during exercise due to poor blood circulation in the extremities. Femoral artery: Main artery in the groin and thigh that provides oxygenated blood to the tissues of the leg. Guidewire: A device to position a catheter, tube, or other device into a tubular structure. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time, X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Intravascular stent: An expandable mesh tube to open a stenosed or narrowed vessel; the provider inserts the deflated stent into the narrowed portion of the vessel and then expands it against the wall of the vessel to open it; once expanded, the stent remains in position to keep the vessel open. Ischemia: Deficient supply of blood to a body part such as the heart or brain due to an obstruction of the inflow of arterial blood due to narrowing of arteries by spasm or disease. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD): A condition of impaired blood circulation in the extremities due to narrowing of the vessels, typically due to the accumulation of plaques (fatty deposits on the vessel walls). Popliteal artery: A continuation of the femoral artery that runs deep in the muscles along the back of the leg. Stent: A thin, plastic or metal tubelike device that is inserted into a tubular structure, such as a vessel or duct, to open or widen a narrowed area or support a weakened part of the structure. short_description: Macular pigment optical density measurement by heterochromatic flicker photometry, unilateral or bilateral, with interpretation and report
lay_term: The provider measures macular pigment optical density (MPOD), or attenuation of blue light, using heterochromic flicker photometry (HFP) to determine the amount of lutein and zeaxanthin in macular pigment in one or both eyes. Lutein and zeaxanthin are thought to play a protective role against age–related macular degeneration and cataract. This code covers the procedure itself as well as interpretation and report. Explanation The provider exposes the macula of one or both eyes to alternating wavelengths of light (e.g., blue light at 460 nm) absorbed by the macular carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin and wavelengths that are not absorbed (e.g., green at 540 nm). The patient experiences these alternating wavelengths of light as a flickering disk or ring. The patient participates in this procedure by adjusting the intensity of the blue light until she no longer sees the flicker. The average intensity of the blue light is recorded at minimal flicker. The stimuli are repeated aimed at a point where the MPOD is thought to be insignificant. A standard formula or equation is used to calculate central MPOD. HFP is a noninvasive procedure but requires both patient and provider training. It is useful in assessing macular degeneration and cataract maturity. The provider interprets the findings and prepares a report. Terminology Attenuation: The reduction in strength, amplitude, or force of something, such as a sound signal or wavelength of light. Macula: A point within the retina or the inner surface of the eye, which is the point of sharpest vision. Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. short_description: Near infrared dual imaging (ie, simultaneous reflective and transilluminated light) of meibomian glands, unilateral or bilateral, with interpretation and report Notes: (For external ocular photography, use 92285) (For tear film imaging, use 0330T) (For pulse-echo ultrasound bone density measurement resulting in indicator of axial bone mineral density, tibia, use 76999)
lay_term: The provider uses a special device called a transilluminator that inverts the eyelid and shines a near–infrared light through the eyelid, and a camera that captures high–resolution images to assess the meibomian glands, sebaceous glands at the edges of the eyelid that secrete an oily substance that prevents evaporation of tears and keeps the surface of the eye from becoming too dry. He assesses one or both eyes, interprets the images, and prepares a report. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepared and topical anesthesia applied to the eye(s), the provider places a transilluminator on the eye, which everts (turns inside out) the eyelid and shines a near–infrared light through the eyelid. Simultaneous reflective light from external sources and the near–infrared light shining through the eyelid allow a camera to capture high–quality, high–definition images that the provider uses to assess the structure of the meibomian glands. The provider performs the procedure on one or both eyes, evaluates and analyzes the images, and prepares a report. Terminology Infrared light: An invisible form of light with a wavelength beyond the visible range; light waves invisible to the human eye; also referred to as infrared waves. Transillumination: Holding an object against light to highlight and examine its details. short_description: Electroretinography (ERG) with interpretation and report, pattern (PERG) Notes: (For full-field ERG, use 92273) (For multifocal ERG, use 92274) Electroretinography (ERG) is used to evaluate function of the retina and optic nerve of the eye, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells. A number of techniques that target different areas of the eye, including full field (flash and flicker) (92273) for a global response of photoreceptors of the retina, multifocal (92274) for photoreceptors in multiple separate locations in the retina, including the macula, and pattern (0509T) for retinal ganglion cells, are used. If the technique used is not specifically named in the code descriptors for 92273, 92274, 0509T, use the unlisted procedure code 92499.
lay_term: The provider performs pattern electroretinography (PERG), an electrophysiologic technology to assess the function of both the retina and macula. The retina is tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation, and the macula is the point of sharpest vision on the retina. The provider also interprets the findings of the PERG and prepares a report. Explanation The test is performed on a patient who has been dark adapted and fitted with a recording contact lens and a reference electrode attached to the patient's forehead. Using a specialized device and software, the provider exposes the retina to a specific pattern of stimuli (visual patterns with optimized contrast and spatial frequencies) similar to those used in visual–evoked potentials; the device records the retinal responses generated by these patterns. The provider uses software to analyze the results and assess the function of the various retinal cell types, including the photoreceptors (rods and cones), inner retinal cells (bipolar and amacrine cells) and the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and the macula. He then prepares a report. ERG is used to help diagnose and manage glaucoma, age–related macular degeneration (AMD), and diabetic edema (swelling due to fluid collection). Terminology Electrophysiologic: Relating to the electrical impulse generation phenomena of cells and tissues. Visual evoked potential (VEP): Electrical signals produced or evoked mainly in the brain's occipital region in response to visual stimuli, such as an alternating checkerboard pattern on a computer screen. Tips The Diopsys® NOVA–ERG Vision Testing System is a proprietary system for use with this procedure. short_description: Insertion of gastrostomy tube, percutaneous, with magnetic gastropexy, under ultrasound guidance, image documentation and report Notes: (Do not report 0647T in conjunction with 76942)
lay_term: The provider inserts a gastrostomy tube (feeding tube) through the skin, using magnets to bring the stomach to the abdominal wall. She uses ultrasound guidance, including documentation and report. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider navigates a catheter, such as a balloon catheter, from the mouth (or nose) to the stomach. She confirms the catheter’s position in the stomach using ultrasound guidance. She uses an external magnet to pull the catheter to the front of the stomach and up to the abdominal wall. Using ultrasound, the provider evaluates the site for the gastrostomy tract. She punctures the abdominal wall, inserting a needle and guidewire into the stomach. The catheter in the stomach snares the guidewire, allowing the provider to pull both the catheter and guidewire toward the mouth. Holding the guidewire taut, she maneuvers the gastrostomy tube over the guidewire to the stomach, pulling the tube partially out through the abdominal wall. A bumper end inside the stomach ensures one end of the gastrostomy tube stays in the stomach. After securing the gastrostomy tube, she removes all instruments and applies sterile dressings. She stores image documentation from the ultrasound and creates a report. The provider may use this treatment for patients suffering from abnormalities of the mouth, esophagus (the tube connecting the throat and stomach), or stomach, or with an impaired mechanism of swallowing. Terminology Abdominal wall: Refers to the muscles covering the abdomen or to the skin, fascia, muscle, and membranes marking the boundaries of the abdominal cavity. Gastrostomy tube (G tube): A tube inserted through a surgically created opening through the skin and into the stomach, typically through a small incision in the abdomen. short_description: Transperineal focal laser ablation of malignant prostate tissue, including transrectal imaging guidance, with MR-fused images or other enhanced ultrasound imaging Notes: (Do not report 0655T in conjunction with 52000, 76376, 76377, 76872, 76940, 76942, 76998)
lay_term: The provider uses laser to ablate (destroy) malignant prostate tissue using a transperineal approach and transrectal imaging guidance. The procedure also includes enhanced ultrasound imaging such as MR–fused images, which combine an MR image of the prostate with the real–time ultrasound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an imaging probe, such as an ultrasound probe, into the rectum, allowing the provider to view the prostate on a screen. The prostate is a small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder. The provider uses enhanced ultrasound imaging for the procedure, such as MR–fused images, which align a magnetic resonance (MR) image of the prostate with real–time ultrasound to improve precision. The provider inserts the laser device through the perineum (the area between the anus and scrotum) and into the prostate lesion. He performs focal laser ablation, which uses heat to destroy cancerous tissue while preserving surrounding healthy tissue. The provider removes the surgical instruments. The provider may use thoracoscopy for the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the lumbar (lower) or thoracolumbar (middle/lower) spine, such as through a small incision in the side. The provider may insert a thoracoscope (thin tube with a camera) for visualization. The provider then revises, replaces, or removes thoracolumbar or lumbar vertebral body tethering, which uses screws and a flexible cable, typically to treat spinal curvature caused by scoliosis. For revision, the provider may address an issue with the initial placement or otherwise change the previously placed tethering and screws. Alternatively, the provider may replace the system, replacing screws at target vertebral levels and/or replacing the strong cord that connects the screws. Or the provider may remove the screws and cord. The provider removes the surgical instruments and closes access sites. short_description: Automated quantification and characterization of coronary atherosclerotic plaque to assess severity of coronary disease, using data from coronary computed tomographic angiography; data preparation and transmission, computerized analysis of data, with review of computerized analysis output to reconcile discordant data, interpretation and report Notes: Automated quantification and characterization of coronary atherosclerotic plaque is a service in which coronary computed tomographic angiography (CTA) data are analyzed using computerized algorithms to assess the extent and severity of coronary artery disease. The computer-generated findings are provided in an interactive format to the physician or other qualified health care professional who performs the final review and report. The coronary CTA is performed and interpreted as a separate service and is not included in the service of automated analysis of coronary CTA.
lay_term: This code represents the complete service of preparing and transmitting quantitative coronary computed tomographic angiography data, the computerized analysis of the data, review of the computerized analysis, and an interpretation and report. The service helps with assessing how severe a patient’s coronary disease is. Explanation Quantitative coronary computed tomographic angiography (CTA) is a noninvasive imaging service that provides quantitative information about a patient’s coronary stenosis. Quantitative refers to data based on quantities (measurable) rather than being subjective. Using the coronary CTA data, specialized software performs automatic quantitative work to provide information such as lesion length, plaque volumes, and plaque type. This data helps with understanding the severity of the patient’s coronary disease, a condition in which the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle become stenosed (narrowed) due to the deposit of plaques (fatty substances) on the inner walls of the blood vessels, resulting in decreased blood flow and ultimately heart failure, if not treated. Use 0623T to report all the components, including coronary CTA data preparation, transmission, and computerized analysis. This code also includes reviewing the computerized analysis to check for and reconcile data that doesn’t match. The provider also must complete an interpretation and report to meet this code’s requirements. Terminology Computed tomography angiography (CTA): An imaging procedure in which dye is injected during computed tomography (CT) scanning, to produce images of the blood vessels. Tips Code 0623T is appropriate to report all of the components involved in automated quantification and characterization of coronary atherosclerotic plaque using coronary CTA data. If you are reporting less than the complete service, see 0624T, 0625T, and 0626T, which represent the individual components. short_description: Automated quantification and characterization of coronary atherosclerotic plaque to assess severity of coronary disease, using data from coronary computed tomographic angiography; review of computerized analysis output to reconcile discordant data, interpretation and report Notes: (Use 0623T, 0624T, 0625T, 0626T one time per coronary computed tomographic angiogram) (Do not report 0623T in conjunction with 0624T, 0625T, 0626T) (Do not report 0623T, 0624T, 0625T, 0626T in conjunction with 76376, 76377) (For noninvasive estimate of coronary fractional flow reserve [FFR] derived from augmentative software analysis of the data set from a coronary computed tomography angiography, with interpretation and report by a physician or other qualified health care professional, use 75580)
lay_term: This code represents the work involved in reviewing computerized analysis of data from coronary computed tomographic angiography, reconciling discordant data, and completing an interpretation and report. The service helps with assessing how severe a patient’s coronary disease is. Explanation Quantitative coronary computed tomographic angiography (CTA) is a noninvasive imaging service that provides quantitative information about a patient’s coronary stenosis. Quantitative refers to data based on quantities (measurable) rather than being subjective. Using the coronary CTA data, specialized software performs automatic quantitative work to provide information such as lesion length, plaque volumes, and plaque type. This data helps with understanding the severity of the patient’s coronary disease, a condition in which the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle become stenosed (narrowed) due to the deposit of plaques (fatty substances) on the inner walls of the blood vessels, resulting in decreased blood flow and ultimately heart failure, if not treated. Use 0626T to report only the work involved in reviewing computerized analysis of data from coronary computed tomographic angiography, reconciling discordant data, and completing an interpretation and report. Terminology Computed tomography angiography (CTA): An imaging procedure in which dye is injected during computed tomography (CT) scanning, to produce images of the blood vessels. If you are reporting less than the complete service, see 0624T, 0625T, and 0626T, which represent the individual components. short_description: Intraprocedural coronary fractional flow reserve (FFR) with 3D functional mapping of color-coded FFR values for the coronary tree, derived from coronary angiogram data, for real-time review and interpretation of possible atherosclerotic stenosis(es) intervention (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0523T in conjunction with 93454, 93455, 93456, 93457, 93458, 93459, 93460, 93461) (Do not report 0523T more than once per session) (Do not report 0523T in conjunction with 75580, 76376, 76377, 93571, 93572)
lay_term: The provider reviews and interprets, in real time during ta cardiac catheterization procedure, the results of an imaging procedure that maps the blood flow in the coronary arteries using 3D color mapping to determine whether intervention is needed for coronary stenosis. Explanation During the performance of a cardiac catheterization procedure and after obtaining an angiogram, the provider enters the patient’s mean aortic pressure and possibly other hemodynamic data into a computer displaying the angiographic data. The computer uses proprietary software/algorithm to generate a complete three–dimensional (3D) coronary tree of the left or right coronary system. The computer then scans the entire 3D tree and examines each branch and bifurcation for narrowing of the arterial lumen. The FFR values at each point along the vessels are color–coded and superimposed on the 3D model. FFR angiography does not use a pressure guidewire or pharmacologic (drug–induced) hyperemia (increased blood flow). Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Atherosclerosis: Buildup of plaque (fatty deposits) on the walls of an artery; hardening and thickening the artery walls, which can lead to coronary artery disease; sometimes used interchangeably with arteriosclerosis (thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries). Cardiac catheterization: The insertion of a catheter (tube) into a major vessel in the groin or another location, and advanced to the heart to perform diagnostic tests, such as dye studies and therapeutic procedures. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubelike cavity, or the interior of a catheter or tube. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure, such as an artery, valve, the colon, or ear canal. Read Less

short_description: Electrical impedance spectroscopy of 1 or more skin lesions for automated melanoma risk score
lay_term: The provider examines one or more skin lesions by applying an electrical signal through the lesion(s) using different frequencies and depths. The device uses an algorithm to classify the lesion and calculate a melanoma risk score based on the data. Explanation The provider positions the patient, prepares the lesion site(s), and sets up the device to perform electrical impedance spectroscopy, which is a measure of resistance in tissue at alternating currents of different frequencies. Electrical properties of skin vary under different medical conditions. The provider typically performs a reference measurement of healthy skin near the lesion first and then repeats the process on the lesion suspected of being melanoma, a potentially deadly form of skin cancer. The process involves using a probe with an electrode system to apply an electrical signal through the target site. The provider performs the measurement at multiple frequencies and depth settings, covering the lesion in width and depth. The device uses an algorithm to classify the lesion using the data from the reference measurement and the lesion measurement. The device provides a score reflecting the lesion’s risk of melanoma by showing the degree to which the lesion differs from normal. The provider uses visual inspection and the score to inform clinical decision–making. The provider may repeat the process on one or more lesions. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Melanoma: A deadly form of cancer, primarily of the skin, but it can affect other organs that contain melanocytes, cells that produce the pigment melanin. Spectroscopy: Study of absorption and emission of radiation or light from an object usually reflected by the object. short_description: Implantation of anterior segment intraocular nonbiodegradable drug-eluting system, internal approach Notes: (Report medication separately)
lay_term: The provider inserts an implant into the eye that delivers a drug at a controlled rate into the anterior segment (front–most region of the eye) to treat a condition such as glaucoma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision and examines the anterior chamber angle using an ab interno (from inside the eye) approach. The anterior chamber angle is part of the eye between the cornea (clear outer layer of the eye) and iris (colored part of the eye), and it contains the trabecular meshwork, which is translucent tissue at the base of the cornea that filters the thick, watery substance called aqueous humor that flows out of the eye. The provider implants the drug–eluting system, possibly in the trabecular meshwork. The drug–eluting system may include an anchor, a drug reservoir, and a membrane to allow controlled release of the drug. The provider removes the tools used for implantation and completes the procedure. Terminology Aqueous humor: Thick watery substance that fills the space between the lens and the cornea; also known as aqueous fluid. Glaucoma: Eye disorder characterized by increased intraocular pressure, the pressure caused by the fluid inside the eye, the aqueous humor, that helps maintain the shape of the eye. Tips See 0661T for removal and reimplantation. short_description: Scalp cooling, mechanical; initial measurement and calibration of cap Notes: (Report 0662T once per chemotherapy treatment period)
lay_term: The provider takes patient measurements and calibrates the cooling cap to ensure proper fit and function for the patient, who will wear the cap during future chemotherapy sessions. The intent of cooling is to reduce hair loss. Explanation The provider follows the instructions from the scalp cooling system manufacturer to get the necessary measurements of the patient’s head to ensure the best fit of the scalp cooling cap. In some systems, selecting the correct cap size involves the patient trying on the different cap sizes available. The goal is to have a snug fit with consistent contact across the entire scalp. The purpose of the cooling is to reduce hair loss in a patient undergoing chemotherapy. The system may have one cap or it may have a cooling cap or wrap that fits close to the head as well as a cap to wear over that to offer insulation and improve scalp contact. Tips See +0663T for placement, monitoring, and removal of the device in conjunction with a chemotherapy session. short_description: Donor hysterectomy (including cold preservation); open, from cadaver donor
lay_term: The provider harvests a uterus from a deceased donor and preserves the uterus on ice and in cold preservation solution for transplantation into the recipient. Explanation When the brain–dead or cadaver donor is appropriately prepped, the provider makes an incision to access the uterus. The provider grasps the top of the uterus with a clamp and enters the retroperitoneal space. He excises the uterus and anatomic structures required for transplant, such as the cervix, part of the vagina, blood vessels, vascular pedicles (tissue containing vessels), and bladder peritoneum (membrane lining the abdominal cavity). The provider may close the incision. He flushes the acquired uterine graft with a preservative solution and stores it in a sealable container on ice for transplantation. Terminology Uterus (womb): The part of the female reproductive system where the fertilized egg is implanted and that nourishes the developing fetus; the uterus is a hollow, muscular, pear–shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part (the isthmus) and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips See 0664T–0670T for uterus transplantation services. short_description: Endovaginal cryogen-cooled, monopolar radiofrequency remodeling of the tissues surrounding the female bladder neck and proximal urethra for urinary incontinence
lay_term: The provider inserts a small probe into the vagina. The probe emits cryogen cooling and radiofrequency waves that heat tissue. The goal is to stimulate production of collagen, the tissue’s structural proteins, to treat urinary incontinence (unintentional passing of urine). Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider inserts the probe of a cryogen–cooled, monopolar radiofrequency (CMRF) energy delivery system into the patient’s vagina. The provider uses the probe to deliver several energy pulses to multiple locations in the vagina. The controlled cooling protects the vaginal mucosal surface and allows the radiofrequency energy to reach deeper into the lamina propria (connective tissue in mucosa) to reach the muscularis (outermost layer of mucosa). The intent is to activate fibroblasts, the cells that make the structural protein collagen, to make new collagen and improve the structural integrity of the tissues around the bladder neck and proximal urethra. The bladder neck is a muscular area where the bladder connects to the urethra, the tube that connects the bladder to the outside of the body. Bladder neck muscles contract to hold urine in the bladder and relax to let urine into the urethra. The goal of the procedure is to treat urinary incontinence (unintentional passing of urine). After delivering the pulses, the provider removes the probe. Terminology Incontinence: Lack of control; as in inability to control urine or feces. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. Radiofrequency (RF): Electrical current from a radio wave (a type of electromagnetic wave) used to transmit signals. short_description: Ablation, benign thyroid nodule(s), percutaneous, laser, including imaging guidance Notes: (Do not report 0673T in conjunction with 76940, 76942, 77013, 77022)
lay_term: The provider ablates (destroys) one or more benign thyroid nodules using a laser. The approach is percutaneous (through the skin). The code includes imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses imaging guidance to assist with insertion of one or more needles through the skin and into the benign thyroid nodule. The provider may ablate one or more benign thyroid nodules during the session. When ablation is complete, the provider removes the needle(s) and completes the procedure. Terminology Benign neoplasm: An abnormal mass of cells that lacks the ability to penetrate the nearby tissues. Laser ablation or resection: Using heat produced by an adjustable focused light energy to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue. Nodule: A small swelling or aggregation of cells in the body, commonly abnormal. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Tips This code includes imaging guidance, so you should not report that service separately. short_description: Laparoscopic insertion of new or replacement of permanent implantable synchronized diaphragmatic stimulation system for augmentation of cardiac function, including an implantable pulse generator and diaphragmatic lead(s) Notes: (Do not report 0674T in conjunction with 0675T, 0676T, 0677T, 0678T, 0679T, 0680T, 0681T, 0682T, 0683T, 0684T, 0685T)
lay_term: The provider uses a laparoscopic approach to insert or replace a synchronized diaphragmatic stimulation system, including one or more leads and a pulse generator. The system is intended to help cardiac function in patients with heart failure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes one or more small incisions to insert a laparoscope, a tubular surgical instrument used to view the interior of the abdomen. The provider uses a laparoscopic implant tool to insert one or more leads on the underside of the diaphragm, the flat muscular membrane that separates the lungs from the stomach area. If this is a replacement procedure, the provider may remove the previously placed leads. After placing the lead(s), the provider removes the laparoscope. The provider makes an incision in the abdomen and creates a small pocket under the skin. They place the system’s pulse generator in the pocket, connect the lead or leads to the generator, and close the pocket. The implanting provider also may perform interrogation and programming of the device as part of this procedure. The device, an implantable synchronized diaphragmatic stimulation system, uses small shocks from the lead electrodes to stimulate the diaphragm below the heart. The stimulation is synchronized with the cardiac cycle (the events from the beginning of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next) and changes the pressures in the chest cavity with the goal of allowing better filling and emptying of the heart in patients with heart failure. Terminology Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Laparoscopic approach or procedure: A surgical procedure in which the provider views and accesses the abdominal and/or pelvic contents with a laparoscope (a tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera) to examine the interior structures of a body cavity; usually, several incisions are made, one for the laparoscope and additional incisions for surgical instruments. Tips See 0674T–0685T for services related to an implantable synchronized diaphragmatic stimulation system that augments cardiac function. lay_term: The provider performs in–person programming device evaluation of a synchronized diaphragmatic stimulation system, making repeated adjustments to find the optimal programmed settings. short_description: Histotripsy (ie, non-thermal ablation via acoustic energy delivery) of malignant hepatocellular tissue, including image guidance
lay_term: The provider uses a special device to deliver ultrasound energy into the body to destroy cancerous liver tissue. The provider monitors the treatment using image guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider uses a special device that delivers pulsed ultrasound energy to destroy malignant hepatocellular tissue (cancerous liver tissue). In a typical procedure, the treatment does not require incisions or needles. The provider uses a special device to deliver ultrasound pulses in the targeted cancerous liver tissue to determine the energy required to create microbubbles from gases present in the targeted tissue. When the bubble clouds form and collapse, they destroy cells and tissues. After determining the energy requirement, the provider initiates treatment, and the system moves the microbubbles through the planned area to destroy the cancerous liver tissue. The provider uses imaging guidance to monitor the treatment in real–time. Terminology Liver: Largest internal organ of the body, it helps in metabolism, production, and storage of various substances. Ultrasound: High–frequency sound waves; may be used to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions, or may be used for therapeutic purposes. Tips Code 0686T includes imaging guidance, so do not report that service using a separate code. short_description: Treatment of amblyopia using an online digital program; device supply, educational set-up, and initial session
lay_term: The provider performs initial services for an online digital amblyopia (lazy eye) treatment program, including device supply, education, and the first session. Explanation The provider supplies the patient with a device specially designed for online digital amblyopia treatment. Amblyopia, also called lazy eye, can result in decreased vision because the brain favors one eye over the other. lay_term: The provider uses ultrasound imaging data and software to analyze tissue quantitatively, and then provides an interpretation and report. Explanation The provider uses specialized software to evaluate ultrasound images for quantitative tissue characterization. Ultrasound refers to high–frequency sound waves that can be used to view internal tissues. A quantitative measurement measures quantity. This is an objective assessment as opposed to a subjective evaluation based on the provider’s visual inspection. For instance, the software may divide the image into areas of 3x3 pixels and assign numerical values to each area to indicate its lightness and darkness relative to the other areas in the image. Depending on the structure, healthy tissue may appear darker while bright speckles may indicate the tissue is not healthy. The service is non–elastographic; elastography helps determine the stiffness of structures in the body. The provider interprets the data and prepares a report. This code is appropriate when there is not a diagnostic ultrasound of the same area (such as organ, gland, tissue, or target structure) at the same session. lay_term: Automated analysis of an existing computed tomography (CT) dataset checks for vertebral fractures. The analysis also may assess bone density. The code includes data preparation, interpretation, and report. Explanation The provider prepares previously acquired computed tomography (CT) data for automated analysis to detect one or more vertebral fractures. Vertebrae are the interlocking bones that form the spine. The service involves analysis by an assistive augmented intelligence (AI) system, meaning that artificial intelligence technology assists and enhances human intelligence. The automated analysis may check for bone mineral density (BMD), but this is not required. BMD refers to the amount of minerals, like calcium, in the bones. Low BMD is connected to diagnoses such as osteoporosis, a thinning of the bones with reduction in bone mass that may increase the risk of fracture. The provider interprets the data and provides a report. Terminology Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of cross–sectional two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. lay_term: The provider uses an ultrafiltration machine to remove excess fluid from a patient, such as a patient with heart failure. Explanation The provider inserts a tube (cannula or catheter) in the patient’s blood vessel. Blood travels through the tube to the ultrafiltration machine, which passes the blood through a special filter to remove excess water and components such as salt. The blood then returns to the patient, possibly by separate venous access. After the therapy is complete, the provider removes the tube or tubes from the patient. The provider may perform this therapy on patients with heart failure whose bodies retain fluid because the heart cannot pump normal amounts of blood. Excess fluid can lead to issues such as swelling and difficulty breathing. Terminology Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, inserted into the body to deliver or drain fluids or supply oxygen and through which instruments and monitoring devices can be inserted. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. short_description: Comprehensive full body computer-based markerless 3D kinematic and kinetic motion analysis and report
lay_term: The provider uses cameras and analytical software to collect and quantify full–body human kinematics and kinetics, which relate to motion. The system does not use markers placed on the patient’s body. The system collects, quantifies, and documents information during patient movement. short_description: Body surface-activation mapping of pacemaker or pacing cardioverter-defibrillator lead(s) to optimize electrical synchrony, cardiac resynchronization therapy device, including connection, recording, disconnection, review, and report; at time of implant or replacement Notes: (Use 0695T in conjunction with 33224, 33225, 33226)
lay_term: The provider uses body surface–activation mapping, such as by multiple–lead electrocardiography, to optimize electrical synchrony of a biventricular pacing or biventricular pacing–defibrillator system at the time of implant or replacement. The goal is to restore electrical synchrony in dyssynchronous heart ventricles, which pump out of sync because of erratic electrical impulses. Explanation At the time of implanting a cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) device, which may be a biventricular pacing or biventricular pacing–defibrillator system, the provider uses body surface–activation mapping (BSAM) to optimize electrical synchrony. CRT aims to restore electrical synchrony in dyssynchronous heart ventricles, which pump out of sync because of erratic electrical impulses. For BSAM, the provider may place multiple leads on the body that then record electrocardiogram data. BSAM generates a visual representation related to electrical impulses in the heart. The provider disconnects the BSAM device, reviews the data, and uses that data with the CRT device to improve electrical synchrony. The provider completes a report as part of the service. Terminology Biventricular pacing: Contraction of both the ventricles in synchronization and together that improves the symptoms of heart failure. Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Pacing cardioverter defibrillator: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate the abnormal or fast rhythm of the heart when needed. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips Report 0695T along with the appropriate code for device insertion or replacement, such as 33224–33226. See 0696T for the same service during a follow–up interrogation or programming device evaluation. short_description: Injection, posterior chamber of eye, medication Notes: The anterior segment of the eye includes the cornea, lens, iris, and aqueous. The aqueous is divided into anterior and posterior chambers. The anterior chamber is by far the larger, including all of the aqueous in front of the lens and iris and behind the cornea. The posterior chamber includes the narrow area behind the iris and in front of the peripheral portion of the lens and lens zonules.
lay_term: The provider injects medication in the posterior chamber of the eye, typically for therapeutic purposes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle into the eye. They gently inject a medication in the posterior chamber of the eye. The posterior chamber is located between the iris (the colored part of the eye) and the lens. The provider then removes the needle. short_description: Molecular fluorescent imaging of suspicious nevus; first lesion
lay_term: The provider uses a fluorescent dye, special imaging device, and analysis software to assess a suspicious mole for tissue changes and cell abnormalities. This code applies to the first lesion. Explanation The provider applies a fluorescent peptide (strings of amino acids) dye that binds to biomarker protein–receptors in the mole (nevus) and surrounding area. A biomarker is a measurable substance that can indicate an abnormal process. The provider uses the imager to excite the dye and capture fluorescence to mark tissue undergoing changes from benign to abnormal. Analysis software may use the data and mole characteristics, like size, shape, and color, to assess likelihood that the tissue is undergoing changes. This code applies to the first lesion. This code applies to each additional lesion after the first. Explanation The provider applies a fluorescent peptide (strings of amino acids) dye that binds to biomarker protein–receptors in the mole (nevus) and surrounding area. A biomarker is a measurable substance that can indicate an abnormal process. The provider uses the imager to excite the dye and capture fluorescence to mark tissue undergoing changes from benign to abnormal. Analysis software may use the data and mole characteristics, like size, shape, and color, to assess likelihood that the tissue is undergoing changes. This code applies to each additional lesion after the first. Tips Because this code is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you unless you report it with an appropriate primary code. See 0700T for the first lesion. short_description: Remote treatment of amblyopia using an eye tracking device; device supply with initial set-up and patient education on use of equipment
lay_term: The provider performs initial services for a remote amblyopia (lazy eye) treatment program that uses an eye–tracking device. The service includes device supply, initial setup, and patient education. Explanation The provider performs initial services related to remote amblyopia treatment. Amblyopia, also called lazy eye, can result in decreased vision because the brain favors one eye over the other. The treatment system includes an eye–tracking device that can transmit data to a surveillance center. The provider performs setup so the system is ready for the patient and supplies the device to the patient. The provider also educates the patient, and possibly caregivers, so they understand how to use the system. Tips Codes 0704T–0706T represent different aspects of remote amblyopia treatment services. short_description: Intradermal cancer immunotherapy; preparation and initial injection
lay_term: The provider prepares the cancer immunotherapy and performs an initial intradermal injection. Explanation The provider assembles the equipment and prepares the immunotherapy for injection. Cancer immunotherapy is a type of treatment that helps the immune system fight cancer. The provider selects the area on the skin for injection and cleanses the area. The provider places the needle almost flat against the patient’s skin and inserts the needle within the skin layers (intradermal). The provider slowly injects the immunotherapy solution and then withdraws the needle. This code is specific to preparation and initial injection. Tips See +0709T for each additional injection.
