short_description: Insertion of wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing, including device interrogation and programming, and imaging supervision and interpretation, when performed; complete system (includes electrode and generator [transmitter and battery])
lay_term: The provider places a generator (battery) and a transmitter for a wireless cardiac stimulator in separate subcutaneous pockets and connects them with a cable through a subcutaneous tunnel; he also inserts a wireless electrode into the left ventricle after which tests the system and adjusts the programming. Imaging supervision and interpretation, if performed, are included in this code. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the midaxillary line and dissects subcutaneous tissue to create a pocket into which he places the generator battery and secures the battery in place. He then makes an incision in the chest wall, typically between the 4th and 6th intercostal spaces lateral to the left edge of the sternum and creates a pocket for the transmitter. The transmitter must be located so that there is no bone or lung between it and the electrode in the left ventricle in order for there to be a clear acoustic window for the ultrasound pulses that will stimulate the electrode. To ensure an acoustic line of sight, he cuts down to the intercostal muscle and inserts an ultrasound probe in a sterile sleeve. He secures an accessory in place and then places the transmitter in the accessory and secures it. Next, he creates a subcutaneous tunnel between the two pockets, inserts a 30 cm cable through the tunnels and attaches an end to the battery and the other end to the transmitter. He closes the incisions over the battery and transmitter. Next, the provider administers heparin to prevent blood clots. Under fluoroscopic guidance, he makes a small incision over the femoral vein and advances a delivery sheath retrograde to the LV through which he inserts a delivery catheter preloaded with the wireless electrode to within about 5 to 10 mm of the tip of the delivery sheath. He connects the cathode of the electrode through the delivery catheter so that he can monitor the signals and test electrical pacing thresholds. Now, he advances the electrode to the tip of the delivery sheath and tests multiple pacing sites before anchoring the electrode in the inside wall of the left ventricle. He places a proprietary programming device over the chest and tests and programs the wireless pacing electrode. He withdraws the delivery catheter and sheath and closes the small incision. Note: To synchronize biventricular pacing, a separate standard pacemaker, transvenous defibrillator, or other cardiac resynchronization therapy device is required. Sensing electrodes placed on the skin over the transmitter and battery pockets detect right ventricular (RV) pacing pulses from the separately implanted device. On sensing the RV pacing output, the transmitter triggers an ultrasound pulse that is received by the wireless cardiac stimulator electrode and converted to electrical energy for near–simultaneous pacing of the LV. Terminology Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Intercostal space: Space between two ribs. Midaxillary line: An imaginary line down the side of the thoracic that serves as a landmark; it is the midpoint between the anterior and posterior (front and back) axillary lines that originate on either side of the axilla (armpit). Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. lay_term: The provider inserts a pulse generator battery and transmitter for a wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing. The system provides pacing for the heart. The provider may use imaging guidance for the procedure and perform device interrogation and programming. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision and dissects tissue to create a subcutaneous pocket in the chest wall. The provider places the pulse generator battery for a wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing. The provider secures the battery in place. The provider makes a separate incision in the chest wall and creates a subcutaneous pocket for a transmitter. The provider creates a subcutaneous tunnel between the two pockets, inserts a cable through the tunnel, and attaches one end to the battery and the other end to the transmitter. The provider also may perform device interrogation and programming to ensure the device is working and has proper settings for the patient. The provider closes the incisions over the battery and transmitter. Terminology Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips CPT® provides several codes related to wireless cardiac stimulators for left ventricular pacing. Review code descriptors carefully to ensure you have the correct code for your service. A wireless cardiac stimulator system for left ventricular pacing has a wireless electrode implanted in the lining of the left ventricle and a pulse generator consisting of a transmitter and battery. The system senses right ventricular pacing from a previously implanted conventional pacemaker or defibrillator and sends an ultrasound pulse to the wireless left ventricular electrode. The electrode emits a left ventricular pacing pulse. short_description: Relocation of pulse generator for wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing, including device interrogation and programming; transmitter component only Notes: (Do not report 0863T in conjunction with 0515T, 0517T, 0518T, 0519T, 0520T, 0521T, 0522T, 0861T)
lay_term: The provider relocates a pulse generator transmitter for a wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing. The system provides pacing for the heart. The provider also performs device interrogation and programming. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to open a previously created subcutaneous pocket in the chest wall. The provider removes the pulse generator transmitter for a wireless cardiac stimulator for left ventricular pacing, disconnecting the transmitter from the cable connecting the battery to the transmitter if necessary. The provider creates a new subcutaneous pocket and relocates the transmitter there. The provider secures the transmitter in place. If needed, the provider creates a subcutaneous tunnel between the pockets for the battery and transmitter components of the pulse generator, inserts a cable through the tunnel, and attaches one end to the battery and the other end to the transmitter. The provider also performs device interrogation and programming to ensure the device is working and has proper settings for the patient. The provider closes the incisions. Terminology Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Subcutaneous pocket: Pocket made up within the subcutaneous (just beneath the skin) tissue. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips CPT® provides several codes related to wireless cardiac stimulators for left ventricular pacing. Review code descriptors carefully to ensure you have the correct code for your service. Base code choice on factors such as components involved (electrode, transmitter, battery) and service provided (insertion, removal, removal and replacement, relocation, device interrogation, programming). A wireless cardiac stimulator system for left ventricular pacing has a wireless electrode implanted in the lining of the left ventricle and a pulse generator consisting of a transmitter and battery. The system senses right ventricular pacing from a previously implanted conventional pacemaker or defibrillator and sends an ultrasound pulse to the wireless left ventricular electrode. The electrode emits a left ventricular pacing pulse. lay_term: The provider inserts a catheter into a varicose vein after isolating the area to be treated with a balloon and uses a liquid or foam chemical to ablate the varicose portion of the vein under imaging guidance. short_description: Removal of intracardiac ischemia monitoring system, including all imaging supervision and interpretation; complete system (electrode and implantable monitor)
lay_term: The provider withdraws the electrode and removes the monitoring component of an intracardiac ischemia monitoring system under imaging guidance. This code covers all imaging supervision and interpretation. Explanation Techniques for lead removal vary based various factors such as the patient’s condition, the condition of the previously placed electrode, and the personal preferences of the provider. Leads are designed to be permanent, but may need to be removed because of infection, breakage, or (rarely) malfunction. Depending on how long the lead has been in place, removal could be a high–risk procedure due to migration of the lead. Scar tissue may cause the lead to be firmly attached to the blood vessel or chamber wall anywhere along the route. Leads may break before or during removal. The lead tip may have become imbedded in the ventricular wall requiring specialized tools to remove it. The vessel wall may be punctured during removal. Prophylactic antibiotics are generally given prior to the procedure. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, the provider typically removes the monitor first. He incises the skin over the subcutaneous pocket where the monitor was placed, cuts through any sutures securing the monitor, and removes it. He irrigates the pocket with antimicrobial solution and closes the pocket in layers. Then, he turns his attention to removing the lead. He may employ a number of different tools to remove the lead. Under imaging guidance, he may insert a thin wire called a stylet through a channel in the lead and advance it to the end and just beyond the lead tip where a hook can be attached to the tip. Using twisting and traction, he pulls the lead out. Alternatively, he may advance a catheter sheath over the lead and advance it to the tip. The catheter will have some means by which the provider grasps the tip and, again, using twisting and traction, he pulls out the catheter sheath with the lead. Some sheaths, called power sheaths, actually have an energy source such as a laser or electrocautery at their tip, that can help cut through scarred tissue, making it easier to free up the lead and remove it with less traction. Such a device may be used if the lead has been in place for an extended period of time. Once the lead has been extracted, the provider uses real–time imaging guidance to assess for bleeding or clots. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Ischemia: Deficient supply of blood to a body part such as the heart or brain due to an obstruction of the inflow of arterial blood due to narrowing of arteries by spasm or disease. Read Less

Explanation Techniques for lead removal vary based various factors such as the patient’s condition, the condition of the previously placed electrode, and the personal preferences of the provider. Leads are designed to be permanent, but may need to be removed because of infection, breakage, or (rarely) malfunction. Depending on how long the lead has been in place, removal could be a high–risk procedure due to migration of the lead. Scar tissue may cause the lead to be firmly attached to the blood vessel or chamber wall anywhere along the route. Leads may break before or during removal. The lead tip may have become imbedded in the ventricular wall requiring specialized tools to remove it. The vessel wall may be punctured during removal. Prophylactic antibiotics are generally given prior to the procedure. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, the provider may employ a number of different tools to remove the lead. Under imaging guidance, he may insert a thin wire called a stylet through a channel in the lead and advance it to the end and just beyond the lead tip where a hook can be attached to the tip. Using twisting and traction, he pulls the lead out. Alternatively, he may advance a catheter sheath over the lead and advance it to the tip. The catheter will have some means by which the provider grasps the tip and, again, using twisting and traction, he pulls out the catheter sheath with the lead. Some sheaths, called power sheaths, actually have an energy source such as a laser or electrocautery at their tip, that can help cut through scarred tissue, making it easier to free up the lead and remove it with less traction. Such a device may be used if the lead has been in place for an extended period of time. Once the lead has been extracted, the provider uses real–time imaging guidance to assess for bleeding or clots. Terminology Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits or treats bacterial infections. Antimicrobial agent: Substance that repels or destroys microorganisms. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Ischemia: Deficient supply of blood to a body part such as the heart or brain due to an obstruction of the inflow of arterial blood due to narrowing of arteries by spasm or disease. Read Less

short_description: Myocardial imaging by magnetocardiography (MCG) for detection of cardiac ischemia, by signal acquisition using minimum 36 channel grid, generation of magnetic-field time-series images, quantitative analysis of magnetic dipoles, machine learning-derived clinical scoring, and automated report generation, single study
lay_term: The provider uses multichannel magnetocardiography (MCG) imaging to detect cardiac ischemia in a patient who reports with chest pain. The MCG has a minimum of 36 channels and generates magnetic–field, time–series images, performs quantitative (numerical) analysis of magnetic dipoles, provides a clinical score, and generates an automatic report. Report this code for a single study. Explanation The provider performs a 36–channel MCG. For routine studies, the patient may be exercised to reach a certain target heart rate. For patient’s presenting with chest pain, exercise would not be performed. The patient lies supine on a table with the sensor positioned as close as possible to the chest directly over the heart. The sensor was located as close to the thorax as possible, directly over the heart. The provider carries out magnetic field registration generating magnetic–field time–series images in a total of 36 positions with a 6 × 6 rectangle grid. Data were recorded every 30 seconds. The procedure generally takes no more than a total of six minutes. The signals were then processed and analyzed by a computer using proprietary software. Positive and negative magnetic poles were quantified (counted) and analyzed and a computer learning–derived clinical score and automated report generated. The raw data are stored for further review, analysis, and interpretation by the provider. Like electrocardiograms (ECGs), MCG can recognize P, QRS, and T waves. Unlike ECGs, MCG has minimal signal distortion, magnetic field conductivity is not affected by body composition, there is no electrode skin interference, and MCG requires no direct–current filtering. It records magnetic fields directly from primary cardiac current so can evaluate the absolute value of the heart current. Newer systems, such as the 36–channel MCG do not require shielded rooms. MCG is especially useful in monitoring the fetal heart for bradycardia, tachycardia, Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, long QT syndrome, and enlarged heart. It is more sensitive than ECG in detecting coronary stenosis and can detect HIS bundle potential and partial atrial standstill. Terminology Atrial: Referring to one of the two upper chambers of the heart. Bradycardia: Slow, or lower than normal, heart rate. Bundle of His: The bundle of cardiac muscle fibers that conducts the electrical impulses that regulate the heartbeat; also known as atrioventricular bundle or AV bundle. Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Ischemia: Deficient supply of blood to a body part such as the heart or brain due to an obstruction of the inflow of arterial blood due to narrowing of arteries by spasm or disease. Long QT syndrome: A heart rhythm irregularity characterized by fast chaotic heartbeats. Stenosis: Narrowing in a tubular or hollow structure, such as an artery, valve, the colon, or ear canal. Supine position: Lying on the back with legs extended. Tachycardia: Rapid or increased heartbeat. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome: A heart rhythm problem in which an extra electrical pathway in the heart causes episodes of a fast heart rate. Read Less

short_description: Transapical mitral valve repair, including transthoracic echocardiography, when performed, with placement of artificial chordae tendineae Notes: (For transesophageal echocardiography image guidance, use 93355)
lay_term: The provider approaches the valve between the left upper chamber and left lower pumping chamber of the heart (mitral valve) through the top (apex) of the left ventricle and places artificial fibrous bands (chordae tendineae) to hold the valve in place to prevent prolapse and treat mitral valve regurgitation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepared and anesthetized, the provider makes a small, 5 cm thoracotomy incision in the patient’s chest over the left ventricle. This procedure is performed on a beating heart, and the patient is not placed on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), although standby CPB procedures may be in place. The provider makes a small incision in the apex of the left ventricle and under echocardiographic guidance inserts a specialized grasping mechanism with a fiberoptic monitor and needle system through the incision. He advances the instrumentation across the mitral valve and into the left atrium in the chordal free zone. He grasps the free edge of the mitral valve leaflet, pierces it with the needle, and attaches one or more e–PTFE Gore–Tex® sutures to the leaflet. The other ends of the sutures are brought back and tied to the papillary muscles in the left ventricular apex after tension is adjusted to reduce mitral regurgitation. He removes the instrument, closes the incision in the ventricle, inserts a pleural drain, and closes the chest incision in layers. Terminology Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, and the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; "on pump" means the provider performed CPB. Chordae tendineae (tendinous cords): Cords or strings of fibrous connective tissue connecting the tricuspid valve and the bicuspid, or mitral, valve to the papillary muscles of the heart; also called heart strings because of their resemblance to strings. Echocardiogram (Echo): The use of high–frequency sound waves or sonography (ultrasound) to create a two–dimensional image of the heart. Fiberoptic: A light source that uses bundles of glass or plastic fibers to send reflected light and transmit images back. Flail: Floppy, uncontrolled movement, as in a flail heart valve leaflet (cusp). Leaflets: Leaf–shaped flaps of tissue; two or three leaflets come together in the center of a heart valve, opening to allow blood to flow from one heart chamber to another and closing to stop the flow of blood between chambers; also known as cusps. Left ventricle: The left lower chamber of the heart of the heart that receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Mitral regurgitation: A condition in which the mitral valve fails to close properly resulting in reverse flow of blood from the left ventricle to the left atrium; major causes include myxomatous degeneration, a genetic disorder that causes elongation of the valve leaflets, ischemic heart disease, and left ventricular dilatation; treatment includes valvuloplasty or valve replacement; also known as mitral insufficiency or mitral incompetence. Mitral valve: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, name because its two cusps look like a bishop's hat or a mitered joint in carpentry; also called bicuspid or atrioventricular valve. Papillary muscles of the heart: Muscles that originate in the ventricular wall and attach to the mitral or tricuspid valves via bands of fibrous connective tissue called chordae tendineae. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTF or PTFE): The generic name for a man–made suture and graft material with applications in cardiac surgery; an expanded PTFE (ePTFE) has also been developed. Prolapse: The dropping, falling, sinking, or sliding of an organ or structure from its normal position or location in the body. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): A imaging study in which an ultrasound transducer is inserted through the esophagus to make detailed pictures of the heart and the arteries through the use of sound waves (ultrasound). Thoracotomy: Surgical incision to open the chest wall. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips Transthoracic echocardiography is included in this procedure when performed; if transesophageal echocardiogram is performed, you may also report 93355. lay_term: The provider inserts an adjustable annulus device via a catheter inserted percutaneously through the skin and across the interatrial septum to reconstruct and tighten the dilated annulus of the mitral valve (the valve between the left upper chamber and left lower pumping chamber of the heart) to treat mitral regurgitation. Explanation This procedure is performed on a beating heart, and the patient is not placed on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), although standby CPB procedures may be in place. When the patient is appropriately prepared and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision through the skin and femoral vein. He inserts a catheter and advances it up to the inferior vena cava under fluoroscopic imaging guidance. Typically, using transesophageal echocardiographic (TEE) guidance, he punctures the interatrial septum over the posterior medial mitral valve commissure. He advances a transseptal steerable sheath (TSS) over a guidewire into the left atrium. He delivers the implant through the sheath and aligns the tip of the implant catheter near the anterior lateral trigone. Next, he inserts a series of anchors through the implant fabric into the annular tissue surrounding the mitral valve, maneuvering the implant catheter to each targeted anchoring point under fluoroscopic and TEE guidance. After deploying the last anchor, the provider disconnects the implant from the implant catheter and inserts a size adjustment tool through the TSS over a wire to the implant adjustment mechanism and rotates the adjustment knob to reduce the implant size and control mitral regurgitation. Finally, the size adjustment tool and the transseptal steerable sheath are removed, leaving the implant in place. The provider removes the catheter and applies pressure over the femoral vein to control bleeding. After ensuring hemostasis, he closes the incision in layers. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; "on pump" means the provider performed CPB. Commissure: The area where the heart valve leaflets (cusps) meet or come together. Dilation or dilatation: Stretching or expansion of an opening or passageway. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Inferior vena cava: The major trunk of the venous circulatory system that brings blood back from the lower body circulation, the abdominal and pelvic organs, and the extremities. Mitral valve: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, name because its two cusps look like a bishop's hat or a mitered joint in carpentry; also called bicuspid or atrioventricular valve. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Septum: Wall or partition between two cavities or open spaces; examples include the septa between the ventricles and the atria of the heart and the nasal septum. short_description: Radiofrequency spectroscopy, real time, intraoperative margin assessment, at the time of partial mastectomy, with report Notes: (Use 0546T only once for each partial mastectomy site) (Do not report 0546T for re-excision)
lay_term: The provider employs radiofrequency spectroscopy, a type of imaging using electromagnetic waves, after a partial mastectomy (partial breast excision) or lumpectomy to determine whether the margins are free of cancer. Explanation Immediately after a lumpectomy or partial breast excision, while the patient is still on the operating table, the provider applies a special probe that emits electromagnetic waves similar to FM radio waves to the margins of the excised tissue. The probe emits electromagnetic waves in a wide range of frequencies and detects differences between uptake in breast cancer cells and normal breast tissue, which it sends back to a computer console to which it is attached. The device assesses margins up to 1 mm in depth. The technology can detect both ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive breast cancer. The provider typically takes 5 to 8 measurements at evenly spaced intervals along the margins of the excised tissue. The computer uses an algorithm to interpret the results and displays them as positive or negative on a monitor. If any of the readings is positive, the provider will excise more tissue. Terminology Lumpectomy: Removal of an entire lesion of the breast and a margin of tissue around it. Probe (noun): A device, usually attached to a computer, that sends and receives sound waves or electromagnetic waves; it may be used for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes; also called a transducer. Radiofrequency (RF): Electrical current from a radio wave (a type of electromagnetic wave) used to transmit signals. Tips You may report this code once for each partial mastectomy or lumpectomy site, but do not report it again for re–excision. short_description: Bone-material quality testing by microindentation(s) of the tibia(s), with results reported as a score Notes: (To report unilateral or bilateral insertion, removal, or fluid adjustment of a periurethral adjustable balloon continence device, see 53451, 53452, 53453, 53454)
lay_term: The provider inserts a reference point indenter through the skin into the shaft of the tibia to assess bone stiffness and toughness, which may be useful in providing bone quality information in joint replacement surgery and fracture potential in patients with osteoporosis or osteopenia. Results are reported as a score. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepared and using local anesthesia, the provider performs reference point indentation or microindentation of the tibial shaft. He inserts a probe through the skin of the midshaft of the tibia down to the bone surface. He activates the instrument, which produces a microfracture where it indents the cortical surface. Indentation force and depth of indentation are measured. Keeping the probe perpendicular to the bone surface, he makes multiple indentations 1 to 2 mm apart, which are relayed through the probe back to a computer, which uses an algorithm to interpret the results as bone material strength index and reports the results as a score. Terminology Cortical: Pertaining to the cortex, the outermost layer of an organ such as the brain or kidneys or a structure such as bone. Osteopenia: A bone mineral density that is lower than normal, which signifies a bone condition that may result in osteoporosis. Osteoporosis: A thinning of the bones with reduction in bone mass due to depletion of calcium and bone protein commonly occurring as a result of hormonal changes, or a deficiency of calcium or vitamin D. Tibia: The larger and stronger of the two bones in the lower leg; also known as the shin bone. lay_term: The provider assesses bone strength and risk of fracture using computer equations to calculate the relationship between the biomechanical properties of bone and its response to various loads in conjunction with CT scan of bone mineral density; this code includes scan data retrieval and transmission of bone strength, fracture risk, and bone mineral density and interpretation and report. short_description: Autologous cellular implant derived from adipose tissue for the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knees; tissue harvesting and cellular implant creation Notes: (Do not report 0565T in conjunction with 15769, 15771, 15772, 15773, 15774)
lay_term: Report this code for the harvesting (removal) of fat tissue and the creation of a cellular implant for injection into the knee joint of the same patient. Explanation The provider performs liposuction to remove adipose (fat) tissue from a patient. The harvested tissue, called lipoaspirate, is then “digested” with collagenase to break down the matrix (connective tissues). This releases mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) or adipose tissue–derived stem cells (ASCs) from the adipose tissue matrix. The ASCs are isolated using centrifugation and flushing out of the precipitate (dilution), and the collagenase is washed off. This process is repeated until only a few milliliters is left. This end–product referred to as stromal vascular fractions (SVFs), which can then be injected back into the patient’s knee(s) to treat osteoarthritis. Terminology Autologous: Describes tissue or blood taken from and returned to the same individual. Centrifugation: Process that rotates a mixture around a fixed axis at a high speed to separate it into its component parts. Collagenase: An enzyme that breaks down collagen, an insoluble fibrous protein, chief constituent of connective tissue. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Liposuction: A procedure to extract fat from deposits beneath the skin and between tissues in the body. Mesenchymal stem cells: Stromal cells that have the potential to develop into other types of cells including bone cells (osteoblasts), cartilage cells (chondrocytes), muscle cells (myocytes) and (fat cells which give rise to marrow adipose tissue (adipocytes). Meniscus: A rubbery C–shaped cartilage that acts as a shock absorber in the knee joint. Osteoarthritis: A degenerative condition of a joint due to wear and tear that causes the cartilage or cushion in the joints between bones to break down and results in pain, stiffness, and swelling. Osteonecrosis: A bone disease caused by lack of blood supply to an area resulting in the bone breaking down faster than the body can make enough new bone. Pericytes: Cells that wrap around endothelial cells and support small blood vessel (capillary) integrity. Tendons: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips For injection of the cellular implant into a single knee, see 0566T. Do not confuse 0565T and 0566T with 15771, +15772, 15773, and +15774 for harvesting of autologous fat by liposuction technique and grafting it to specific areas of the body. Codes 15771 to 15774 do not involve culturing and preparation or injection of an autologous cellular implant. Although this code is specifically for harvesting and preparation of adipose tissue for a cellular implant to treat osteoarthritis of the knee, SVFs contain a variety of cell types from which cartilage, bone, and tendons can be generated to treat osteoarthritis (OA), chondromalacia (softening of the cartilage underneath the patella), meniscus tear, osteonecrosis of the femoral head, and tendon injuries. lay_term: After placing a prosthetic device to repair the tricuspid valve (the three–leaflet valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle) and reduce regurgitation (backflow of blood), the provider places another device like the first via percutaneous catheter insertion. Explanation During the same procedure as the initial placement of a tricuspid valve (TV) prosthetic device, the provider places another device. He may inject contrast and perform angiography and roadmapping to guide placement of the prosthesis. He may also use fluoroscopy to guide the prosthesis repair system through the catheter and, choosing from three different balloon sizes (12, 15 and 18 mm), places another balloon spacer to provide better coaptation of the TV leaflets and reduce regurgitation. Coaptation refers to the fitting together of the tricuspid valve leaflets when the valve closes. He may adjust the position of the spacer until he feels it is in optimum position. He stabilizes the spacer by anchoring a rail at the right ventricular apex. He withdraws the catheter and closes the incisions, ensuring hemostasis as he does so. If the provider places additional spacers, each additional placement is reported separately with this same code. The provider may perform right and/or left heart catheterization for hemodynamic monitoring, intracardiac echocardiography for guidance, and/or right ventricular angiography to assess tricuspid valve regurgitation in conjunction with this procedure. If so, these procedures and all the procedures described above are included and should not be reported separately. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): Technique that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs and maintains the circulation of blood and the oxygen content of the body during surgery, giving the provider a motionless operative field; known as a heart–lung machine or pump; "on pump" means the provider performed CPB. Hemodynamic monitoring: Measurement of systemic, arterial, and venous blood pressure, blood flow, cardiac output, and oxygen via insertion of a catheter tipped with a monitoring device into a vein, a ventricle of the heart, or an artery. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Prosthesis (pl. prostheses): An artificial or man–made replacement for a body part; also known as a prosthetic or prosthetic device. Transcatheter delivery: A minimally invasive delivery method of medication or a device via a catheter placed through a small incision. Tricuspid valve: Valve consisting of three triangular membranous flaps (called leaflets or cusps) situated at the opening of the right atrium of the heart into the right ventricle. Ventricular assist device (VAD): A mechanical pump that helps pump blood from the ventricles (lower chambers of the heart) to other organs of the body to support a weakened heart or in heart failure. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips Report +0570T for each additional prosthesis placed in conjunction with 0569T. Guidelines for use of 0569T and +0570T are extensive. Be sure to examine them carefully to avoid reporting included procedures. If a ventricular assist device is required, that procedure may be reported separately. If cardiopulmonary bypass is employed, use an appropriate add–on code (33367, 33368, 33369). Transesophageal echo (TEE), if performed by a separate operator, may be reported separately. Two other systems that may be used for tricuspid valve repair include TriClip® implantation, which is a modification of the MitraClip® system. This device is inserted percutaneously through the internal jugular or femoral vein and consists of clipping together two continuous or opposing leaflets, basically turning the tricuspid valve into a bicuspid one. The Pascal® system involves placing a spacer, paddles, and clasps that attach the device to the valve leaflets for independent leaflet capture. The system includes a steerable guide, implantation catheter, and sheath. lay_term: The provider implants a prosthetic tricuspid valve, or replaces one, using a catheter that he inserts through a small incision in the skin and which he threads through a vessel to the heart. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision through the skin to reach the vessel selected for access. He inserts a catheter and navigates it through blood vessels to reach the heart. He may insert a temporary pacemaker for rapid pacing. He may use angiography (vessel imaging) and intracardiac echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart) to guide the procedure. He catheterizes the right heart. He implants or replaces the prosthetic tricuspid valve. The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart, allowing blood to flow from the right atrium (upper chamber) to the right ventricle (lower chamber). The provider then ensures a return to normal heart function in the patient. He withdraws the catheter, applies pressure over the access site to control any bleeding, and closes the small incision. The procedure may help reduce tricuspid regurgitation, where the valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow back into the right atrium and causing the heart to work harder. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. short_description: Insertion or replacement of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator system with substernal electrode(s), including all imaging guidance and electrophysiological evaluation (includes defibrillation threshold evaluation, induction of arrhythmia, evaluation of sensing for arrhythmia termination, and programming or reprogramming of sensing or therapeutic parameters), when performed Notes: (Use 0571T in conjunction with 0573T, 0580T for removal and replacement of an implantable defibrillator pulse generator and substernal electrode) (Do not report 0571T in conjunction with 93260, 93261, 93644, 0572T, 0575T, 0576T, 0577T) (For insertion or replacement of permanent subcutaneous implantable defibrillator system with subcutaneous electrode, use 33270)
lay_term: The provider either replaces or implants a new implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) system with one or more substernal electrodes and performs necessary testing and programming of the system. ICDs sense and regulate the heart rate. Substernal ICDs may be indicated when subcutaneous or transvenous electrodes are not feasible. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin between the left midaxillary and anterior axillary lines below the armpit. He dissects down through tissues to the submuscular space and creates a pocket where he places the pulse generator and secures it to the fascia. Next, he makes a subxiphoid incision to access the retrosternal space. He places one or more leads behind the sternum (breastbone) deep to the left sternal border but outside the pericardial cavity and secures the lead(s) to the subxiphoid fascia. Under fluoroscopic guidance and using a specially designed tunneling tool inside a hemostatic sheath, he creates a tunnel from the lead(s) to the generator, threads the lead(s) through the tunnel, and attaches the lead(s). He evaluates the function of the electrode(s) and generator by inducing tachycardia and evaluating defibrillation thresholds. He evaluates electrode sensing of termination of irregular heart rate, and programs or reprograms the sensing or therapeutic settings. He removes all instruments and after checking and controlling bleeding closes the incisions. If the provider is replacing an existing system, he opens the previous incisions and removes the generator and electrodes. He may irrigate the areas with antibiotic solution if infection was the reason for removal. He closes the incisions. He then essentially follows the above procedure to place another generator and electrode(s) in similar positions. Implantable cardioverter–defibrillator systems with one or more substernal electrodes have similar benefits to traditional, transvenous ICDs, that is, they can administer defibrillation therapy and anti–tachycardia and post–shock pacing. The pulse generator is the same size and shape (smaller than a subcutaneous ICD generator) and is expected to last as long as transvenous ICDs. The main advantage is that ICDs with substernal electrodes avoid having to place electrodes in the veins or in or on the heart. Terminology Arrhythmia: Irregular rate or rhythm of the heartbeat. Cardioverter–defibrillator electrodes or leads: Flexible insulated electrical conductors with one end connected to an external pulse generator and the other end to the heart. Cardioverter–defibrillator pulse generator: An implantable electronic device that senses abnormal heart rhythm and controls it. Cardioverter–defibrillator system: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate the abnormal or fast rhythm of the heart when needed. Defibrillation: A controlled electric shock to the exterior of the chest wall or directly to the exposed heart muscle, to normalize the rhythm of the heart or restart the heart of a patient who has no pulse and is unresponsive. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Pericardial: Relates to the pericardium, which is the membrane covering the heart. Substernal: Under the breastbone. Tips If you are reporting 0571T for replacement of a substernal implantable ICD, you can report 0573T for removal of the electrode and 0580T for removal of the pulse generator. Placement of electrode(s) and pulse generator, repositioning, testing (interrogation), and programming, as well as imaging guidance, are included with 0571T, so those procedures should not be reported separately. There are many codes for various procedures involving implantable cardioverter–defibrillators, pacemakers, and defibrillators and their components, testing, and programming. Study the procedure documentation, the codes in the Category III subsection for Implantable Cardioverter–defibrillator Procedures (0571T to 0580T and 0614T), the codes in the Pacemaker or Pacing Cardioverter–Defibrillator Procedures (33202–33275), and Implantable and Wearable Cardiac Device Evaluations (93264–93298) sections to make sure you choose the correct code for the procedure you are reporting. lay_term: The provider inserts a substernal implantable defibrillator electrode and attaches it to a pulse generator. Defibrillators sense and regulate the heart rate. lay_term: The OQHCP or physician provider performs an in–person evaluation and repeatedly adjusts the programmed settings of the components of an already implanted cardioverter–defibrillator system to select the optimal permanent programmed values; this code includes the analysis, review, and report of his findings and the programmed settings. Explanation The provider, a physician or OQHCP, connects an ECG monitor to the patient and a portable programmer to the pulse generator of the implanted cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) system to establish a communication link between it and the programmer. The provider repeatedly analyzes and reviews several parameters of the stored data, comparing it to current readings, making adjustments, and retesting. He then determines whether to change the programming of the device to optimize performance. When he has completed his testing and adjustments, he prepares a report of the findings and the programmed settings. Implantable cardioverter–defibrillator systems with one or more substernal electrodes have similar benefits to traditional, transvenous ICDs, that is, they can administer defibrillation therapy and anti–tachycardia and post–shock pacing. The pulse generator is the same size and shape (smaller than a subcutaneous ICD generator) and is expected to last as long as transvenous ICDs. Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Iterative: Refers to the process of concluding a decision or result based on repetitive action and analysis. Other qualified healthcare professional (OQHCP): An individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure and/or regulation, when applicable, and facility privileging, when applicable, who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service; distinct from clinical staff, individuals who works under the supervision of a provider or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation, and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service but who does not individually report that professional service; other policies may also affect who may report specified services. Pulse generator: Electronic device that stimulates the nerves that control muscles with electrical impulses. lay_term: The OQHCP or physician provider performs an in–person interrogation and evaluation of the components of an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) system, including connecting and disconnecting the device components and recording the results as well as analysis, review, and report of his findings and the programmed settings. This code can be reported for each patient encounter to interrogate the ICD system. Explanation The provider, a physician or OQHCP, connects an electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor to the patient and a portable programmer to the pulse generator of the implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) system to establish a communication link between it and the programmer. He retrieves the stored and measured data about one or more components. The provider connects and disconnects the system and records the results. He analyzes and reviews the results and prepares a report. Use this code to report in–person interrogation of the components of an ICD system. Implantable cardioverter–defibrillator systems with one or more substernal electrodes have similar benefits to traditional, transvenous ICDs, that is, they can administer defibrillation therapy and anti–tachycardia and post–shock pacing. The pulse generator is the same size and shape (smaller than a subcutaneous ICD generator) and is expected to last as long as transvenous ICDs. The main advantage is that ICDs with substernal electrodes avoid having to place electrodes in the veins or in or on the heart. Terminology Arrhythmia: Irregular rate or rhythm of the heartbeat. Cardioverter–defibrillator system: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate the abnormal or fast rhythm of the heart when needed. Defibrillation: A controlled electric shock to the exterior of the chest wall or directly to the exposed heart muscle, to normalize the rhythm of the heart or restart the heart of a patient who has no pulse and is unresponsive. Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. lay_term: The provider ablates, or destroys, one or more small malignant tumors in one breast in a minimally invasive surgical procedure using cryotherapy, or extreme cold, applied through a percutaneous needle. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and with only local anesthesia, the provider guides one, two, or more thin, needlelike devices (cryoprobes) through the skin directly into the tumor under ultrasound or MR imaging guidance. He blasts liquid nitrogen through the cryoprobe to freeze and destroy the cancerous tissue. An ice ball forms around the tip of the cryoprobe and completely encompasses the tumor and a 1 cm margin of normal tissue. Temperatures of 40 degrees below zero or colder are maintained for about 6 to 8 minutes followed by a 10–minute thaw and then another 6– to 8–minute freeze. If the tumor is close to the skin, saline injections enable the provider to obtain acceptable margins and protect the skin from damage. Warmed bags of saline and vigorous massage may also be used to protect the skin. Once all the tumors have been treated, the provider removes the probe(s) and covers the small incision(s) with an adhesive bandage, and the patient can go home. Terminology Cryoablation, cryosurgery, or cryotherapy: A technique that destroys damaged or abnormal tissues by freezing temperatures. Fibroadenoma of breast: Solid, noncancerous breast tumors; usually painless; they do not increase the risk of breast cancer. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Tips Report 0581T only once per breast regardless of the number of tumors ablated. If the procedure is performed on both breasts, append modifier 50 for a bilateral procedure. Be sure to read parenthetical notes following the descriptor to avoid reporting codes you should not report with this procedure. Using intraoperative imaging and needle guidance, he positions the needle tip of the device directly at the malignant prostate tissue. He injects the heated water vapor into the malignant tissue in bursts circumferentially. He retracts the needle after each injection and repositions it, creating contiguous and overlapping zones, until he is satisfied that he has destroyed all the malignant prostate tissue. The total number of treatments varies depending on the size and shape of the prostate. When enough of the prostatic tissue has been destroyed, he withdraws the instrument. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. lay_term: The provider carries out tympanostomy with insertion of a ventilation tube in a single ear using an automated tube delivery system that also applies iontophoresis local anesthesia. Electrodes within the ear plugs connected to a control unit deliver local anesthetic to the tympanic membrane (eardrum). The local anesthesia is achieved by iontophoresis, that is, the application of constant low–voltage direct electrical current to topical anesthetic molecules, which causes the anesthetic to be absorbed into the tissues. The patient is sent home after the provider ensures proper placement of the ventilation tube. This procedure may be performed in a doctor’s office or outpatient clinic. short_description: Islet cell transplant, includes portal vein catheterization and infusion, including all imaging, including guidance, and radiological supervision and interpretation, when performed; percutaneous
lay_term: The provider transplants pancreatic beta islet cells from the patient’s own pancreas or a donor source to stimulate insulin production in a patient with diabetes. He infuses the cells into the portal vein of the liver through a tube that he inserts through a small skin incision in the abdomen. All imaging, imaging guidance, and radiological supervision and interpretation are included with this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small midline abdominal incision. He dissects down to the liver and identifies the portal vein. Using imaging guidance, he makes a small puncture in the portal vein and inserts a catheter over a guidewire. He then withdraws the guidewire and secures the other end of the catheter to a small incision in the skin of the abdomen. The provider then removes the instruments, checks for bleeding, and closes the incisions. He next slowly infuses a suspension of islet beta cells obtained from the pancreas of a cadaveric donor, known as allotransplantation. He may also use islet beta cells from the patient’s own pancreas, known as autotransplantation, which the provider harvests after removal of the pancreas in a separate procedure. The laboratory purifies and processes the cells to prepare them for transplantation. He may take a scout film of the abdomen prior to the procedure and more abdominal x–rays during the procedure. This procedure includes all imaging, imaging guidance, and radiological interpretation and procedure, so do not report those services separately. Terminology Catheterization: Placement of a long, thin, flexible tube (catheter) into a blood vessel, heart, or any other tubular structure in the body. Diabetes mellitus (DM): A disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs; type 1 DM refers to insulin–dependent diabetes mellitus; type 2 DM refers to a form that can be controlled with oral or injectable noninsulin medications. Imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy (a live, real–time X–ray where the image appears on a television monitor), ultrasound (high–frequency sound waves), or other forms of imaging to view tissues during surgical procedures. Infusion: The administration of medication or other fluids directly into circulation through a vein or artery by gravity drainage through a catheter. Islet cell: Insulin producing cells in the pancreas. Laparoscopy: A surgical procedure where the provider makes small incisions into the abdomen or pelvis; inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure; then inserts trocars (ports) into the incisions to keep the incisions open so that he can insert, through one of the incisions, a laparoscope (a camera attached to a lighted tube to visualize the abdominal or pelvic cavity), and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments to perform the procedure; he removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Radiologic supervision and interpretation (RS&I): Refers to when a provider oversees an imaging procedure and interprets the results; it may be included as part of a procedure code or be reported separately (if not included in the procedure) using a radiologic procedure code. lay_term: The provider percutaneously implants or replaces an integrated neurostimulation system that stimulates the posterior tibial nerve to treat bladder dysfunction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision, typically just above the inner ankle. The provider also may perform analysis and programming to ensure the system works properly for the patient. lay_term: The provider inserts an interatrial septal shunt device between the left and right atrium via a percutaneous puncture over the femoral vein and advances it through a catheter to the upper chambers (atria) of the heart under imaging guidance. The provider may also perform left and right heart catheterization and intracardiac echocardiography. Explanation The provider, typically an interventional cardiologist, makes a small puncture wound through the skin over the femoral vein and inserts a catheter through the vein and guides it under imaging guidance through other vessels up to the atrium. He inserts an interatrial septal shunt device over a guidewire through the catheter, withdraws the guidewire, punctures the wall between the two atria, passes part of the device through the atrial septum, and secures the device in place. He may perform cardiac catheterization to check pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), which he does by wedging a catheter with a weighted balloon in a small branch of the pulmonary artery. He may perform intracardiac echocardiography to check the pressures in the atria and the ejection fraction. He withdraws the catheter and sutures the incision in the femoral vein and the skin. This procedure includes imaging guidance, cardiac catheterization, and intracardiac echocardiography if performed. Providers perform this procedure to treat heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or elevated left atrial pressure in patients with heart failure (LAP–HF). In heart failure, fluid builds up in the heart and the lungs due to elevated blood pressure, making respiration difficult. The ejection fraction is the measure of the percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with every heartbeat. lay_term: The provider uses an automated system to analyze eye movements, such as to assess concussion. This includes evaluating the coordination of both eyes, quick eye movements, and how pupils respond to light. This code includes the interpretation and report of the results. short_description: Cystourethroscopy with transurethral anterior prostate commissurotomy and drug delivery, including transrectal ultrasound and fluoroscopy, when performed Notes: (Do not report 0619T in conjunction with 52000, 52441, 52442, 52450, 52500, 52601, 52630, 52640, 52647, 52648, 52649, 53850, 53852, 53854, 76872)
lay_term: The provider performs a cystourethroscopy during which he incises the anterior prostate at the bladder neck (commissurotomy) and injects a drug or places a drug implant to help treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). He examines the urethra and bladder. The provider may inject sterile saline water into the bladder to improve the view of the bladder. He may employ ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance when he makes a small incision in the capsule of the prostate at the junction of the prostate and bladder (the anterior prostatic commissure). He may leave an indwelling catheter in the patient’s urethra to help with voiding until the tissues heal. short_description: Trabeculostomy ab interno by laser
lay_term: In a procedure also known as microinvasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), the provider uses a laser to create holes in the eye’s trabecular meshwork. The procedure uses the ab interno approach, meaning inside the eye. Trabecular meshwork drains most of the aqueous humor from the eye, and creating holes assists this flow and lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma patients. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider makes a tiny incision in the cornea, the clear transparent outer layer of the eye. She advances a probe through the incision into the anterior chamber of the eye. The probe makes direct contact with the trabecular meshwork, which is translucent tissue at the base of the cornea that filters aqueous humor that flows out of the eye. She uses the probe to apply laser energy that creates microchannels (tiny holes). A typical case may involve 10 microchannels. She removes the instruments and completes the procedure. Terminology Anterior chamber of eye: The space between the cornea and the iris that contains aqueous humor, a thick watery substance, and communicates through the pupil with the posterior chamber at the back of the eye. Aqueous humor: Thick watery substance that fills the space between the lens and the cornea; also known as aqueous fluid. Tips See 0622T for the same procedure using an ophthalmic endoscope. short_description: Transcutaneous visible light hyperspectral imaging measurement of oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, and tissue oxygenation, with interpretation and report, per extremity Notes: (Do not report 0631T in conjunction with 94760, 94761, 94762, 0061U)
lay_term: The provider uses a hyperspectral imaging device that differentiates light absorption between oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, which may help with finding ischemic tissue. The provider interprets the data and completes a report. This code applies per extremity. Explanation The provider uses a hyperspectral imaging device, which images and quantifies light absorption in hemoglobin molecules using light and a spectrometer. Hemoglobin is the protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs. A spectrometer is a device to measure the properties of light and differentiate between them. The data is presented as color–coded images to reveal concentrations of oxyhemoglobin (the combination of hemoglobin and oxygen), deoxyhemoglobin (hemoglobin without oxygen), and oxygen saturation (the relative amount of oxygen, expressed in percent, that is dissolved or carried in the blood). The provider uses software to analyze areas in the image to locate ischemic tissue, meaning tissue with restricted blood supply. For instance, the provider may use the service to evaluate a diabetic foot ulcer or other non–healing wounds. The provider interprets the data and completes a report. Use this code once per extremity. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous transcatheter ultrasound ablation of nerves innervating the pulmonary arteries, including right heart catheterization, pulmonary artery angiography, and all imaging guidance Notes: (Do not report 0632T in conjunction with 36013, 36014, 36015, 75741, 75743, 75746, 93451, 93453, 93456, 93460, 93503, 93505, 93568, 93593, 93594, 93596, 93597) (For percutaneous transcatheter thermal ablation of nerves innervating the pulmonary arteries, including right heart catheterization, pulmonary artery angiography, and all imaging guidance, use 0793T)
lay_term: The provider performs a minimally invasive procedure that uses ultrasound to interrupt the pulmonary artery nerve supply. The code includes services required to complete the procedure such as imaging guidance and right heart catheterization. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small opening through the skin to access a blood vessel. She inserts a catheter (a flexible tube) in the vessel and uses imaging guidance to navigate the catheter to the target area. She performs right heart catheterization, passing the catheter through the right atrium and the tricuspid valve of the heart, into the right ventricle, across the pulmonary valve to reach the pulmonary artery. She performs pulmonary artery angiography to assess the area and uses the catheter to apply ultrasound energy (high–frequency sound waves) to ablate (destroy) nerves innervating the pulmonary arteries. The procedure may help treat pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary artery circulation. She removes the instruments and completes the procedure. lay_term: The provider uses a catheter navigated through the blood vessels to insert a reduction device in the coronary sinus, the largest cardiac venous structure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the target blood vessel, possibly using ultrasound guidance. She navigates the catheter to the heart and performs right heart catheterization and coronary sinus catheterization. She uses angiography to examine the structures. She may perform interventions in the coronary sinus, a large venous structure that drains the heart and lies in the groove that separates atria (upper heart chambers) from ventricles (lower heart chambers). She places the coronary sinus reduction device, typically using imaging to guide the placement. She may use intracardiac echocardiography during the procedure. After placing the device and removing catheters and wires, the provider closes the access site. The device may help reduce angina (chest pain) in patients with coronary artery disease. Angina may be caused by the heart muscle not getting enough oxygen–rich blood. The device helps by increasing pressure in the coronary sinus to redistribute blood to the heart muscle that is not getting enough blood. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. lay_term: The provider provides software and is responsible for collection, transmission, and storage of data for a remote autonomous algorithm–based recommendation system for insulin dose calculation and titration. This code is reportable each 30 days. Explanation The provider provides software and is responsible for collection, transmission, and storage of data for a remote recommendation system for insulin dose calculation and titration. It is an autonomous system, meaning it can function and perform certain tasks without human control, including insulin dose calculation and titration for a patient with diabetes. Insulin titration adjusts the dose based on blood glucose data. The system uses mathematical dosing algorithms based on factors such as blood glucose and weight. Code 0741T covers up to 30 days of service, with a minimum of 16 days required. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Diabetes mellitus (DM): A disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs; type 1 DM refers to insulin–dependent diabetes mellitus; type 2 DM refers to a form that can be controlled with oral or injectable noninsulin medications. Glucose: The main type of sugar in the blood; the major source of energy for the body's cells. Titration: The process of gradually increasing the concentration of a substance, such as a drug dosage, to achieve a specific result. Tips See 0740T for initial system setup and patient education. short_description: Absolute quantitation of myocardial blood flow (AQMBF), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), with exercise or pharmacologic stress, and at rest, when performed (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0742T in conjunction with 78451, 78452) (For absolute quantification of myocardial blood flow [AQMBF] with positron emission tomography [PET], use 78434)
lay_term: As an add–on to a primary SPECT myocardial (heart muscle) perfusion imaging study, the provider performs absolute quantitation of myocardial blood flow (AQMBF). The test is performed under stress and possibly at rest. Explanation In conjunction with a primary single photon emission computerized tomography (SPECT) myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) study, the provider performs absolute quantitation of myocardial blood flow (AQMBF). SPECT is a type of scan that uses a radioactive substance and a special camera to produce three–dimensional (3D) images. The myocardium is the muscular layer of the heart. MPI shows how well blood flows through the heart muscle and shows how well the heart muscle is pumping. The provider performs the SPECT AQMBF with the patient under stress, either by having the patient exercise or by administering a drug to increase blood flow. The code also includes SPECT AQMBF with the patient at rest, when performed. AQMBF provides more accurate classification of coronary artery disease (CAD) than static MPI. AQMBF also may help with quantifying and identifying other cardiac diseases. Terminology Coronary artery disease (CAD): A condition in which the vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle become stenosed (narrowed) due to the deposit of plaques (fatty substances) on the inner walls of the blood vessels, resulting in decreased blood flow and ultimately heart failure, if not treated; also known as coronary heart disease or atherosclerotic heart disease. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. short_description: Bone strength and fracture risk using finite element analysis of functional data and bone mineral density (BMD), with concurrent vertebral fracture assessment, utilizing data from a computed tomography scan, retrieval and transmission of the scan data, measurement of bone strength and BMD and classification of any vertebral fractures, with overall fracture-risk assessment, interpretation and report Notes: (Do not report 0743T in conjunction with 0554T, 0555T, 0556T, 0557T, 0691T)
lay_term: The provider assesses bone strength and risk of fracture using computer analysis known as finite element analysis. The service also includes classifying any vertebral fractures and assessing overall fracture risk. Explanation The provider calculates bone strength and fracture risk for a patient using finite element analysis. Finite element analysis has been developed by laboratory testing of the effects of stress and strain, loading conditions, external shape and internal architecture, and material properties of bone. At the same time, the service assesses the patient for vertebral fractures. Vertebrae are the interlocking bones that form the spine. The code includes retrieval and transmission of a previously acquired computed tomography (CT) scan), measuring bone strength and bone mineral density (BMD), classifying any vertebral fractures, providing an overall fracture risk assessment, and completing an interpretation and report. short_description: Insertion of bioprosthetic valve, open, femoral vein, including duplex ultrasound imaging guidance, when performed, including autogenous or nonautogenous patch graft (eg, polyester, ePTFE, bovine pericardium), when performed Notes: (Do not report 0744T in conjunction with 34501, 34510, 76998, 93971)
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to implant a bioprosthetic valve in the large femoral vein of the thigh. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the femoral vein of the thigh. The provider applies clamps to either end of a small portion of the vein to restrict blood flow. The provider makes an incision into that area of the vein between the clamps and inserts the bioprosthetic valve, anchoring it in place such as by suture. Bioprosthetic valves involve animal material, such as one or more pig heart valves on a stainless–steel frame. During the procedure, the provider may use duplex ultrasound guidance, which combines traditional ultrasound with Doppler ultrasound to measure speed and flow of blood. The provider closes the vein and closes the surgical access site. The provider may use a graft using tissue from the patient (autogenous) or using material from another source (nonautogenous), such as polyester, ePTFE (expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, a common material for grafts), or bovine pericardium (sac surrounding a cow’s heart). Terminology Bioprosthetic valve: An artificial valve usually made of animal tissue. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Open procedure: A surgical procedure requiring a large incision that allows the provider to directly visualize the target anatomy.
