short_description: Digitization of glass microscope slides for morphometric analysis, tumor immunohistochemistry (eg, Her-2/neu, estrogen receptor/progesterone receptor), quantitative or semiquantitative, per specimen, each single antibody stain procedure, manual (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0763T in conjunction with 88360)
lay_term: This code describes clinical staff work performed to scan and digitize images from glass microscope slides for immediate or later pathologic diagnosis. This add–on code specifically describes digitization of slides prepared for a manual quantitative/semiquantitative single antibody immunohistochemistry exam (morphometric analysis) (88360). Explanation Using a slide scanning microscope, the clinical staff scans and digitizes glass slides prepared from a tissue specimen, possibly using artificial intelligence (AI) to focus on specific regions of the slide. As a separate service, a pathologist or other healthcare professional will evaluate the digitized images for diagnosis, possibly using computer–assisted image analysis AI algorithms. The digitized slide evaluation may occur remotely in real time, or at a later time from a server or cloud–based digital image archive. Code +0763T specifically describes the work to digitize glass slides prepared for a manual quantitative/semiquantitative single antibody immunohistochemistry exam (morphometric analysis) described by code 88360. Following the +0763T service, the pathologist uses digital images, not just glass slides viewed directly through the microscope, to diagnose the immunohistochemistry stain slides. Code +0763T does not describe slide digitization performed solely for archiving or other non–diagnostic purposes. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Digital image: A picture converted to numerical data for storage and viewing on a computer. Immunohistochemistry: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood; also called immunoassay. Morphometric: A quantitative or semiquantitative analysis of form, such as counting specific types of cells in a microscope field. Pathologic examination: Microscopic analysis of tissue for abnormalities in structure or function. Tips Report one unit of this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides only in addition to an 88360 manual quantitative/semiquantitative single antibody immunohistochemistry exam (morphometric analysis) for pathologic diagnosis. Do not report this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides solely for purposes other than pathologic diagnosis, such as archiving slides after pathologic diagnosis is complete, educational purposes, or database creation. short_description: Assistive algorithmic electrocardiogram risk-based assessment for cardiac dysfunction (eg, low-ejection fraction, pulmonary hypertension, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); related to concurrently performed electrocardiogram (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0764T in conjunction with 93000, 93010) (Use 0764T only once for each unique, concurrently performed electrocardiogram tracing)
lay_term: Concurrent with performing a separately reportable electrocardiogram (ECG), the provider uses algorithms enhanced by artificial intelligence to assess the patient for cardiac issues. Explanation The provider performs a separately reportable electrocardiogram (ECG) and, as an add–on service, uses algorithms enhanced by artificial intelligence to assess the patient’s risk for cardiac dysfunction. For instance, specific algorithms applied to the ECG data may assess patient risk for low–ejection fraction (low percentage of blood pumped out of a filled ventricle with every heartbeat), pulmonary hypertension (elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary artery circulation), or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (abnormally thick heart muscle). Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. lay_term: The provider locates the peripheral nerve for treatment and defines the appropriate magnetic stimulation amplitude. The provider may use nerve conduction to confirm the nerve location. short_description: Virtual reality (VR) procedural dissociation services provided by the same physician or other qualified health care professional performing the diagnostic or therapeutic service that the VR procedural dissociation supports, requiring the presence of an independent, trained observer to assist in the monitoring of the patient's level of dissociation or consciousness and physiological status; initial 15 minutes of intraservice time, patient age 5 years or older
lay_term: A qualified healthcare professional (QHP) performing a separate diagnostic or therapeutic procedure also provides virtual reality (VR) procedural dissociation services to increase patient comfort. This code represents the first 15 minutes of VR intraservice time for a patient who is at least 5 years of age. Explanation While performing a separately reportable diagnostic or therapeutic service, a qualified healthcare professional (QHP) provides virtual reality (VR) procedural dissociation services for a patient who is 5 years of age or older. A trained, independent observer is present. The observer must be qualified to monitor the patient, be trained in immersive technology, be able to adjust the tech under provider supervision, and not have other duties during the procedure. VR is a simulated environment that lets people interact with virtual surroundings. Users typically wear a headset. VR procedural dissociation involves a computer–generated audio, visual, and proprioceptive immersive environment. Proprioception is the body’s ability to sense movement, action, and location. The resulting state of altered consciousness improves patient comfort and tolerance for the procedure while decreasing the patient’s pain. Patients can still respond to spoken instructions and stimuli. The provider is responsible for periodically assessing the patient, checking how well they are tolerating the procedure, and also monitoring oxygen saturation, heart rate, pain, neurological status, and global anxiety. The codes also require changing the VR program to optimize the patient’s state. Examples of optimization techniques include changing the software program, adjusting the volume or visual environment, making changes necessary to reposition the patient, changing programming to maintain the dissociated state, and using a feedback loop to achieve the desired dissociated state level. The service does not include interventions to maintain cardiovascular function, a patent (open) airway, or spontaneous ventilation (breathing). The service also does not include medication administration for pain control or sedation. VR intraservice time starts with administration of the VR technology and continues while there is continuous face–to–face QHP attendance. VR intraservice time ends when the VR administration and continuous face–to–face time end. This code applies to the initial 15 minutes of intraservice time. Tips Codes 0771T (initial 15 minutes) and +0772T (each additional 15 minutes) apply when a single QHP performs both the VR service and the diagnostic or therapeutic service performed at the same session. Codes 0773T (initial 15 minutes) and +0774T (each additional 15 minutes) apply to the VR service when one QHP performs the VR service and another QHP performs the related diagnostic or therapeutic service. Don’t separately report VR services lasting fewer than 10 minutes. After that, use the halfway rule for coding based on time. For instance, use the initial codes for services lasting 10–22 minutes. Once you hit 23 minutes, report the initial code and one unit of the add–on code. That’s 15 minutes (initial code) and eight minutes (add–on code) to reach the total of 23 minutes. lay_term: A qualified healthcare professional (QHP) performing a separate diagnostic or therapeutic procedure also provides virtual reality (VR) procedural dissociation services to increase patient comfort. This add–on code represents each additional 15 minutes of VR intraservice time for a patient who is at least 5 years of age. Explanation While performing a separately reportable diagnostic or therapeutic service, a qualified healthcare professional (QHP) provides virtual reality (VR) procedural dissociation services for a patient who is 5 years of age or older. A trained, independent observer is present. The observer must be qualified to monitor the patient, be trained in immersive technology, be able to adjust the tech under provider supervision, and not have other duties during the procedure. VR is a simulated environment that lets people interact with virtual surroundings. Users typically wear a headset. VR procedural dissociation involves a computer–generated audio, visual, and proprioceptive immersive environment. Proprioception is the body’s ability to sense movement, action, and location. The resulting state of altered consciousness improves patient comfort and tolerance for the procedure while decreasing the patient’s pain. Patients can still respond to spoken instructions and stimuli. The provider is responsible for periodically assessing the patient, checking how well they are tolerating the procedure, and also monitoring oxygen saturation, heart rate, pain, neurological status, and global anxiety. The codes also require changing the VR program to optimize the patient’s state. Examples of optimization techniques include changing the software program, adjusting the volume or visual environment, making changes necessary to reposition the patient, changing programming to maintain the dissociated state, and using a feedback loop to achieve the desired dissociated state level. The service does not include interventions to maintain cardiovascular function, a patent (open) airway, or spontaneous ventilation (breathing). lay_term: The provider performs in–person measurement and recording of dynamic joint motion and muscle function. The service requires multiple inertial measurement unit (IMU) with concurrent surface mechanomyography (sMMG) sensors. A cloud–based processing platform processes the data from multiple sensors and produces an automated report. Explanation The provider prepares the patient by placing multiple inertial measurement unit (IMU) with concurrent surface mechanomyography (sMMG) sensors. The provider uses the wireless sensors to measure and record dynamic joint motion and muscle function bilaterally with the patient physically present (not remote). IMU sensors measure body acceleration, velocity, positioning, rotation, and orientation during movement. sMMG sensors quantify muscle activation (ability to switch on and work) and contraction. The sensor data uploads to a cloud–based application, which produces an automated report that helps the provider track patient progress during the episode of care. short_description: Bronchoscopy, rigid or flexible, with insertion of esophageal protection device and circumferential radiofrequency destruction of the pulmonary nerves, including fluoroscopic guidance when performed; bilateral mainstem bronchi
lay_term: The provider inserts a specialized catheter through a bronchoscope and completes a circumferential radiofrequency ablation in the main bronchus of each lung to destroy pulmonary nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a rigid or flexible bronchoscope through the nose or mouth, advancing the scope to the bronchus, the main passageway to the lung. The provider positions an esophageal protection device. In a typical procedure, the provider inserts a specialized catheter through the working channel of the bronchoscope and positions the catheter in the right or left mainstem bronchus. The provider brings the catheter electrode in contact with the airway wall, such as by inflating a balloon on the catheter. The provider activates the radiofrequency energy, typically in multiple positions to complete circumferential (around in a circle) ablation. The provider performs the service in both the right and left mainstem bronchi and then removes the instruments. Terminology Bronchoscopy: A procedure in which the provider inserts a flexible or rigid tube (bronchoscope) through the nose or mouth to perform visual examination of the airways. Bronchus (pl. bronchi): One of two main air passageways from the end of the trachea (windpipe) into the lungs; also known as the right and left bronchi. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA): Use of heat produced by focused radio waves (a type of electromagnetic wave) to destroy areas of abnormal, damaged, or diseased tissue. short_description: Transcutaneous auricular neurostimulation, set-up, calibration, and patient education on use of equipment
lay_term: The provider performs setup, calibration, and patient education for the use of a transcutaneous auricular neurostimulation device. The device may have a noninvasive earpiece that is wired to a unit to deliver electrical stimulation, such as to the auricular branch of the vagus nerve and trigeminal nerve. Explanation The provider sets up a transcutaneous auricular neurostimulation device. Transcutaneous means across the skin and refers to a noninvasive approach. Auricular refers to the ear. The device may have an earpiece that is wired to a unit to deliver electrical stimulation, such as to the auricular (ear) branch of the vagus nerve. The provider calibrates the device, running a system check to make sure it is accurate. The provider also educates the patient on proper use of the device. Terminology Vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X, one of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. short_description: Transcatheter insertion of permanent dual-chamber leadless pacemaker, including imaging guidance (eg, fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, right atrial angiography, right ventriculography, femoral venography) and device evaluation (eg, interrogation or programming), when performed; complete system (ie, right atrial and right ventricular pacemaker components) Notes: (Do not report 0795T in conjunction with 75820, 76000, 76937, 77002, 93566, 0796T, 0797T)
lay_term: The provider uses a catheter to implant a complete dual–chamber leadless pacemaker system in the heart. The provider may use imaging guidance for the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider punctures the skin to insert a catheter into a vein and navigates the catheter through the blood vessels to reach the heart, typically using imaging guidance. The provider may perform right atrial angiography and right ventriculography, injecting dye to visualize the heart chambers. The provider uses the catheter to implant a pulse generator (with a built–in battery and electrode) in the right atrium (upper chamber) of the heart and implants a second pulse generator in the right ventricle (lower chamber). The provider then removes the catheter and controls any bleeding. The provider may interrogate (test) the pacemaker’s function and adjust the programming parameters after insertion. Terminology Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips Codes 0795T–0804T represent dual–chamber leadless pacemaker insertion, removal, removal and replacement, and programming device evaluation. short_description: Transcatheter superior and inferior vena cava prosthetic valve implantation (ie, caval valve implantation [CAVI]); percutaneous femoral vein approach Notes: Codes 0805T, 0806T are used to report transcatheter superior and inferior vena cava prosthetic valve implantation (ie, caval valve implantation [CAVI]). Codes 0805T, 0806T include the work, when performed, of vascular access, placing the access sheath, transseptal puncture, advancing the caval valve delivery systems into position, repositioning the device(s) as needed, and deploying the device(s). Angiography and radiological supervision and interpretation performed to guide CAVI (eg, guiding device placement and documenting completion of the intervention) are included in these codes. Diagnostic right and left heart catheterization codes (93451, 93452, 93453, 93456, 93457, 93458, 93459, 93460, 93461, 93593, 93594, 93595, 93596, 93597, 93598) should not be used with 0805T, 0806T to report: 1. Contrast injections, angiography, road-mapping, and/or fluoroscopic guidance for the transcatheter CAVI, 2. Left ventricular angiography to assess tricuspid regurgitation for guidance of the transcatheter CAVI, or 3. Right and left heart catheterization for hemodynamic measurements before, during, and after transcatheter superior and inferior vena cava prosthetic valve implantation for guidance. Diagnostic right and left heart catheterization codes (93451, 93452, 93453, 93456, 93457, 93458, 93459, 93460, 93461, 93593, 93594, 93595, 93596, 93597, 93598) and diagnostic coronary angiography codes (93454, 93455, 93456, 93457, 93458, 93459, 93460, 93461, 93563, 93564) may be reported with 0805T, 0806T, representing separate and distinct services from CAVI, if: 1. No prior study is available and a full diagnostic study is performed, or 2. A prior study is available, but as documented in the medical record: a. There is inadequate visualization of the anatomy and/or pathology, or b. The patient's condition with respect to the clinical indication has changed since the prior study, or c. There is a clinical change during the procedure that requires new evaluation. For same session or same day diagnostic cardiac catheterization services, the appropriate diagnostic cardiac catheterization code(s) may be reported by appending modifier 59 indicating separate and distinct procedural service from the transcatheter superior and inferior vena cava prosthetic valve implantation procedures. Percutaneous coronary interventional therapeutic procedures may be reported separately, when performed. When transcatheter ventricular support is required in conjunction with CAVI, the appropriate ventricular assist device (VAD) procedure codes (33990, 33991, 33992, 33993, 33995, 33997) or balloon pump insertion codes (33967, 33970, 33973) may be reported. When cardiopulmonary bypass is performed in conjunction with CAVI, 0805T and 0806T may be reported with the appropriate add-on code for percutaneous peripheral bypass (33367), open peripheral bypass (33368), or central bypass (33369).
lay_term: The provider uses a percutaneous femoral vein approach to implant prosthetic valves in the vena cava using a catheter. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision for percutaneous (minimally invasive, through the skin) access to the femoral vein of the thigh. The provider inserts a catheter into the vein and navigates the catheter to the implant site. The provider deploys one or more devices in the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava. The procedure may include placing an access sheath to assist with catheter insertion, advancing the valve delivery systems to the implant sites, and repositioning the device(s). The provider may use angiography (blood vessel imaging), contrast injections, fluoroscopic guidance, and other radiological supervision and interpretation services to guide aspects of the procedure, such as device placement and confirming the procedure is complete. To guide the caval valve implantation (CAVI), the provider may perform left ventricular angiography to visualize the left, lower ventricle of the heart and assess the patient’s tricuspid regurgitation. Providers may use CAVI to treat tricuspid regurgitation in which the heart’s tricuspid valve does not close properly, allowing blood to leak backward and making the heart work harder. The provider may perform right and left heart catheterization for hemodynamic measurements before, during, and after CAVI for guidance. The provider may need to perform a transseptal puncture, puncturing the wall that divides the left and right sides of the heart, as part of the procedure. Once the provider confirms the caval valve implants are in place, the provider removes the catheter and closes the access site. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Hemodynamics: Study of blood flow or circulation in the body. Superior and inferior venae cavae: The major trunks of the venous circulatory system; the superior vena cava brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation while the inferior vena cava brings it back from the lower body circulation. Tricuspid insufficiency: Impaired function of the tricuspid valve, such as when a leaking valve lets blood flow backward and causes regurgitation; in Ebstein anomaly the displacement of the posterior and septal leaflets cause backward flow of blood into the right atrium. Tricuspid valve: Valve consisting of three triangular membranous flaps (leaflets or cusps) situated at the opening of the right atrium of the heart into the right ventricle. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. short_description: Subretinal injection of a pharmacologic agent, including vitrectomy and 1 or more retinotomies Notes: (Report medication separately) (Do not report 0810T in conjunction with 67036, 67039, 67040, 67041, 67042, 67043)
lay_term: The provider removes vitreous fluid from the eye to access the posterior segment of the eye and cuts the retina one or more times. This procedure also includes injection of a pharmacologic agent beneath the retina. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may place a special contact lens on the patient’s cornea, the transparent membrane of the outer layer of the eyeball. The provider may use different types of equipment to incise the eye to expose the sclera (white part of the eye) and make incisions about the entire circumference of the cornea. The provider may make small incisions to insert a lighted cannula, an infusion cannula, and cutting and suction instruments. Once the instruments are in place, the provider removes vitreous from the eye (called vitrectomy). The vitreous humor is the semi–liquid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. In this procedure, the provider removes this substance to gain surgical access to the back of the eye. The provider makes one or more incisions in the retina (called retinotomy). The provider also injects a pharmacologic agent in the subretinal space, a potential space between the retina and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a thin layer of pigmented cells that absorb light. Once the procedure is complete, the provider removes the instruments and closes the incisions. The provider may inject a sterile solution into the eye to restore pressure. The provider also may apply a pressure patch with an antibiotic ointment. Terminology Cannula: A tube, not as flexible perhaps as a catheter, inserted into the body to deliver or drain fluids or supply oxygen and through which instruments and monitoring devices can be inserted. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina; also called crystalline lens. Posterior segment: The back part of the eye. Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Sclera: The white outer part of the eye that covers all of the eyeball except for the cornea. Vitrectomy: Surgical method to remove some or all of the vitreous humor, a semifluid substance that fills the region between the lens and the retina of the eye. short_description: Remote multi-day complex uroflowmetry (eg, calibrated electronic equipment); set-up and patient education on use of equipment
lay_term: The provider sets up specialized electronic equipment for a test that measures urine flow. The provider educates the patient on the use of the equipment. short_description: Ultrasound-based radiofrequency echographic multi-spectrometry (REMS), bone-density study and fracture-risk assessment, 1 or more sites, hips, pelvis, or spine
lay_term: The provider uses ultrasound–based radiofrequency echographic multi–spectrometry (REMS) for a bone–density study and fracture–risk assessment. The test involves placing a noninvasive probe at one or more sites (hips, pelvis, spine) to collect detailed information about the bone’s structure and then using that data to assess bone health. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider places the probe on the skin to visualize the target bone. The test may involve one or more sites (hip, pelvis, and/or spine). The provider sets the values for the equipment, such as scan depth. Software may identify the regions of interest for evaluation. The provider performs the scan. The ultrasound signals are unfiltered, meaning they contain a lot of detailed information about the tissues they pass through. This is different from conventional ultrasound methods, which filter out some of this information. The software used in REMS analysis may compare these signals to reference models of healthy and diseased bone condition to help determine the health status of the bone being examined. The data collected provides information about the internal structure of the bone, which can help estimate its strength and predict the risk of fractures. lay_term: A physician or other qualified healthcare professional (QHP) provides continuous, in–person monitoring and intervention during a patient’s psychedelic medication therapy. This service is necessary due to potential emotional and physiological issues that can occur during the therapy. Report this code per hour. This code is specific to the first physician or other QHP. Explanation The provider begins by supervising the patient’s self–administration of a psychedelic medication in a therapeutic setting. These medications are known to induce distinctive alterations in perception, which can potentially place the patient at risk for emotional vulnerability and physiological instability. Physiological refers to the normal functions and processes that occur in the body. Following the administration of the medication, the provider is responsible for continuous in–person monitoring of the patient. This is crucial as the pharmacological risks of the medication can last for several hours. During this monitoring period, the provider may need to intervene to support the patient’s physical, emotional, and psychological safety. This could involve psychotherapy, crisis intervention, or other methods, depending on the patient’s needs. The goal of these interventions is to optimize treatment outcomes, ensuring that the patient is safe and that the therapy is as effective as possible. This code is specific to the first physician or other qualified healthcare professional. Report this code per hour. Tips See +0821T for the second physician or other QHP, concurrent with the first. See +0822T for clinical staff concurrent with the first physician or other QHP. short_description: Transcatheter insertion of permanent single-chamber leadless pacemaker, right atrial, including imaging guidance (eg, fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, right atrial angiography and/or right ventriculography, femoral venography, cavography) and device evaluation (eg, interrogation or programming), when performed Notes: (Do not report 0823T in conjunction with 33274, 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0802T)
lay_term: The provider uses a catheter to implant a permanent right atrial pacemaker in the heart. The provider may use imaging guidance for the procedure and perform device evaluation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider punctures the skin to insert a catheter into a vein and navigates the catheter through the blood vessels to reach the heart, typically using imaging guidance. For instance, the provider may use fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, right atrial angiography and right ventriculography (injecting dye to visualize the heart chambers), femoral venography, and cavography (vena cava angiography). The provider uses the catheter to implant a pulse generator with a built–in battery and electrode in the right atrium (upper chamber) of the heart. The provider then removes the catheter from the body and controls any bleeding. The provider may interrogate (test) the pacemaker’s function and adjust the programming parameters after insertion. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Venae cavae (sing. vena cava): The large veins that carry deoxygenated blood into the heart; the superior vena cava carries blood from the upper parts of the body, and the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower parts of the body; these two empty into the right atrium of the heart. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips For right atrial, single–chamber leadless pacemaker systems, choose the code based on the service provided: insertion (0823T), removal (0824T), removal and replacement (0825T), programming device evaluation (0826T). short_description: Transcatheter removal and replacement of permanent single-chamber leadless pacemaker, right atrial, including imaging guidance (eg, fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, right atrial angiography and/or right ventriculography, femoral venography, cavography) and device evaluation (eg, interrogation or programming), when performed Notes: (Do not report 0825T in conjunction with 33274, 0795T, 0796T, 0797T, 0802T)
lay_term: The provider uses a catheter to remove and replace a permanent right atrial pacemaker in the heart. The provider may use imaging guidance for the procedure and perform device evaluation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider punctures the skin to insert a catheter into a vein and navigates the catheter through the blood vessels to reach the heart, typically using imaging guidance. For instance, the provider may use fluoroscopy, venous ultrasound, right atrial angiography and right ventriculography (injecting dye to visualize the heart chambers), femoral venography, and cavography (vena cava angiography). The provider uses the catheter to remove a previously placed leadless pacemaker (pulse generator with a built–in battery and electrode) from the right atrium (upper chamber) of the heart. The provider then uses the catheter to place a new right atrial pacemaker. The provider removes the catheter from the body and controls any bleeding. The provider may interrogate (test) the pacemaker’s function and adjust the programming parameters after insertion. Terminology Angiography: A medical imaging technique in which the provider injects a dye into blood vessels and uses plain X–rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to visualize the inside (lumen) of the vessels; more specific terms include arteriography when performed on the arteries or venography when performed on the veins; angiography can also be used to study blood supply to organs such as the heart, kidneys, and liver. Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Fluoroscopy: A live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Venae cavae (sing. vena cava): The large veins that carry deoxygenated blood into the heart; the superior vena cava carries blood from the upper parts of the body, and the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower parts of the body; these two empty into the right atrium of the heart. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips For right atrial, single–chamber leadless pacemaker systems, choose the code based on the service provided: insertion (0823T), removal (0824T), removal and replacement (0825T), programming device evaluation (0826T). short_description: Opto-acoustic imaging, breast, unilateral, including axilla when performed, real-time with image documentation, augmentative analysis and report (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0857T in conjunction with 76641, 76642)
lay_term: As an add–on service to conventional breast ultrasound, the provider uses a probe to perform real–time noninvasive opto–acoustic imaging of the breast. The service includes imaging of the axilla (armpit area), when performed. The service also includes image documentation, augmentative analysis, and a report. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, and as an add–on service to conventional breast ultrasound, the provider places a probe on the patient’s skin to perform opto–acoustic imaging of a single breast. The provider may image the axilla (armpit area), as well. Opto–acoustic imaging uses light (such as laser) to enable visualization of the target site. The probe sends pulses of light into breast tissue and receives light energy converted to sound pressure waves, similar to ultrasound. The combination of opto–acoustic imaging and ultrasound produces high–resolution images that help identify whether target tissue contains characteristics of a malignant tumor. For instance, compared to benign tumors, areas around malignant tumors tend to have increased blood concentration with decreased oxygen content. The service also includes image documentation, augmentative analysis, and a report. Augmentative refers to a machine (software) analyzing or quantifying data in a clinically meaningful way. As an example, the machine may provide image reference keys to help the provider and may provide a likelihood of malignancy. The provider interprets what the machine provides and creates a report. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. short_description: Externally applied transcranial magnetic stimulation with concomitant measurement of evoked cortical potentials with automated report Notes: (Do not report 0858T in conjunction with 95836, 95957, 95961, 95965, 95966) Code 0858T represents measurement of evoked cortical potentials associated with transcranial magnetic stimulation of two or more cortical areas using multiple, externally applied scalp electrode channels. Upon stimulation, the device performs automated signal processing indicating brain physiological features of connectivity, excitability, and plasticity, which may be impaired with structural and functional brain deficits. Because these physiological features may be altered in certain types of brain disease, the device's automated report of analyzed data is intended to provide clinical insight of brain function within the context of certain brain disease states.
lay_term: The provider applies electrodes on the patient’s scalp to deliver magnetic stimulation through the skull and measures the electrical activity of the brain in response to the stimuli. The testing device automatically processes signals and generates an automated report to assist the provider’s assessment for certain conditions affecting the brain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider places external electrodes on the patient’s scalp and uses them to perform transcranial (through the skull) magnetic stimulation. The test measures evoked cortical potentials, meaning it measures electrical activity in areas of the brain in response to the stimuli. The testing device processes the signals automatically to check certain physiological features of the brain. Physiological relates to the way a body or part functions. The test checks connectivity (how brain regions work together), excitability (strength of neuron response to stimulation), and plasticity (the brain’s ability to change and adapt). The device provides an automated report with data analysis to give the provider information to use when assessing the patient for certain structural and functional brain conditions. short_description: Digitization of glass microscope slides for cytopathology, smears, any other source; preparation, screening and interpretation (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0833T in conjunction with 88161)
lay_term: Code +0833T describes clinical staff work performed to scan and digitize whole–slide images from glass microscope slides to use for immediate or later pathologic diagnosis. Report one unit of this add–on code for digitizing slides from one unit of cytopathology code 88161, which describes cytopathology (cellular material) slides of specimens not from other listed sources (meaning 88161 is appropriate when the specimen is not represented in another code). Code 88161 involves preparation such as touching a tissue specimen to a slide to gather cells for examination, called a “touch prep.” Explanation Using a slide–scanning microscope, the clinical staff scans and digitizes glass slides to create whole–slide images for diagnosis. Code +0833T specifically describes the work to digitize glass slides prepared for a cytopathology exam of “other” cytopathology (cellular material) such as touch–preparation slides described by a single unit of 88161. The separate digital–slide exam may occur remotely in real time, or at a later time from a server or cloud–based digital image archive. To complete the 88161 service, a pathologist or other healthcare professional will evaluate and diagnose the digitized images, not just glass slides viewed directly through the microscope. The digitized–slide exam may include using computer–assisted image analysis and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Cytopathology: Specialized study of cells to evaluate disease processes. Digital image: A picture converted to numerical data for storage and viewing on a computer. Pathologic examination: Microscopic analysis of cellular material or tissue for abnormalities in structure or function. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. Report one unit of this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides only in addition to an 88161 cytopathology exam for pathologic diagnosis. Do not report this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides solely for purposes other than pathologic diagnosis, such as archiving slides after pathologic diagnosis is complete, educational purposes, or database creation. Do not report this code for sharing static or video images of a glass microscope slide using a mobile smartphone or tablet. Read Less

short_description: Digitization of glass microscope slides for in situ hybridization (eg, FISH), per specimen; initial single probe stain procedure (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0848T in conjunction with 88365)
lay_term: Code +0848T describes clinical staff work performed to scan and digitize whole–slide images from glass microscope slides to use for immediate or later pathologic diagnosis. Report one unit of this add–on code for digitizing slides for one unit of code 88365, which describes an initial single–probe in situ hybridization stain procedure. Explanation Using a slide–scanning microscope, the clinical staff scans and digitizes glass slides to create whole–slide images for diagnosis. Code +0848T specifically describes the work to digitize glass slides prepared for an initial single–probe in situ hybridization stain procedure for a surgical pathology specimen, described by a single unit of 88365. The separate digital–slide exam may occur remotely in real time, or at a later time from a server or cloud–based digital image archive. To complete the 88365 service, a pathologist or other healthcare professional will evaluate and diagnose the digitized images, not just glass slides viewed directly through the microscope. The digitized–slide exam may include using computer–assisted image analysis and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Digital image: A picture converted to numerical data for storage and viewing on a computer. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): A laboratory test in which a special stain that includes a DNA or RNA probe, which selectively attaches to a target segment of DNA or RNA, is applied to a tissue sample in situ hybridization (ISH); the probe includes some kind of marker, often a fluorescent molecule, which can be analyzed with a fluorescence microscope to detect and localize the target in the tissue (fluorescence ISH, or FISH); fluorescence describes a substance which absorbs and emits light. Hybridization: Forming a double–stranded DNA or RNA molecule by combining two complementary single strands, usually to identify a genetic mutation. In situ hybridization (ISH): A laboratory test in which a special strain that includes a DNA or RNA probe, which selectively attaches to a target segment of DNA or RNA, is applied to a tissue sample; the tissue can then be analyzed with a microscope to identify antigens and/or cell types. Pathologic examination: Microscopic analysis of cellular material or tissue for abnormalities in structure or function. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. Report one unit of this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides only in addition to an 88365 initial single–probe in situ hybridization stain procedure for pathologic diagnosis. Do not report this code if the referring physician submits digital images of the slides. Do not report this code for scanning and digitizing glass slides solely for purposes other than pathologic diagnosis, such as archiving slides after pathologic diagnosis is complete, educational purposes, or database creation. Do not report this code for sharing static or video images of a glass microscope slide using a mobile smartphone or tablet. Read Less

short_description: Quantitative magnetic resonance image (MRI) analysis of the brain with comparison to prior magnetic resonance (MR) study(ies), including lesion identification, characterization, and quantification, with brain volume(s) quantification and/or severity score, when performed, data preparation and transmission, interpretation and report, obtained without diagnostic MRI examination of the brain during the same session Notes: (Do not report 0865T in conjunction with 70551, 70552, 70553)
lay_term: The provider uses imaging data and software for quantitative MRI brain analysis, including comparison to previous MRI studies. The provider prepares the data, transmits the data for analysis and provides an interpretation and report. Explanation For quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) analysis of the brain, the provider uses specialized software to evaluate imaging data. A quantitative measurement measures quantity. This is an objective assessment, using computer algorithms, as opposed to a subjective evaluation based on the provider’s visual inspection. The service includes comparison to one or more prior magnetic resonance (MR) studies, and includes lesion identification, characterization, and quantification. This may include brain volume quantification and a severity score. The provider prepares the data, transmits the data, and provides an interpretation and report. This code is appropriate when the service is performed without same–session diagnostic MRI of the brain. Tips See +0866T for the service when obtained with diagnostic MRI examination of the brain. short_description: Implantation of subcutaneous peritoneal ascites pump system, percutaneous, including pump-pocket creation, insertion of tunneled indwelling bladder and peritoneal catheters with pump connections, including all imaging and initial programming, when performed Notes: (Do not report 0870T in conjunction with 49082, 49083, 49405, 49406, 49418, 51100, 51101, 51102, 76942, 76989, 77002, 0871T, 0872T, 0873T, 0874T, 0875T)
lay_term: The provider uses a minimally invasive approach to implant a peritoneal ascites pump system, including placing the pump in a pocket under the skin and inserting tubes to carry fluid from the abdomen’s peritoneal space to the bladder. The provider may use imaging for the procedure and program the pump. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to create a pocket under the skin for the peritoneal ascites pump, such as in the right or left upper quadrant of the abdomen. The provider then inserts catheters (tubes), tunneling them through tissue, possibly suturing them in place. One tube extends from the pump to the peritoneal space, which is the space between the two layers of the peritoneum, the membrane that lines the abdominal wall and covers the abdominal organs. A second tube extends from the pump to the bladder. The provider may use imaging to guide and complete the procedure. The provider connects the tubes to the pump, ensures the pump is properly placed in the pocket, and confirms the system is functioning properly. The pump is designed to treat peritoneal ascites, a medical condition characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity. The provider may program the system, such as to ensure that the optimal amount of ascites is removed each day on a schedule based on the patient’s individual daily routine. The provider closes the pump pocket to complete the procedure. short_description: Esophagoscopy, flexible, transoral, with initial transendoscopic mechanical dilation (eg, nondrug-coated balloon) followed by therapeutic drug delivery by drug-coated balloon catheter for esophageal stricture, including fluoroscopic guidance, when performed Notes: (Do not report 0884T in conjunction with 43191, 43195, 43196, 43200, 43213, 43214, 43220, 43226, 76000)
lay_term: The provider passes a flexible endoscope through the mouth and into the esophagus, the tube from the mouth to the stomach. The provider uses mechanical means to dilate an esophageal stricture (narrowing). The provider then uses a drug–coated balloon catheter to deliver drug therapy for the stricture. The provider may use fluoroscopic guidance for the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the esophagoscopy. The provider inserts a flexible endoscope through the patient’s mouth and down into the esophagus, which is the muscular tube that connects the throat to the stomach. An endoscope is a flexible tube with a light and a camera on the end, which allows the provider to see the inside of the esophagus. Once the endoscope is in place, the provider performs an initial transendoscopic mechanical dilation. Transendoscopic means the procedure is performed through an endoscope. Mechanical dilation is the process of widening a narrow area, in this case, the esophagus. An example is inflating a balloon (not drug–coated) inside the esophagus to stretch the tissue. After the initial dilation, the provider delivers a therapeutic drug using a device known as a drug–coated balloon catheter. A catheter is a thin, flexible tube, and in this case, it has a balloon on the end that’s coated with medication. The balloon is inflated in the esophagus, allowing the drug to be delivered directly to the tissue. The provider may also use fluoroscopic guidance during this procedure. Fluoroscopy is a type of imaging that uses X–rays to create real–time moving images of the inside of the body. This can help the provider guide the endoscope and the balloon catheter to the correct location in the esophagus. The procedure is performed to treat a condition known as esophageal stricture, which is a narrowing of the esophagus that can make it difficult to swallow. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes the endoscope. short_description: Histotripsy (ie, non-thermal ablation via acoustic energy delivery) of malignant renal tissue, including imaging guidance
lay_term: The provider uses a special device to deliver ultrasound energy into the body to destroy cancerous renal (kidney) tissue. The provider monitors the procedure using image guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider uses a special device that delivers pulsed ultrasound energy to destroy malignant renal tissue (cancerous kidney tissue). In a typical procedure, the treatment does not require incisions or needles. The provider uses a special device to deliver ultrasound pulses in the targeted cancerous renal tissue to determine the energy required to create microbubbles from gases present in the targeted tissue. When the bubble clouds form and collapse, they destroy cells and tissues. After determining the energy requirement, the provider initiates treatment, and the system moves the microbubbles through the planned area to destroy the cancerous tissue. The provider uses imaging guidance to monitor the treatment in real–time. short_description: Personalized target development for accelerated, repetitive high-dose functional connectivity MRI-guided theta-burst stimulation derived from a structural and resting-state functional MRI, including data preparation and transmission, generation of the target, motor threshold-starting location, neuronavigation files and target report, review and interpretation Notes: (Report 0889T once per personalized target development) (Do not report 0889T in conjunction with 70551, 70552, 70553, 70554, 70555, for the same session) (Do not report 0889T in conjunction with 77022)
lay_term: The provider performs the services necessary for personalized target development for a noninvasive brain stimulation technique called accelerated, repetitive high–dose functional connectivity MRI–guided theta–burst stimulation. The provider uses structural and resting–state functional MRI data and provides data preparation and transmission, target generation, motor threshold–starting location (the specific area on the scalp where magnetic pulses are first applied), neuronavigation files and target report, and a review and interpretation. Explanation The provider performs services for personalized target development for accelerated, repetitive high–dose functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)–guided theta–burst stimulation. The service is a noninvasive brain stimulation technique. It uses magnetic fields to stimulate specific areas of the brain. The procedure is guided by functional connectivity MRI, which provides images of brain activity and helps identify the areas of the brain to be targeted. Functional connectivity is determined using resting–state functional MRI (fMRI) and describes brain regions that activate together. Theta–burst stimulation is a specific pattern of stimulation that may be more efficient and effective than traditional repetitive transcranial (through the skull) magnetic stimulation patterns. It involves bursts of high–frequency stimulation, which can either increase or decrease the excitability of the targeted brain area, depending on the pattern of stimulation used. For personalized target development, the provider performs data preparation and transmission, which includes collecting and processing the patient’s structural and resting–state fMRI scans. Once the data is prepared, it is transmitted to the system that will be used for the theta–burst stimulation procedure. During the target generation step, a specific target area in the brain is identified. This target area is the part of the brain that will be stimulated during the theta–burst stimulation procedure. The target is determined based on the patient’s specific condition, MRI data, and the goals of the treatment. The provider determines the motor threshold–starting location, determining the specific area on the scalp where magnetic pulses are first applied. The service also involves neuronavigation files. Neuronavigation is a technology used to accurately target specific areas of the brain. For instance, the individual’s MRI scans may be used to create a 3D model of the brain, which is then used to guide the placement of the stimulation device. The provider generates a target report, detailing the target area for the theta–burst stimulation, which may explain why the area was chosen, how it will be targeted, and what the expected outcomes are. Finally, the provider reviews and interprets all the information gathered and prepared in the previous steps. This review ensures that the procedure is planned accurately and safely for the individual patient. short_description: Noninvasive assessment of blood oxygenation, gas exchange efficiency, and cardiorespiratory status, with physician or other qualified health care professional interpretation and report
lay_term: The provider uses a noninvasive approach to assess the patient’s blood oxygenation, gas exchange efficiency, and cardiorespiratory status. For instance, a typical service may involve having the patient breathe into a special device connected to a monitor that displays the resulting measurements. A physician or other qualified healthcare professional then interprets the data and writes a report. Explanation The provider uses a specialized device to perform a noninvasive assessment of blood oxygenation, gas exchange efficiency, and cardiorespiratory status. Blood oxygenation refers to the level of oxygen in the blood. It’s a measure of how well oxygen is being delivered to the body’s tissues and organs. Gas exchange efficiency refers to how effectively the lungs are able to transfer oxygen from the air into the blood and remove carbon dioxide from the blood into the air. This process occurs in the tiny air sacs in the lungs, called alveoli. Cardiorespiratory status is a broad term that refers to the health and functioning of the heart and lungs. Assessing cardiorespiratory status can help healthcare providers detect conditions such as heart disease or lung disease. An example of a device for the service is a handheld device the patient breathes into. The device is connected to a monitor that displays the precise measurements. A physician or other qualified healthcare professional then interprets the data and writes a report. short_description: Connection of liver allograft to normothermic machine perfusion device, hemostasis control; initial 4 hours of monitoring time, including hourly physiological and laboratory assessments (eg, perfusate temperature, perfusate pH, hemodynamic parameters, bile production, bile pH, bile glucose, biliary bicarbonate, lactate levels, macroscopic assessment)
lay_term: The provider connects a liver allograft to a perfusion device that helps preserve the organ for transplantation. This code represents the first four hours of monitoring and assessments. Explanation The provider connects a liver allograft to the normothermic perfusion device using tubes (cannulas) previously placed in the liver. A liver allograft is a liver transplant graft from another human. The normothermic perfusion device circulates a warm, oxygenated blood–based solution through the liver, which helps to preserve the organ and assess its function before transplantation. The provider ensures hemostasis, which involves checking for and controlling any bleeding from the cannulation sites or other areas of the liver. Once the liver is connected and stable, the initial four hours of monitoring begins. This includes hourly physiological and laboratory assessments. Parameters that are typically monitored include perfusate temperature, perfusate pH, hemodynamic parameters, bile production, bile pH, bile glucose, biliary bicarbonate, lactate levels, and a macroscopic assessment of the liver. Perfusate temperature is the heat level of the fluid being circulated through the organ during the perfusion process. The acidity or alkalinity of this fluid, known as the perfusate pH, is crucial to maintain for the health of the organ during perfusion. Hemodynamic parameters are measurements that relate to blood flow. Bile pH refers to the acidity or alkalinity of bile, a fluid the liver creates that aids in digestion, especially in breaking down fats. Bile also contains a certain amount of glucose. Biliary bicarbonate is a substance within bile that helps maintain a balanced pH. Lactate levels refer to the amount of lactate, a chemical produced often in response to low oxygen levels. High lactate levels in the blood can indicate organ dysfunction. Lastly, a macroscopic assessment is a visual examination of the organ that allows the provider to identify any obvious signs of disease or damage. Any abnormalities in these parameters are addressed as needed to ensure the liver remains viable for transplantation. Tips See 0894T for the cannulation and decannulation service. See +0896T for each additional hour of the perfusion service. short_description: Noninvasive augmentative arrhythmia analysis derived from quantitative computational cardiac arrhythmia simulations, based on selected intervals of interest from 12-lead electrocardiogram and uploaded clinical parameters, including uploading clinical parameters with interpretation and report Notes: (Do not report 0897T in conjunction with 93000, 93005, 93010, when performed on the same day)
lay_term: The provider uses a noninvasive, artificial intelligence (AI)–based approach to mapping heart arrhythmias (irregular heartbeats), using data from a 12–lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and certain patient health data. The provider completes an interpretation and report. Explanation The provider performs or collects the data from a 12–lead electrocardiogram (ECG) on the patient. This is a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart and can help detect any abnormalities or arrhythmias (irregular heartbeats). The provider selects intervals of interest from the ECG. These are specific parts of the ECG waveform that the provider believes may indicate an arrhythmia or other cardiac issue. The provider uploads these intervals of interest, along with other clinical parameters (measurable patient health data), into a computational cardiac arrhythmia simulation. This is a computer program that uses mathematical models to simulate the electrical activity of the heart, allowing the provider to analyze the potential effects of different arrhythmias. For instance, it may generate 3D cardiac maps beat–by–beat. The technology provides augmentative analysis, which means the technology analyzes or quantifies the data to yield clinically meaningful output, but it doesn’t provide an independent diagnosis or management decision. The provider will then interpret the results of the simulation and create a report. short_description: Open implantation of integrated neurostimulation system, vagus nerve, including analysis and programming, when performed Notes: (Do not report 0908T in conjunction with 64553, 64568, 0909T, 0910T, 0911T, 0912T)
lay_term: The provider performs open surgery to implant an integrated neurostimulation device on the vagus nerve. This procedure may also include checking and setting up the device to ensure it functions correctly. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision, typically on the left side of the neck, over the vagus nerve. lay_term: The provider uses a percutaneous approach to deliver therapeutic drugs by catheter to a major coronary artery or a branch. The catheter has a balloon that is coated with medication. The procedure also includes mechanical dilation of the artery using a nondrug–coated balloon and imaging techniques to guide and confirm the intervention. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins by making a small incision to access the vascular system percutaneously (minimally invasive access through the skin). The provider inserts a catheter and navigates it to the target coronary artery or branch, using angiography and possibly other imaging techniques, such as intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) or optical coherence tomography (OCT, which uses light waves), to visualize the area. This code includes necessary radiological supervision and interpretation. The provider traverses the lesion, as necessary (navigating through the blockage). Once the catheter is in place, the provider first performs mechanical dilation of the artery using a balloon that is not coated with drugs. This step widens the artery to improve blood flow. Following this, the provider uses a drug–delivery balloon to deliver therapeutic medication directly to the artery walls. The balloon may be coated in a drug or in a substance that releases a drug over time (eluting). The provider inflates the drug–delivery balloon to ensure the medication is evenly applied to the affected area. After completing the drug delivery, the provider may use additional imaging to confirm the success of the intervention. The procedure concludes with the removal of the catheter and closure of the access site. short_description: Insertion of permanent cardiac contractility modulation-defibrillation system component(s), including fluoroscopic guidance, and evaluation and programming of sensing and therapeutic parameters; pulse generator and dual transvenous electrodes/leads (pacing and defibrillation)
lay_term: The provider implants a permanent cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation system, which includes a pulse generator and two transvenous leads. The procedure involves using fluoroscopic guidance to place one lead for pacing and another for defibrillation. After implantation, the provider evaluates and programs the device to ensure it functions correctly. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to create a pocket under the skin in the pectoral (chest) region. The provider inserts a pulse generator into this pocket for a cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation (CCM–D) system. A CCM–D system combines cardiac contractility modulation (CCM), which improves the heart’s pumping ability to alleviate chronic heart failure symptoms, with defibrillation to protect against sudden cardiac arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat). Under fluoroscopic guidance, the provider accesses the venous system and navigates a pacing lead and a defibrillation lead (electrodes) through the veins to the heart. Fluoroscopy is a type of imaging that uses X–rays to create real–time moving images of the inside of the body. The provider places the pacing lead on the high septum of the right ventricle, which is the upper part of the wall that separates the heart’s lower chambers. The provider places the defibrillation lead (which provides an electric shock to restore heart rhythm) in the middle part of the septum. After securing the leads, the provider connects them to the pulse generator. The provider then evaluates and programs the device, adjusting sensing and therapeutic parameters to ensure optimal function. Once the device is properly set up, the provider closes the incisions. guidelines: Cat III Guidelines Code Specific Guideline A cardiac contractility modulation-defibrillation (CCM-D) system combines cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) for symptom relief from chronic heart failure with defibrillation protection against sudden cardiac arrhythmia into a single therapy. A CCM-D system consists of a pulse generator and two transvenous electrodes (leads): one defibrillation lead and one pacemaker lead. An implantable CCM-D system’s electrodes (leads) are placed transvenously under fluoroscopic guidance. One right ventricular pacing lead is placed on the high septum and a second defibrillation lead is placed in the mid-septum. The pulse generator is implanted in a subcutaneous pocket in the pectoral region. A CCM-D differs from a CCM system (0408T-0418T). A CCM system consists of a pulse generator and two ventricular pacemaker electrodes (leads) and does not include a defibrillator component. Do not report CCM-D services in conjunction with 0408T-0418T. All services associated with CCM-D implantation, revision, extraction, and follow-up should be reported utilizing Category III codes 0915T-0931T. Do not report CCM-D services with existing Category I codes for pacemaker and defibrillator services (33206-33275). All catheterization and imaging guidance required to complete a CCM-D procedure are included in the work of each code. Contractility evaluation and programming of sensing and therapeutic parameters (0926T, 0927T) are performed each time a pulse generator or lead is implanted or replaced and cannot be reported separately. For the implantation of a CCM-D system (generator plus dual leads), report 0915T. If only a pulse generator is implanted without insertion of transvenous electrodes, report 0916T for the implantation or 0923T for the removal and replacement. When CCM-D leads are placed without insertion of a pulse generator, report 0917T for a single-lead insertion or 0918T when both leads are inserted. In certain circumstances, relocation of the skin pocket is required and is reported using 0925T. Skin pocket relocation includes all services associated with the initial pocket (eg, opening the pocket, incision and drainage of hematoma or abscess if performed, and any closure performed), in addition to the creation of a new pocket for the new generator to be placed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the venous system and navigates to the two transvenous leads. Using fluoroscopic guidance, the provider breaks up scar tissue as needed and carefully extracts both the pacing lead and the defibrillation lead from the heart and the veins. Fluoroscopy is a type of imaging that uses X–rays to create real–time moving images of the inside of the body. A cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation (CCM–D) system combines cardiac contractility modulation (CCM), which improves the heart’s pumping ability to alleviate chronic heart failure symptoms, with defibrillation, which protects against sudden cardiac arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat). The provider disconnects the leads from the pulse generator if necessary. After removing the leads, the provider inspects the site and ensures there is no bleeding or complications. The provider then closes the incision. lay_term: The provider removes and replaces the pulse generator of a permanent cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation system. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the pocket under the skin in the pectoral (chest) region where the pulse generator is located. The provider carefully removes the pulse generator component of the cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation (CCM–D) system. The provider then implants the new pulse generator and connects it to the existing leads, if appropriate. Finally, the provider evaluates and programs the new device, adjusting sensing and therapeutic parameters to ensure optimal function, and closes the incision. short_description: Programming device evaluation (in person) with iterative adjustment of the implantable device to test the function of the device and select optimal permanent programmed values with analysis, including review and report, implantable cardiac contractility modulation-defibrillation system Notes: (Do not report 0926T in conjunction with 33206-33275, 0915T, 0916T, 0917T, 0918T, 0919T, 0920T, 0921T, 0922T, 0923T, 0924T, 0927T, 0930T, 0931T)
lay_term: The provider conducts an in–person programming device evaluation for an implantable cardiac contractility modulation–defibrillation system. The session includes making adjustments to test the device’s function, selecting optimal programmed values, and performing an analysis with a review and report of the findings. Explanation The provider evaluates the implantable contractility modulation–defibrillation (CCM–D) system in person. A CCM–D system includes a pulse generator and two leads (electrodes). It combines cardiac contractility modulation (CCM), which improves the heart’s pumping ability to alleviate chronic heart failure symptoms, with defibrillation, which protects against sudden cardiac arrhythmia, offering both therapies in a single device. The provider makes iterative adjustments (progressive changes) to the device’s settings to test its function, ensuring it operates correctly and effectively. This process includes checking the device’s response to different settings and selecting the optimal programmed values. The provider analyzes the data collected during the adjustments, reviews the results, and prepares a report. The entire process ensures the device is functioning optimally and delivering the best possible therapeutic benefit to the patient. short_description: Noninvasive detection of heart failure derived from augmentative analysis of an echocardiogram that demonstrated preserved ejection fraction, with interpretation and report by a physician or other qualified health care professional Notes: (Use 0932T in conjunction with a concurrent echocardiography [separately reported] or a previously performed transthoracic echocardiography [ie, 93306, 93307, 93308, 93350, 93351])
lay_term: The provider performs a noninvasive detection of heart failure using augmentative analysis of an echocardiogram, which shows a preserved ejection fraction. The service involves analyzing the echocardiogram to detect signs of heart failure, even though the heart’s pumping function appears normal. The physician or other qualified healthcare professional interprets the results and prepares a report. Explanation Using data from a separately reported echocardiogram (a type of ultrasound imaging that evaluates the heart’s structure and function), the provider uses augmentative analysis to detect potential heart failure. Augmentative analysis means the machine analyzes or quantifies data to produce clinically meaningful information. The echocardiogram demonstrates a preserved ejection fraction, meaning that the heart is pumping blood effectively. However, the service looks for other signs of heart failure that may not be immediately apparent from the ejection fraction alone. This analysis helps to identify heart failure in patients whose hearts are still pumping normally. A physician or other qualified healthcare professional then interprets the findings and prepares a report. short_description: Transcatheter implantation of wireless left atrial pressure sensor for long-term left atrial pressure monitoring, including sensor calibration and deployment, right heart catheterization, transseptal puncture, imaging guidance, and radiological supervision and interpretation Notes: (Do not report 0933T in conjunction with 33289, 36013, 36014, 36015, 75741, 75743, 75746, 76000, 93451, 93453, 93456, 93457, 93460, 93461, 93568, 93569, 93573, 93593, 93594, 93596, 93597, 93598) (For implantation of a wireless pulmonary artery pressure sensor, use 33289)
lay_term: The provider uses a catheter to implant a small, wireless sensor in the left atrium of the heart. This sensor monitors left atrial pressure over time. The procedure includes right heart catheterization (insertion of a catheter into the right side of the heart), a transseptal puncture (piercing the septum to access the left atrium), and the use of imaging to guide the placement and calibration of the sensor. The code also includes radiological supervision and interpretation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins by performing a right heart catheterization. This involves inserting a catheter into a large vein, typically in the groin, and threading it through the vascular system into the right side of the heart. The provider then performs a transseptal puncture, which involves puncturing the septum, the wall separating the right and left sides of the heart, to access the left atrium. Using imaging guidance, the provider carefully positions and implants the wireless sensor in the left atrium. The sensor is calibrated to monitor the pressure within the left atrium, which is crucial for assessing the patient’s heart function. Radiological supervision and interpretation are included in this code. Once the sensor is in place and functioning correctly, the provider removes the catheter and completes the procedure. short_description: Remote monitoring of a wireless left atrial pressure sensor for up to 30 days, including data from daily uploads of left atrial pressure recordings, interpretation(s) and trend analysis, with adjustments to the diuretics plan, treatment paradigm thresholds, medications or lifestyle modifications, when performed, and report(s) by a physician or other qualified health care professional Notes: (Report 0934T only once per 30 days) (Do not report 0934T, if monitoring period is less than 16 days) (Do not report 0934T in conjunction with 93264) (For remote monitoring of an implantable wireless pulmonary artery pressure sensor, use 93264)
