short_description: Cystourethroscopy with renal pelvic sympathetic denervation, radiofrequency ablation, retrograde ureteral approach, including insertion of guide wire, selective placement of ureteral sheath(s) and multiple conformable electrodes, contrast injection(s), and fluoroscopy, bilateral Notes: (Do not report 0935T in conjunction with 52000, 52005, 76000, 0338T, 0339T)
lay_term: The provider uses a cystourethroscope to examine the urinary tract and performs renal pelvic sympathetic denervation, a process that reduces nerve activity in the kidney, using radiofrequency ablation. The procedure is performed by accessing the kidney through the ureter, and it includes inserting a guide wire, placing a ureteral sheath, and using fluoroscopy to guide the procedure. This code represents a bilateral service. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins by inserting a cystourethroscope through the urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body) and into the bladder. A cystourethroscope is a thin tube with a camera and light that allows the provider to see the inside of the urinary tract. The provider then uses a retrograde approach, meaning they move the scope against the normal flow of urine, to access the ureters (the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder) and renal pelvis (the central part of the kidney). To accomplish this, the provider inserts a guide wire to help navigate through the ureter and places one or more ureteral sheaths (protective tubes). The provider then uses radiofrequency ablation, a technique that uses heat to destroy nerve tissue, to perform sympathetic denervation in the renal pelvis. The provider uses multiple conformable electrodes (flexible electrodes that can adapt to the tissue’s shape) to complete the service. Sympathetic denervation reduces the nerve signals that can contribute to high blood pressure or other kidney–related issues. Throughout the procedure, the provider uses one or more contrast injections and fluoroscopy, a type of real–time X–ray imaging, to guide the instruments and ensure accurate placement. This is a bilateral service, so the provider repeats the work of navigating the second ureter and performing ablation in the second kidney. After completing the ablation, the provider removes the instruments. short_description: Photobiomodulation therapy of retina, single session Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 0936T with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider uses a light therapy technique known as photobiomodulation to treat the retina, the light–sensitive layer at the back of the eye. This procedure involves a single session where the provider applies low–level light to the retina to stimulate healing, reduce inflammation, and promote cell repair. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider begins the photobiomodulation therapy session. The therapy involves applying low–level light directly to the retina, the part of the eye that detects light and sends visual signals to the brain. The light used in photobiomodulation is typically in the red or near–infrared spectrum and is known to promote cellular repair and reduce inflammation in the treated area. The provider carefully administers the light to the retina, targeting areas that require healing or reduction in inflammation. This noninvasive therapy session is completed in a single treatment. short_description: External electrocardiographic recording for greater than 15 days up to 30 days by continuous rhythm recording and storage; including recording, scanning analysis with report, review and interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional
lay_term: The provider uses an external device to continuously record and store the patient’s heart rhythm for more than 15 days and up to 30 days. After the monitoring period, the provider scans the recorded data, interprets it, and generates a report on the findings. This helps assess the patient’s heart function over an extended period. Explanation The provider connects the patient’s external electrocardiographic recording device and instructs the patient to wear the device for more than 15 days and up to 30 days. The device continuously records the heart’s electrical activity, capturing any irregularities in rhythm over an extended period. After the monitoring period is complete, the provider retrieves the device and scans the recorded data. The provider then carefully reviews and interprets the data, looking for signs of abnormal heart rhythms or other issues that could indicate heart disease or other conditions. Based on this analysis, the provider generates a report summarizing the findings, which may be used to guide further treatment or intervention. This code includes all aspects of the recording, data analysis, and professional interpretation by a physician or other qualified healthcare provider. Tips To report individual components, choose from 0938T (recording, including initial connection and recording), 0939T (scanning analysis with report), and 0940T (review and interpretation by a physician or other qualified healthcare professional). short_description: Cystourethroscopy, flexible; with insertion and expansion of prostatic urethral scaffold using integrated cystoscopic visualization Notes: (For insertion of permanent urethral stent, use 52282) (For placement of temporary prostatic urethral stent, use 53855)
lay_term: The provider uses a flexible cystourethroscope to insert and expand a prostatic urethral scaffold, a device designed to support and widen the urethra in patients with conditions that cause narrowing. The provider uses the integrated camera in the cystourethroscope to visualize the urethra during the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a flexible cystourethroscope through the urethra (tube that carries urine out of the body). The cystourethroscope is a thin, flexible tube with a light and a camera that allows the provider to see the inside of the urinary tract. The provider then advances a prostatic urethral scaffold through the cystourethroscope to the site of narrowing within the urethra. The scaffold is expanded to support and maintain the urethral opening, preventing further narrowing. The procedure is performed under visualization using the camera integrated into the cystourethroscope, ensuring precise placement of the scaffold. Once the scaffold is securely in place and the urethra is adequately supported, the provider removes the cystourethroscope. short_description: 3D contour simulation of target liver lesion(s) and margin(s) for image-guided percutaneous microwave ablation Notes: (Report 0944T once per liver microwave ablation procedure) (Do not report 0944T in conjunction with 76376, 76377)
lay_term: The provider uses advanced software to create a 3D simulation of one or more liver lesions and surrounding tissue to plan the microwave ablation procedure. This simulation includes calculating the volume of tissue that will be ablated, overlaying the ablation plan onto CT images of the liver, and comparing the volumes before and after the procedure to ensure the treatment was effective. Explanation For a patient who will undergo image–guided percutaneous microwave ablation of one or more liver lesions, the provider uses specialized software to generate a 3D model of the liver lesions and their margins, which are the surrounding tissues that may also need to be treated. The provider uses this model to simulate the probe pathways and determine the best locations for the ablation needles. The software calculates the expected volume of the ablation cavity and overlays this information onto computed tomography (CT) images, helping the provider plan the procedure with precision. After the ablation, the provider uses the software to analyze additional CT images to compare the actual ablation volume with the planned volume, ensuring that the lesions were effectively treated. Report this code once per ablation session, regardless of the number of lesions targeted. short_description: Intraoperative assessment for abnormal (tumor) tissue, in-vivo, following partial mastectomy (eg, lumpectomy) using computer-aided fluorescence imaging (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 0945T in conjunction with 19301) (Report 0945T once per procedure) (Do not report 0945T in conjunction with 88172, 0546T)
lay_term: During a partial mastectomy, the provider performs the add–on service of using computer–aided fluorescence imaging to assess the surgical site for any remaining abnormal (tumor) tissue. This imaging technique helps the provider ensure the provider removes all tumor tissue during the procedure. Explanation At the same session as partial mastectomy, such as a lumpectomy, the provider uses computer–aided fluorescence imaging to evaluate the surgical site for any remaining abnormal tissue. The service is in–vivo, meaning it takes place in the patient. The fluorescence imaging involves the use of special dyes or agents that cause the abnormal tissue to light up under specific lighting conditions. The patient may receive the imaging agent by infusion in the hours prior to the surgery. During the surgical session, the provider images the cavity for analysis by software. If the software indicates abnormal tissue is still present, the surgeon removes additional tissue and repeats the imaging and software analysis. The assessment helps ensure the thorough removal of the tumor, reducing the likelihood of residual cancerous tissue. Use this code in addition to the primary partial mastectomy procedure code to reflect the use of advanced imaging technology during the operation. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in conjunction with an appropriate primary code. short_description: Magnetic resonance image guided low intensity focused ultrasound (MRgFUS), stereotactic blood-brain barrier disruption using microbubble resonators to increase the concentration of blood-based biomarkers of target, intracranial, including stereotactic navigation and frame placement, when performed
lay_term: The provider uses MR–guided low–intensity focused ultrasound to disrupt the blood–brain barrier in a targeted area of the brain. This procedure uses microbubble resonators to enhance the concentration of blood–based biomarkers at the target site. Stereotactic navigation and frame placement may be included if performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and positioned, which may include stereotactic frame placement to keep the patient’s head still, the provider uses magnetic resonance (MR) guidance to target a specific intracranial area. The procedure involves the use of low–intensity focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) to temporarily disrupt the blood–brain barrier, a protective layer that regulates the movement of substances between the bloodstream and the brain. Microbubble resonators are injected into the bloodstream, and when exposed to the focused ultrasound, they oscillate, helping to temporarily open the blood–brain barrier at the targeted site. This allows for an increased concentration of blood–based biomarkers, which are measurable substances in the blood that can indicate the presence, severity, or progression of a disease or condition. By analyzing these biomarkers, clinicians can monitor the extent of BBB disruption, detect potential side effects like inflammation or infection, and evaluate the delivery and efficacy of the therapeutic agents in the brain. If needed, the provider may also use stereotactic navigation to precisely locate the target area within the brain. Once the treatment is complete, the provider removes any equipment used for navigation and frame placement. short_description: Totally implantable active middle ear hearing implant; initial placement, including mastoidectomy, placement of and attachment to sound processor
lay_term: The provider surgically places a totally implantable active middle ear hearing implant (AMEI) in a patient with hearing loss. The procedure includes performing a mastoidectomy to prepare the surgical site, implanting the device, and attaching the sound processor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision behind the ear and performs a mastoidectomy, removing a portion of the mastoid bone to create space for the device. The totally implantable active middle ear hearing implant (AMEI) is a hearing device that directly stimulates the middle ear structures to improve hearing. The provider secures the implant components, including the vibrating transducers, which convert sound into mechanical vibrations that enhance sound perception. The provider attaches the sound processor, which detects external sounds and transmits them to the implanted system. After securing all components, the provider closes the incision. lay_term: The provider performs an assistive algorithmic analysis of acoustic and electrocardiogram recordings to help detect cardiac dysfunction (heart problems). After the algorithm processes the data, a physician or other qualified healthcare professional reviews and interprets the findings. Explanation The provider collects acoustic and electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings from the patient. The acoustic recording captures sounds produced by the heart, while the ECG measures the heart's electrical activity. The data is analyzed using an algorithm that helps identify potential abnormalities, such as reduced ejection fraction (a measurement of how effectively the heart pumps blood), cardiac murmurs (unusual sounds caused by turbulent blood flow), or atrial fibrillation (an irregular and often rapid heart rhythm). A physician or other qualified healthcare professional reviews and interprets the results to determine if the patient has signs of cardiac dysfunction. The provider may use the findings to guide further diagnostic testing or treatment decisions. short_description: Anoscopy with directed submucosal injection of bulking agent into anal canal Notes: (Do not report 0963T in conjunction with 46600)
lay_term: The provider inserts an anoscope into the anal canal and injects a bulking agent beneath the mucosal layer to add volume and improve function. Explanation After preparing the patient, the provider inserts an anoscope (a short, tube–like instrument with a light) into the anal canal to examine the tissue. The anal canal is the passageway through which stool exits the body. The provider identifies the appropriate site for treatment and uses a needle to inject a bulking agent into the submucosal (beneath the inner lining) tissue of the anal canal. This bulking agent adds volume, helping to improve the function of the anal sphincter, which controls bowel movements. The provider removes the anoscope once the injection is complete. This procedure is typically performed to treat fecal incontinence by improving the closure of the anal sphincter. short_description: Transanal insertion of endoluminal temporary colorectal anastomosis protection device, including vacuum anchoring component and flexible sheath connected to external vacuum source and monitoring system
lay_term: The provider inserts a temporary protective device into the colon through the anus to protect a newly created colorectal anastomosis (surgical connection between two sections of the colon or rectum). The device uses vacuum technology to anchor it in place and includes a flexible sheath connected to an external vacuum source and monitoring system to help maintain its position and function. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a temporary protective device through the anus and into the colon at the site of a colorectal anastomosis, which is a surgical connection between two sections of the colon or rectum. This device helps protect the anastomosis as it heals, reducing the contact of fecal content at the anastomotic site. It includes a vacuum anchoring component that keeps it securely in place. The provider also places a flexible sheath, which is a soft, tube–like structure that connects the internal device to an external vacuum source and monitoring system. The vacuum source maintains the device’s positioning and ensures it functions correctly. The monitoring system allows the provider to assess the device's status and make necessary adjustments. Once the device is in place and functioning properly, the provider completes the procedure. If a Category III code is available, this code must be reported instead of a Category I unlisted code. This is an activity that is critically important in the evaluation of health care delivery and the formation of public and private policy. The use of the codes in this section allows physicians and other qualified health care professionals, insurers, health services researchers, and health policy experts to identify emerging technology, services, procedures, and service paradigms for clinical efficacy, utilization and outcomes. The inclusion of a service or procedure in this section does not constitute a finding of support, or lack thereof, with regard to clinical efficacy, safety, applicability to clinical practice, or payer coverage. The codes in this section may not conform to the usual requirements for CPT® Category I codes established by the Editorial Panel. short_description: Removal of epicranial neurostimulator system Notes: (For removal of cranial neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver other than skull mounted, use 61888) (For removal of skull-mounted cranial neurostimulator pulse generator or receiver, use 61892)
lay_term: The provider removes an epicranial neurostimulator system, which includes an electrode array placed beneath the scalp and a pulse generator that delivers electrical signals. The provider disconnects and extracts all components of the system. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the scalp to access the implanted neurostimulator system. The provider carefully removes the electrode array from beneath the scalp (epicranial refers to the area overlying the skull). The provider also removes the pulse generator, which was previously implanted under the skin, along with any connecting leads. Once the entire system is extracted, the provider ensures hemostasis (control of bleeding) before closing the incision. short_description: Ablation, benign breast tumor (eg, fibroadenoma), percutaneous, laser, including imaging guidance when performed, each tumor Notes: (Do not report 0970T in conjunction with 76641, 76642, 76940, 76942) (Report 0970T only once per tumor) 003 : (For cryosurgical ablation of fibroadenoma, use 19105) 002 : (For cryoablation of malignant breast tumor[s], use 0581T) 001 : (For laser ablation of malignant breast tumor[s], use 0971T)
lay_term: The provider uses laser energy to ablate (destroy) a benign breast tumor, such as a fibroadenoma. The provider accesses the tumor percutaneously, meaning through the skin, and may use imaging guidance to visualize the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin to insert a thin probe. The provider advances the probe to the benign tumor in the breast and delivers laser energy to heat and destroy the abnormal tissue. The term ablation refers to the process of removing or destroying tissue, in this case using laser energy. Imaging guidance, if performed, helps the provider ensure precise targeting of the tumor. The provider then removes the probe and closes the incision as needed. Report this code per tumor ablated. short_description: Assistive algorithmic classification of burn healing (ie, healing or nonhealing) by noninvasive multispectral imaging, including system set-up and acquisition, selection, and transmission of images, with automated generation of report
lay_term: The provider uses a specialized imaging system to assess burn healing by capturing images at multiple wavelengths without physically touching the skin. The provider sets up the system, obtains images, selects the most relevant ones, and transmits them. The system then uses artificial intelligence (AI)–based analysis to generate an automated report indicating whether the burn is healing or nonhealing. Explanation The provider begins by setting up a noninvasive imaging system designed to evaluate burn healing. Multispectral imaging captures images at different wavelengths of light, allowing for a detailed assessment of tissue characteristics beyond what the human eye can see. The provider positions the system to scan the burned area, ensuring proper image acquisition without direct contact. Once images are captured, the provider selects the most relevant ones for further analysis and transmits them for processing. The imaging system applies an assistive algorithmic classification, which means it uses artificial intelligence (AI) to classify the burn as healing or nonhealing. An automated report is then generated, which assists in guiding further treatment decisions. short_description: Selective enzymatic debridement, partial-thickness and/or full-thickness burn eschar, requiring anesthesia (ie, general anesthesia, moderate sedation), including patient monitoring, trunk, arms, legs; first 100 sq cm Notes: Selective Enzymatic Debridement Codes 0973T, 0974T, 0975T, 0976T describe selective enzymatic debridement of partial-thickness and/or full-thickness burn eschar. For nonselective enzymatic debridement, use 97602. Codes 0973T, 0974T, 0975T, 0976T require general anesthesia or moderate sedation that is separately reported and includes initial wound cleansing, preparation, and topical application of a selective enzyme agent (ie, anacaulase-bcdb), repeated dressing soaks, mechanical debridement, and patient monitoring.
lay_term: The provider removes dead burn tissue from the trunk, arms, and legs using an enzyme that targets damaged tissue while preserving healthy skin. The procedure requires anesthesia and includes wound cleansing, enzyme application, and mechanical removal of the loosened tissue. The provider also monitors the patient throughout the procedure. This code applies to the first 100 sq cm. Explanation After the patient is under general anesthesia or moderate sedation, the provider cleans the burn wound to prepare it for enzymatic debridement. The provider applies a selective enzyme, anacaulase–bcdb, to the burned area. This enzyme breaks down dead tissue while leaving healthy tissue intact. The provider places a dressing over the area and performs repeated dressing soaks to allow the enzyme to work effectively. Once the enzyme has loosened the dead tissue, the provider mechanically removes it. The provider carefully monitors the patient throughout the procedure to ensure safety and effective treatment. This code applies to the first 100 sq cm on the trunk, arms, legs, or some combination of these sites. Tips See +0974T for each additional 100 sq cm. short_description: Upper gastrointestinal blood detection, sensor capsule, with interpretation and report
lay_term: The patient swallows a sensor capsule, allowing it to check for the presence of blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, which includes the esophagus, stomach, and the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). The capsule transmits data, which the provider interprets and documents in a report. Explanation The patient ingests a sensor capsule to assess for blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, which consists of the esophagus (the tube that connects the throat to the stomach), the stomach, and the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine). The capsule, which contains sensors, travels through the digestive system and continuously monitors for the presence of blood. As it moves, it transmits data to an external device. The provider retrieves the data, interprets the information, and prepares a report detailing the findings. This procedure helps detect bleeding that may indicate conditions such as ulcers, inflammation, or other upper gastrointestinal disorders. short_description: Submucosal cryolysis therapy; soft palate, base of tongue, and lingual tonsil
lay_term: The provider applies submucosal cryolysis therapy, a treatment that uses extreme cold, to shrink and modify the tissues of the soft palate, base of tongue, and lingual tonsil. The goal is to improve airflow by reducing excess tissue volume in these areas. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a probe beneath the mucosal surface (the lining of the mouth and throat) into the soft palate, base of tongue, and lingual tonsil. The soft palate is the flexible, muscular part at the back of the roof of the mouth that separates the oral and nasal cavities; the base of the tongue is the back portion of the tongue, extending toward the throat and playing a role in swallowing and speech; and the lingual tonsil is a mass of lymphoid tissue at the base of the tongue that aids in immune defense. The provider applies cryotherapy, a technique that uses extreme cold, to selectively damage the targeted tissues. This controlled injury causes the tissues to shrink over time, reducing obstruction and improving airflow. The procedure is often used to treat conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea. The provider then removes the probe and completes the procedure. lay_term: The provider performs imaging of an intracranial cerebral blood vessel using optical coherence tomography (OCT). This imaging technique uses light waves to produce detailed images of the vessel’s structure, helping the provider diagnose or guide treatment. The procedure includes radiological supervision, interpretation, and reporting. This add–on code applies to each additional intracranial vessel imaged after the first one. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs this add–on procedure of intravascular imaging of an additional intracranial cerebral vessel. The intracranial cerebral vessels are the arteries inside the skull that supply blood to the brain. This imaging may be performed at the same session as a diagnostic evaluation, therapeutic intervention, or both. The provider uses imaging guidance to navigate a catheter inserted into the vascular system to the target vessel. The catheter carries an optical coherence tomography (OCT) probe, which emits light waves that reflect off the vessel walls to create highly detailed images of the vessel’s structure. OCT helps detect conditions such as narrowing or blockages in the arteries. The provider interprets the images, documents the findings, and removes the catheter. This code applies to each additional intracranial vessel imaged after the first one. Tips Because this is an add–on code, you must report it in addition to an appropriate primary code.
